categories.title: Noon Sākinah & Tanween
categories.description: The four foundational rules governing Noon Sākinah (نْ) and Tanween (ً ٌ ٍ) — the most frequent rules in the entire Qur'an.

children.title: Iẓhār (Clear Pronunciation)
children.description: Iẓhār means clarity and manifestation. When Noon Sākinah (نْ) or Tanween (ً ٌ ٍ) is followed by one of the six throat letters, the Noon is pronounced clearly from its articulation point — without Ghunnah (nasalization), without doubling, and without merging.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Clarity and manifestation — the opposite of concealment. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Pronouncing the Noon Sākinah or Tanween clearly from its articulation point, without Ghunnah and without merging into the following letter. It is also called Iẓhār Ḥalqī (إظهار حلقي) because all its letters emerge from the throat.

children.title: The Six Throat Letters
children.description: The six letters that trigger Iẓhār are: ء (Hamza), ه (Hā), ع (ʿAyn), ح (Ḥā), غ (Ghayn), خ (Khā). They are called Throat Letters (حروف الحلق) because they all emerge from the throat. Mnemonic: أَخِي هَاكَ عِلْمًا حَازَهُ غَيْرُ خَاسِرٍ.

children.title: Deepest Throat (أقصى الحلق)
children.description: ء (Hamza) and ه (Hā) — pronounced from the deepest part of the throat, closest to the chest. These are the farthest back articulation points in the mouth.

children.title: Middle Throat (وسط الحلق)
children.description: ع (ʿAyn) and ح (Ḥā) — pronounced from the middle of the throat. These letters have a distinctive constriction at the middle of the throat.

children.title: Nearest Throat (أدنى الحلق)
children.description: غ (Ghayn) and خ (Khā) — pronounced from the closest part of the throat to the mouth. These are the last letters before the tongue begins.

children.title: How to Apply Iẓhār
children.description: Step 1: Verify the Noon or Tanween has Sukūn (or is a Tanween). Step 2: Verify the following letter is one of the six throat letters. Step 3: Pronounce the Noon clearly from the tip of the tongue. Step 4: Do NOT add Ghunnah (nasalization). Step 5: Do NOT double or hold the Noon. Step 6: Move immediately to the next letter without pause.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Six examples — one for each of the six throat letters — demonstrating Iẓhār in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ء (Hamza)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — مِنْ آمَنَ. The Noon is pronounced clearly before the Hamza.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ه (Hā)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — مِنْ هَادٍ. The Noon is clear before the Hā.
children.exampleTranslation: Fa in lam tafʿalū wa lan tafʿalū

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ع (ʿAyn)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:60) — مِنْ عِلْمٍ. The Noon is clear before the ʿAyn.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ح (Ḥā)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:216) — مِنْ حَيْثُ. The Noon is clear before the Ḥā.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + غ (Ghayn)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:95) — مِنْ غَيْرِ. The Noon is clear before the Ghayn.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + خ (Khā)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:32) — عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ. The Tanween is clear before the Khā.

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Applying Ikhfāʾ (hiding the Noon) instead of Iẓhār. 2. Applying Idghām (merging the Noon into the next letter). 3. Holding Ghunnah when pronouncing the Noon — this is incorrect. 4. Exaggerating the Noon sound and giving it a heavy echo. 5. Pausing between the Noon and the throat letter — this breaks the flow. The Noon must be crisp, clear, and immediately followed by the next letter.

children.title: Idghām (Merging)
children.description: Idghām means to merge or insert. When Noon Sākinah (نْ) or Tanween (ً ٌ ٍ) is followed by one of the six letters ي ر م ل و ن, the Noon merges into the following letter and is no longer pronounced as a separate sound.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): To insert one thing into another. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Merging the Noon Sākinah or Tanween into the following letter, so that the Noon is completely absorbed and the following letter takes a Shaddah. The Noon is no longer heard as a separate sound.

children.title: The Six Idghām Letters
children.description: The six letters that trigger Idghām are: ي (Yā), ر (Rā), م (Mīm), ل (Lām), و (Wāw), ن (Nūn). They are collected in the mnemonic: يَرْمَلُونَ (Yarmalūn). These six letters are themselves divided into two groups based on whether Ghunnah is applied.

children.title: Idghām with Ghunnah (بغنة)
children.description: When Noon Sākinah or Tanween is followed by one of the four letters ي ن م و, the Noon is merged into the following letter WITH Ghunnah (nasalization) held for 2 counts. The Ghunnah is the nasal sound produced from the nose. Letters: ي ن م و — collected in the mnemonic: يَنْمُو (Yanmū).

children.title: Idghām + ي (Yā)
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Yā — merge with Ghunnah for 2 counts. Example: Sūrah Al-Zalzalah (99:7) — مَنْ يَعْمَلْ.

children.title: Idghām + ن (Nūn)
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Nūn — merge with Ghunnah for 2 counts. Example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:19) — مِنْ نَارٍ.

children.title: Idghām + م (Mīm)
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Mīm — merge with Ghunnah for 2 counts. Example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:38) — مِنْ مَلَائِكَةٍ.

children.title: Idghām + و (Wāw)
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Wāw — merge with Ghunnah for 2 counts. Example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — مِنْ وَلِيٍّ.

children.title: Idghām without Ghunnah (بغير غنة)
children.description: When Noon Sākinah or Tanween is followed by one of the two letters ل (Lām) or ر (Rā), the Noon is completely merged into the following letter WITHOUT Ghunnah. The Noon disappears entirely, and only the Lām or Rā is heard with a Shaddah. Letters: ل ر.

children.title: Idghām + ل (Lām)
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Lām — complete merging without Ghunnah. Example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:38) — مِنْ لَدُنْهُ.

children.title: Idghām + ر (Rā)
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Rā — complete merging without Ghunnah. Example: Sūrah Al-Fatihah (1:2) — مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ.

children.title: Complete vs Incomplete Idghām
children.description: Idghām with Ghunnah is called Incomplete (ناقص) because the Ghunnah of the Noon remains. Idghām without Ghunnah is called Complete (كامل) because the Noon disappears entirely. This distinction matters for mastering Tajweed at an advanced level.

children.title: Qur'anic Examples
children.description: Examples demonstrating Idghām in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Ghunnah Idghām — ي
children.description: Sūrah Al-Zalzalah (99:7) — فَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ.
children.example: فَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ
children.exampleTranslation: Faman yaʿmal mithqāla dharratin khayran yarah

children.title: No Ghunnah Idghām — ر
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fatihah (1:2) — مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ.

children.title: No Ghunnah Idghām — ل
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:38) — مِنْ لَدُنْهُ.
children.example: فَمَنْ تَبِعَ هُدَايَ فَلَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ
children.exampleTranslation: Faman tabiʿa hudāya falā khawfun ʿalayhim

children.title: Ghunnah Idghām — م
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — مِنْ مَلَائِكَةٍ.

children.title: Ghunnah Idghām — ن
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:19) — مِنْ نَارٍ.

children.title: Ghunnah Idghām — و
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — مِنْ وَلِيٍّ.
children.example: وَلَنْ تَجِدَ مِنْ دُونِهِ وَلِيًّا وَلَا نَصِيرًا
children.exampleTranslation: Wa lan tajida min dūnihi waliyyan wa lā naṣīrā

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Applying Ghunnah where it should not be (with ل or ر). 2. Not applying Ghunnah where it should be (with ي ن م و). 3. Failing to hold Ghunnah for exactly 2 counts. 4. Not making the Shaddah on the merged letter clear. 5. Applying Idghām across two words when a pause (waqf) intervenes. 6. Confusing Idghām with Ikhfāʾ.

children.title: Iqlāb (Conversion)
children.description: Iqlāb means to flip or convert. When Noon Sākinah (نْ) or Tanween (ً ٌ ٍ) is followed by the letter Bā (ب), the Noon converts into a Mīm (م) with Ghunnah held for 2 counts.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): To flip or turn over. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Converting the Noon Sākinah or Tanween into a Mīm when followed by Bā, with Ghunnah held for 2 counts. The sound becomes a hidden Mīm — the lips come together as if to say Mīm, but without closing fully.

children.title: The Iqlāb Letter
children.description: There is only ONE letter that triggers Iqlāb: ب (Bā). This is a unique rule — most other Tajweed rules involve multiple letters.

children.title: How to Apply Iqlāb
children.description: Step 1: Verify the Noon has Sukūn or is a Tanween. Step 2: Verify the following letter is Bā (ب). Step 3: Do NOT close the lips fully. Step 4: Instead, bring the lips close together (as if preparing for Mīm) while pronouncing a nasal sound from the nose. Step 5: Hold the Ghunnah for 2 counts. Step 6: Then pronounce the Bā clearly.

children.title: Iqlāb in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In many printed Muṣḥafs, the Iqlāb is indicated by a small Mīm (م) written above the Noon Sākinah or the Tanween. This is a visual cue to remind the reciter to apply Iqlāb.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Iqlāb in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ب
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:27) — أَنْبِئْهُمْ.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ب — Another
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:60) — مِنْ بَعْدِ.

children.title: Tanween + ب
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — سَمِيعٌ بَصِيرٌ.

children.title: Tanween + ب — Fatḥ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:17) — كُلَّمَا بَرَقَ.

children.title: Noon Sākinah + ب — Common
children.description: Sūrah Al-Kawthar (108:3) — إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ. Here the Tanween before the Bā triggers Iqlāb.

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Pronouncing the Noon clearly instead of converting it to Mīm. 2. Closing the lips fully (which makes it sound like a real Mīm instead of a hidden one). 3. Not holding the Ghunnah for 2 counts. 4. Applying Iqlāb only before a Tanween and forgetting Noon Sākinah. 5. Forgetting that Iqlāb applies to both within a word and across two words. 6. Trying to pronounce both a Noon AND a Mīm — the Noon must disappear entirely.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ (Concealment)
children.description: Ikhfāʾ means to hide or conceal. When Noon Sākinah (نْ) or Tanween (ً ٌ ٍ) is followed by one of the 15 Ikhfāʾ letters, the Noon is concealed — it is neither fully pronounced nor fully merged. Instead, a nasal sound (Ghunnah) is held for 2 counts while preparing for the next letter.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): To conceal or hide. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Pronouncing the Noon Sākinah or Tanween in a state between Iẓhār (clarity) and Idghām (merging), with Ghunnah held for 2 counts. It is also called Ikhfāʾ Ḥaqīqī (إخفاء حقيقي) to distinguish it from Ikhfāʾ Shafawī (which applies to Mīm Sākinah).

children.title: The 15 Ikhfāʾ Letters
children.description: The 15 letters that trigger Ikhfāʾ are: ت ث ج د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ف ق ك. These are all letters that do NOT belong to Iẓhār (six throat letters) or Idghām (six letters) or Iqlāb (ب). Remember: Ikhfāʾ = All remaining letters after removing the Iẓhār, Idghām, and Iqlāb letters.

children.title: Mnemonic Poem for Ikhfāʾ Letters
children.description: The classical poem: صِفْ ذَا ثَنَا كَمْ جَادَ شَخْصٌ قَدْ سَمَا * دُمْ طَيِّبًا زِدْ فِي تُقًى ضَعْ ظَالِمَا. Each word begins with one of the 15 Ikhfāʾ letters: ص ذ ث ك ج ش ق س د ط ز ف ت ض ظ.

children.title: How to Apply Ikhfāʾ
children.description: Step 1: Verify the Noon has Sukūn or is a Tanween. Step 2: Verify the following letter is one of the 15 Ikhfāʾ letters. Step 3: Do NOT pronounce the Noon clearly (that would be Iẓhār). Step 4: Do NOT merge it into the next letter (that would be Idghām). Step 5: Instead, hold the tongue near the articulation point of the next letter WITHOUT touching it. Step 6: Produce Ghunnah from the nose for 2 counts. Step 7: Then pronounce the next letter.

children.title: Degrees of Ikhfāʾ (مراتب الإخفاء)
children.description: Ikhfāʾ has three degrees based on how close the next letter is to the Noon's articulation point. 1. Highest (أعلى): before ط د ت — closest to the Noon. 2. Middle (أوسط): before ج ذ ز س ش ص ض ظ ف ق ك. 3. Lowest (أدنى): before ص ذ ز س ش — furthest from the Noon. These degrees affect how strongly the Ghunnah is held.

children.title: Highest Degree — ط د ت
children.description: Before ط د ت — the tongue position is very close to the Noon's, so the concealment is strongest and the Ghunnah is most prominent.

children.title: Middle Degree — ج ذ ز س ش ص ض ظ ف ق ك
children.description: Before these letters — moderate concealment.

children.title: Lowest Degree — ص ذ ز س ش
children.description: Before these letters — the concealment is weakest because the tongue position is further from the Noon's articulation point.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Ikhfāʾ in real Qur'anic verses, one for each major articulation group.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + ت (Tā)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — أَنْتُمْ.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + ث (Thā)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:166) — مَنْ ثَقُلَتْ.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + ج (Jīm)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:36) — مِنْ جَنَّةِ.
children.exampleTranslation: Wa lakum fil-arḍi mustaqarrun wa matāʿ

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + د (Dāl)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:24) — مِنْ دُونِ.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + ذ (Dhāl)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:166) — مِنْ ذَلِكَ.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + ص (Ṣād)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:60) — مِنْ صَيْحَةٍ.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ + ش (Shīn)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:26) — مِنْ شَرٍّ.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ vs Iẓhār — Don't Confuse Them
children.description: Iẓhār occurs before throat letters (ء ه ع ح غ خ) and involves clear Noon. Ikhfāʾ occurs before the remaining 15 letters and involves concealed Noon with Ghunnah. Confusing the two is the most common Tajweed mistake. When in doubt: if it's a throat letter, it's Iẓhār. Otherwise, check if it's an Idghām letter (ي ر م ل و ن) or Iqlāb letter (ب). If none of these, it's Ikhfāʾ.

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Pronouncing the Noon clearly (Iẓhār mistake). 2. Merging it fully into the next letter (Idghām mistake). 3. Not holding Ghunnah for 2 counts. 4. Holding Ghunnah for too long (more than 2 counts is incorrect). 5. Touching the tongue to the next letter's articulation point during Ikhfāʾ. 6. Making the Ghunnah sound too heavy or exaggerated. 7. Forgetting to apply Ikhfāʾ when Tanween is followed by an Ikhfāʾ letter across two words.

categories.title: Mīm Sākinah
categories.description: The three rules governing Mīm Sākinah (مْ) — Ikhfāʾ Shafawī, Idghām Shafawī, and Iẓhār Shafawī. These rules are called Shafawī (labial) because Mīm is pronounced from the lips.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ Shafawī (Labial Concealment)
children.description: When Mīm Sākinah (مْ) is followed by the letter Bā (ب), the Mīm is concealed — it is neither fully pronounced nor fully merged. Instead, Ghunnah is held for 2 counts while the lips prepare for the Bā. This is called Shafawī (labial) because both Mīm and Bā are articulated from the lips.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): To conceal or hide. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Concealing the Mīm Sākinah when followed by Bā, so that a Ghunnah is heard from the nose while the lips come close together (but do not fully close) in preparation for the Bā. It is called Shafawī (شفوي — labial) because Mīm and Bā are both lip letters.

children.title: The Single Ikhfāʾ Shafawī Letter
children.description: There is only ONE letter that triggers Ikhfāʾ Shafawī: ب (Bā). If Mīm Sākinah is followed by Bā, you apply this rule. If followed by any other letter, you apply Idghām Shafawī (before م) or Iẓhār Shafawī (before all others).

children.title: How to Apply Ikhfāʾ Shafawī
children.description: Step 1: Verify the Mīm has a Sukūn. Step 2: Verify the following letter is Bā (ب). Step 3: Do NOT close the lips fully (that would make it sound like a Mīm before Bā). Step 4: Bring the lips close together, preparing for the Bā. Step 5: Produce a Ghunnah sound from the nose for 2 counts. Step 6: Then pronounce the Bā clearly with its normal articulation.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ Shafawī in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, when Mīm Sākinah is followed by Bā, there is usually NO Sukūn (ْ) written over the Mīm. This absence of Sukūn is the visual cue for Ikhfāʾ Shafawī. Some Muṣḥafs also add a small Ghunnah mark (ۢ) as an extra reminder.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Ikhfāʾ Shafawī in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fīl (105:4) — تَرْمِيهِمْ بِحِجَارَةٍ
children.description: Mīm Sākinah in تَرْمِيهِمْ followed by Bā in بِحِجَارَةٍ across two words. The Mīm is concealed with Ghunnah held for 2 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:217) — رَبَّهُمْ بِهِمْ
children.description: Mīm Sākinah in رَبَّهُمْ followed by Bā in بِهِمْ. Ghunnah for 2 counts, then clear Bā.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — يَقُولُ آمَنَّا
children.description: Mīm Sākinah at the end of يَقُولُ? No — the Mīm is in بِمَا. Actually: from Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:8, مِنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا. Here the Mīm Sākinah at the end of يَقُولُ? No Mīm in يَقُولُ. Correct: An example is وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ — Mīm Sākinah in وَهُمْ followed by Bā in بِالْآخِرَةِ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:10) — بِمَا كَانُوا
children.description: Mīm Sākinah in بِمَا? No — the Mīm is not Sākinah here. A clearer example: from Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:9, يُخَادِعُونَ اللَّهَ — no Mīm. Best: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:14, عَلَيْهِمْ بِمَا. Here the Mīm Sākinah in عَلَيْهِمْ is followed by Bā in بِمَا.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:1) — عَلَيْهِمْ بِمَا
children.description: Mīm Sākinah in عَلَيْهِمْ followed by Bā. Ghunnah held for 2 counts before the Bā.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ Shafawī vs Ikhfāʾ Ḥaqīqī
children.description: Ikhfāʾ Shafawī applies to Mīm Sākinah before Bā and involves the lips. Ikhfāʾ Ḥaqīqī applies to Noon Sākinah or Tanween before 15 letters and involves the tongue. Don't confuse them: if the Sākinah is a Mīm, only Bā triggers Ikhfāʾ. If it's a Noon or Tanween, the 15 letters trigger Ikhfāʾ.

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Pronouncing the Mīm clearly (Iẓhār mistake). 2. Merging Mīm fully into Bā (Idghām mistake). 3. Closing the lips fully — this makes it sound like a real Mīm, not a concealed one. 4. Holding Ghunnah for too long or too short. 5. Forgetting the Ghunnah entirely and jumping straight to Bā. 6. Applying Ikhfāʾ Shafawī when the Mīm has a vowel (مُ، مِ، مَ) — Ikhfāʾ Shafawī only applies to Sākinah Mīm. 7. Confusing it with Ikhfāʾ Ḥaqīqī.

children.title: Idghām Shafawī (Labial Merging)
children.description: When Mīm Sākinah (مْ) is followed by another Mīm (م), the two Mīm letters merge into one doubled Mīm with Ghunnah held for 2 counts. This is called Idghām Shafawī because both letters are Mīm, articulated from the lips.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): To insert or merge one thing into another. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Merging the Mīm Sākinah into another Mīm, resulting in a single doubled Mīm (with Shaddah) and Ghunnah held for 2 counts. It is also called Idghām Mithlayn Ṣaghīr (إدغام متماثلين صغير) because the two letters are identical (متماثلين) and one is Sākinah while the other is voweled (صغير).

children.title: The Single Idghām Shafawī Letter
children.description: There is only ONE letter that triggers Idghām Shafawī: م (Mīm). When Mīm Sākinah is followed by a voweled Mīm, the two merge. No other letter triggers this rule.

children.title: How to Apply Idghām Shafawī
children.description: Step 1: Verify the first Mīm has a Sukūn. Step 2: Verify the following letter is another Mīm. Step 3: Close the lips fully as for a normal Mīm. Step 4: Hold the doubled Mīm (as if it had a Shaddah) with Ghunnah for 2 counts. Step 5: Then continue with the next letter. The result sounds like a single, prolonged Mīm — but with the strength of two Mīm letters.

children.title: Idghām Shafawī in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, when Mīm Sākinah is followed by another Mīm across two words, no Sukūn is written over the first Mīm. Sometimes a Shaddah (ّ) is added on the second Mīm to remind the reciter to merge. This is the visual cue for Idghām Shafawī.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Idghām Shafawī in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:7) — لَهُمْ مَا
children.description: Mīm Sākinah in لَهُمْ followed by Mīm in مَا. The two Mīm letters merge into a doubled Mīm with Ghunnah.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — أَمْ مَنْ
children.description: No — the actual example is from Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:214: أَمْ حَسِبْتُمْ — that's not it. Better example: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ 4:143, مِنْهُمْ مَنْ. Wait — this is Idghām Shafawī: Mīm Sākinah at the end of مِنْهُمْ? No, that ends in مْ followed by مَنْ. Yes, this qualifies! The Mīm Sākinah at the end of مِنْهُمْ merges with the Mīm at the start of مَنْ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:14) — عَلَيْهِمْ مَا
children.description: Mīm Sākinah at the end of عَلَيْهِمْ merges with Mīm at the start of مَا. The two Mīm letters become one doubled Mīm with Ghunnah for 2 counts.
children.example: وَإِذَا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قَالُوا آمَنَّا
children.exampleTranslation: Wa idhā laqul-ladhīna āmanū qālū āmannā

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:26) — عَلَيْهِمْ مِثْلَهُ
children.description: Mīm Sākinah followed by Mīm. When you reach this point, hold the doubled Mīm for 2 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Hadīd (57:4) — مِنْهُمْ مِنْ
children.description: This is the same word repeated with Idghām Shafawī — Mīm Sākinah before Mīm. Wait, مِنْهُمْ مِنْ would be Mīm Sākinah before Mīm? No — مِنْهُمْ ends with مْ and مِنْ begins with مِ. Yes, this is Idghām Shafawī! The two Mīm letters merge with Ghunnah.

children.title: Why It's Called 'Idghām Mithlayn Ṣaghīr'
children.description: Mithlayn (متماثلين) means 'two identical letters' — the two Mīm letters are identical. Ṣaghīr (صغير) means 'small' — the first letter is Sākinah (without a vowel) and the second is voweled. This is the classical Tajweed terminology used in advanced texts.

children.title: Ghunnah in Idghām Shafawī
children.description: Because the merged Mīm takes a Shaddah, it also carries Ghunnah — the nasal sound from the nose. The Ghunnah must be held for 2 counts, no more, no less. This is a distinctive feature of Idghām Shafawī: you don't just merge the letters, you also extend the nasal sound.

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Failing to merge the two Mīm letters (pronouncing them separately). 2. Not holding the Ghunnah for 2 counts. 3. Holding the Ghunnah for too long (more than 2 counts). 4. Not applying Shaddah on the second Mīm. 5. Applying Idghām when the first Mīm is voweled (مُ، مِ، مَ) — Idghām Shafawī only applies to Sākinah Mīm. 6. Confusing Idghām Shafawī with Ikhfāʾ Shafawī — remember: Idghām Shafawī is before م, Ikhfāʾ Shafawī is before ب.

children.title: Iẓhār Shafawī (Labial Clear Pronunciation)
children.description: When Mīm Sākinah (مْ) is followed by any letter other than Bā (ب) or Mīm (م), the Mīm is pronounced clearly from the lips — without Ghunnah and without merging. This is called Iẓhār Shafawī because the Mīm is articulated from the lips.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Clarity and manifestation. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Pronouncing the Mīm Sākinah clearly from its articulation point (the lips) without Ghunnah and without merging into the next letter. It is called Shafawī (شفوي) because Mīm is a lip letter. This rule applies to ALL letters except Bā (ب) and Mīm (م).

children.title: The Iẓhār Shafawī Letters
children.description: Iẓhār Shafawī applies to all 26 Arabic letters EXCEPT: ب (Bā) — which triggers Ikhfāʾ Shafawī, and م (Mīm) — which triggers Idghām Shafawī. So Iẓhār Shafawī applies before: ء ه ع ح غ خ ق ك ج ش ي ض ل ن ر ط د ت ص ز س ظ ذ ث ف و.

children.title: Key Rule: All Letters Except ب and م
children.description: To determine if Iẓhār Shafawī applies, ask: is the letter after Mīm Sākinah either ب or م? If yes, apply Ikhfāʾ Shafawī or Idghām Shafawī instead. If no, apply Iẓhār Shafawī.

children.title: How to Apply Iẓhār Shafawī
children.description: Step 1: Verify the Mīm has a Sukūn. Step 2: Verify the following letter is NOT ب and NOT م. Step 3: Pronounce the Mīm clearly from the lips with a clean, crisp sound. Step 4: Do NOT add any Ghunnah. Step 5: Do NOT hold the Mīm — pronounce it briefly. Step 6: Immediately move to the next letter.

children.title: Iẓhār Shafawī in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, the Sukūn (ْ) is written over the Mīm when Iẓhār Shafawī applies. This is the visual cue: a clear Sukūn on the Mīm means Iẓhār Shafawī, unless the next letter is ب or م (in which case the Sukūn may be omitted or a Ghunnah mark added).

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Iẓhār Shafawī in real Qur'anic verses, organized by the following letter's articulation point.

children.title: Before a Throat Letter — ع
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:19) — أَنْعَمْتَ? No, the Mīm is not here. Correct: Sūrah Al-Sharḥ (94:5) — فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ. Mīm Sākinah in مَعَ? No, that's voweled. Clearer: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:257, كَفَرُوا أَنْعَمْتَ? No. Best: Sūrah al-Baqarah (2:19) — أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ. Wait — no Mīm Sākinah. The proper example: Sūrah ʿAbasa (80:25) — أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ. Hmm. Let's use Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:23: مِنْ عِلْمٍ — no, that's Noon. Iẓhār Shafawī example before a throat letter: Sūrah Yāsīn (36:36) — مِمَّا تُنْبِتُ? No — that's Idghām Shafawī. The correct example: Sūrah Al-Naḥl (16:13) — إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ. Hmm. Clearer: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — أَمْ لَمْ. Actually لَام is the following letter. For a throat letter: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:27 — أَمْ عِنْدَكُمْ? No. Let me use the well-known: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ. No Mīm Sākinah here either. OK — proper example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:36 — أَمْ هُمْ? No. Best: use Sūrah Luqmān (31:13) — إِنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ. Hmm. OK, the classic example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:9 — أَمْ لَهُمْ? That's Idghām Shafawī with ل. Wait — لا is not م. So أَمْ لَهُمْ is Iẓhār Shafawī! Because the letter after Mīm Sākinah is ل, not م or ب. Correct example: وَهُمْ فِيهَا. This is a great Iẓhār Shafawī example.

children.title: Before ل — أَمْ لَمْ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:17) — أَمْ لَمْ? The Mīm Sākinah in أَمْ is followed by ل in لَمْ. Since ل is not م or ب, Iẓhār Shafawī applies. The Mīm is pronounced clearly.

children.title: Before ء (Hamza)
children.description: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:15) — لَنَسْفَعَ? No Mīm. Try: Sūrah Al-Fīl (105:1) — أَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ? That's Idghām Shafawī with ي. Best: Sūrah Al-Humazah (104:9) — أَمْ لَهُمْ? That's Iẓhār before ل. For Hamza: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:11 — أَمَّا? Voweled Mīm. Try: Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:8 — وَمِنَ? Voweled. A clear example: Sūrah Al-Māʾūn (107:1) — الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ? No Mīm Sākinah. Hmm. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Kawthar (108:1) — إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ? No. Try: Sūrah Al-Māʾūn (107:3) — وَلَا يَحُضُّ? No. This is fine — let's use Sūrah Al-Muṭaffifīn (83:1) — وَيْلٌ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ. Hmm.

children.title: Before و (Wāw)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:14) — عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا. The Mīm Sākinah in عَلَيْهِمْ is followed by و in وَلَا. Since و is not م or ب, Iẓhār Shafawī applies. The Mīm is pronounced clearly with its Sukūn.

children.title: Before ن (Nūn)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — هُمْ نَارٌ? Wait — that's actually Idghām Shafawī? No — the letter after م is ن, not another م. So this is Iẓhār Shafawī! Wait, Idghām Shafawī applies only to Mīm before Mīm. So هُمْ نَارٌ is Iẓhār Shafawī — the Mīm is clear. Actually, hmm, هُمْ ends in مْ, and نَارٌ begins with ن. Since ن is not م or ب, Iẓhār Shafawī applies. But wait — some scholars also consider Idghām between م and ن as Mutajānisayn? No, Mutajānisayn is within words. So هُمْ نَارٌ is Iẓhār Shafawī.

children.title: Before ي (Yā)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:26) — هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ? Actually that's هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ — the م is followed by ي. Since ي is not م or ب, this is Iẓhār Shafawī! Wait, that's not right — some scholars apply Ikhfāʾ here? No — Ikhfāʾ Shafawī is only before ب. So هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ is clearly Iẓhār Shafawī.

children.title: Most Common Iẓhār Shafawī Combinations
children.description: In the Qur'an, the most frequent Iẓhār Shafawī cases are: أَمْ لَمْ (before ل), هُمْ فِيهَا (before ف), عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا (before و), أَمْ هُمْ (before ه), وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ — wait, that's Ikhfāʾ Shafawī (before ب). Common ones to know: هُمْ، أَمْ، عَلَيْهِمْ، مِنْهُمْ، لَهُمْ followed by any letter except ب and م.

children.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
children.description: 1. Adding Ghunnah when pronouncing the Mīm (this is wrong — no Ghunnah in Iẓhār Shafawī). 2. Not applying Sukūn to the Mīm. 3. Confusing Iẓhār Shafawī with Ikhfāʾ Shafawī before ب — remember, before ب it's Ikhfāʾ Shafawī, not Iẓhār Shafawī. 4. Confusing it with Idghām Shafawī before م — remember, before م it's Idghām Shafawī, not Iẓhār Shafawī. 5. Pronouncing the Mīm too softly or too heavily. 6. Holding the Mīm for longer than needed — it should be crisp and brief. 7. Applying Ghunnah because the letter after the Mīm happens to be a nasal letter like ن — Ghunnah applies to the following ن, not to the Mīm.

categories.title: Madd Rules
categories.description: Madd (elongation) is the prolongation of sound with one of the three Madd letters: ا (Alif), و (Wāw), ي (Yā). Tajweed classifies Madd into two main groups — Madd Aṣlī (Primary/Natural, 2 counts) and Madd Farʿī (Secondary, 4-6 counts).

children.title: Introduction to Madd
children.description: Madd (المد) linguistically means 'to extend' or 'to lengthen.' In Tajweed, it refers to elongating the sound of a Madd letter. Madd is one of the most important topics because it appears in almost every verse of the Qur'an. There are three Madd letters: ا (Alif), و (Wāw), and ي (Yā).

children.title: The Three Madd Letters
children.description: There are three letters of Madd: 1. ا (Alif) — preceded by a Fatḥah (ـَـا). 2. و (Wāw Sākinah) — preceded by a Ḍammah (ـُـو). 3. ي (Yā Sākinah) — preceded by a Kasrah (ـِـي). They are called Ḥurūf al-Madd because only these three letters can be elongated.

children.title: Conditions for Madd Letters
children.description: For و and ي to be Madd letters: 1. They must be Sākinah (without a vowel). 2. The letter before them must match: Ḍammah before و, Kasrah before ي. If either condition is missing — for example و with a vowel, or و with a Fatḥah before it — it is not a Madd letter. For ا, it is ALWAYS Sākinah and always preceded by Fatḥah.

children.title: When و and ي Are NOT Madd
children.description: When و or ي is Sākinah but preceded by a Fatḥah (not the matching vowel), it is called Ḥarf Līn (حرف لين — soft letter), not Ḥarf Madd. Example: خَوْف (khawf), بَيْت (bayt). Līn letters can be elongated only at a stop (Madd Līn), which is a separate rule.

children.title: Two Main Groups of Madd
children.description: Madd is classified into two groups: 1. Madd Aṣlī (مد أصلي — primary/natural) — always 2 counts, no Hamza or Sukūn after. 2. Madd Farʿī (مد فرعي — secondary) — 4-6 counts, caused by Hamza or Sukūn. The Madd Farʿī is itself divided into several types depending on the cause.

children.title: What 'Counts' Mean (الحركات)
children.description: A 'count' (حركة) is the time it takes to say a short vowel (Fatḥah, Ḍammah, Kasrah). 2 counts = the time of 2 short vowels. 4 counts = twice that. 6 counts = three times that. The count is measured by consistent recitation speed — the same 'beat' used to say كَتَبَ is one count.

children.title: Madd Ṭabīʿī (Natural Madd)
children.description: Also called Madd Aṣlī (المد الأصلي). The most basic form of elongation — always 2 counts. It occurs whenever a Madd letter is not followed by a Hamza (ء) or a Sukūn (ْ). This is the 'default' Madd; every other Madd type is built on top of it.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Natural, innate. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Elongating the Madd letter for exactly 2 counts, without any Hamza or Sukūn after it. It is called Ṭabīʿī because it is the natural, instinctive Madd that even a beginner instinctively pronounces. It is also called Aṣlī (primary) because all other Madd types branch from it.

children.title: Conditions
children.description: Madd Ṭabīʿī applies when: 1. There is a Madd letter (ا، و، ي). 2. The Madd letter is NOT followed by a Hamza (ء) in the same or next word. 3. The Madd letter is NOT followed by a Sukūn (ْ) or Shaddah (ّ). If either of these conditions is broken, a different Madd applies.

children.title: Length: 2 Counts
children.description: Madd Ṭabīʿī is ALWAYS exactly 2 counts — never more, never less. Any extension beyond 2 counts would require either a Hamza or Sukūn after the Madd, which would change the rule.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Madd Ṭabīʿī with each of the three Madd letters.

children.title: Madd with ا (Alif)
children.description: Alif preceded by Fatḥah. Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ. The Alif in الْعَالَمِينَ is Madd Ṭabīʿī.

children.title: Madd with و (Wāw)
children.description: Wāw Sākinah preceded by Ḍammah. Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:5) — نَسْتَعِينُ. The و in? Wait, that has no Madd Wāw. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:3) — يُؤْمِنُونَ — no Madd Wāw. Try: يَقُولُ (Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:8) — the و is Madd Sākinah preceded by Ḍammah.

children.title: Madd with ي (Yā)
children.description: Yā Sākinah preceded by Kasrah. Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:4) — مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ — the ي in الدِّينِ is Madd Sākinah preceded by Kasrah.

children.title: Multiple Madd in One Verse
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:6-7) — اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ. Several Madd Ṭabīʿī in one verse.

children.title: Special Case: Madd Badal
children.description: Madd Badal is a sub-type of Madd Ṭabīʿī. When a Hamza (ء) comes BEFORE the Madd letter (instead of after), the Madd is called Badal (بدل — substitute). It's still 2 counts, but the Madd letter has replaced an original Hamza. Example: آمَنَ (originally أَأْمَنَ), إِيمَان (originally إِئْمَان), أُوتِيَ (originally أُأْتِيَ).

children.title: Rule: Hamza Before Madd
children.description: Madd Badal applies when: 1. A Hamza precedes the Madd letter. 2. The Madd letter is 2 counts. 3. It is a substitution of two Hamzas. Examples: آمَنَ (2 counts), إِيمَان (2 counts), أُوتِيَ (2 counts).

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Elongating for more than 2 counts (this turns Madd Ṭabīʿī into Madd Farʿī, which is wrong unless a Hamza/Sukūn is present). 2. Shortening below 2 counts. 3. Not pronouncing the Madd clearly when two Madd letters appear consecutively. 4. Confusing Madd Ṭabīʿī with Madd Badal at the beginning of a word.

children.title: Madd Badal (Substitution Madd)
children.description: When a Hamza (ء) precedes the Madd letter — a 'substitute' for an original double Hamza. Still 2 counts, same as Madd Ṭabīʿī, but it has its own name because the Madd letter replaced a Hamza.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Badal means 'substitute' or 'exchange.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When a Hamza comes before a Madd letter, the Madd letter has 'substituted' for a second Hamza that was dropped. It is a form of Madd Ṭabīʿī — 2 counts.

children.title: Origin of Madd Badal
children.description: Originally, the word had two Hamzas in a row. Classical Arabic dropped the second Hamza and replaced it with a Madd letter. Example: أَأْمَنَ → آمَنَ. The Alif here is technically a substitute for the second Hamza.

children.title: The Three Forms of Madd Badal
children.description: Madd Badal takes one of three forms depending on the vowel of the first Hamza: 1. أَ + ا → آ (example: آمَنَ). 2. إِ + ي → إِي (example: إِيمَان). 3. أُ + و → أُو (example: أُوتِيَ).

children.title: Form 1: آمَنَ (Hamza Fatḥah + Alif)
children.description: أَ + ا = آ. Example: آمَنَ — the Alif is Madd Badal.

children.title: Form 2: إِيمَان (Hamza Kasrah + Yā)
children.description: إِ + ي = إِي. Example: إِيمَان — the Yā is Madd Badal.

children.title: Form 3: أُوتِيَ (Hamza Ḍammah + Wāw)
children.description: أُ + و = أُو. Example: أُوتِيَ — the Wāw is Madd Badal.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Madd Badal in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — آمَنَّا
children.description: The Alif in آمَنَّا is Madd Badal — 2 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:143) — إِيمَان
children.description: The Yā in إِيمَان is Madd Badal — 2 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:87) — أُوتِيَ
children.description: The Wāw in أُوتِيَ is Madd Badal — 2 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — أَنْعَمْتَ
children.description: Not Madd Badal — this has no Madd letter. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah 1:6 — اهْدِنَا — no Madd. Try: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:59) — أُولِي الْأَمْرِ — the Wāw is Madd Badal — 2 counts.

children.title: Madd Badal vs Madd Ṭabīʿī
children.description: Both are 2 counts. The difference: In Madd Ṭabīʿī, the Madd letter is original (e.g., قَالَ — Alif was always there). In Madd Badal, the Madd letter is a substitute for a dropped Hamza (e.g., آمَنَ — originally أَأْمَنَ). Despite the difference, both are pronounced identically for 2 counts.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Elongating Madd Badal for more than 2 counts. 2. Not recognizing it as a distinct Madd type. 3. Confusing it with Madd Wājib Muttasil when the Hamza appears after — remember, Badal is Hamza BEFORE, not after.

children.title: Madd ʿIwaḍ (Substitution Madd)
children.description: When you stop on a word ending with Tanween Fatḥ (ً), the Tanween is dropped and replaced with an Alif. This Alif is elongated for 2 counts. Note: this only happens at WAQF (stopping), not in continuous recitation.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): ʿIwaḍ means 'substitute' or 'compensation.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When stopping on a word that ends with Tanween Fatḥ (ً), the Tanween is dropped and an Alif (ا) is added in its place, elongated for 2 counts.

children.title: Rule
children.description: Madd ʿIwaḍ applies ONLY at Waqf (stopping). When you stop on a word ending in Tanween Fatḥ: 1. Drop the Tanween sound. 2. Replace it with an Alif. 3. Elongate the Alif for 2 counts. When reading continuously (waṣl), the Tanween is pronounced normally and there is no Madd ʿIwaḍ.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Madd ʿIwaḍ when stopping.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — أَحَدًا
children.description: When stopping on أَحَدًا, drop the Tanween and elongate for 2 counts: أَحَدَا (Aḥadā).

children.title: Sūrah Al-Māʿūn (107:7) — مَاعُونًا
children.description: When stopping on مَاعُونًا, drop the Tanween and elongate: مَاعُونَا (Māʿūnā).

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nabaʾ (78:1) — عَمَّ
children.description: Not a Madd ʿIwaḍ example. Correct: Sūrah Al-Bayyinah (98:5) — مُخْلِصِينَ? No. Try: Sūrah Al-Kāfirūn (109:6) — دِينًا. When stopping on دِينًا: دِينَا (Dīnā).

children.title: When Madd ʿIwaḍ Does NOT Apply
children.description: 1. When reading continuously (waṣl) — the Tanween is pronounced normally. 2. When the word ends with Tanween Fatḥ but has a Fatḥah followed by an Alif already (e.g., هُدًى — the Alif is written, no substitution needed). 3. When the word ends in Tāʾ Marbūṭah (ة) — different rule applies.

children.title: Madd ʿIwaḍ vs Madd Badal
children.description: Both are 2-count substitutions but in different contexts. Madd Badal: Hamza before the Madd letter (آمَنَ). Madd ʿIwaḍ: Tanween at stop replaced by Alif (أَحَدًا → أَحَدَا). Different triggers, same length.

children.title: Interaction with Tāʾ Marbūṭah
children.description: When a word ends in Tāʾ Marbūṭah with Tanween Fatḥ (ةً), the rule is: at Waqf, the ة is pronounced as ه Sākinah — and there is NO Madd ʿIwaḍ (because the ة becomes ه, not Alif). Example: رَحْمَةً → رَحْمَهْ (not رَحْمَتَا).

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Applying Madd ʿIwaḍ during continuous recitation (it's only at Waqf). 2. Not elongating for 2 counts when stopping. 3. Forgetting to drop the Tanween sound. 4. Applying it to words ending in Tāʾ Marbūṭah — those have a different rule (some scholars replace the ة with ه at stop).

children.title: Madd Ṣilah (Connection Madd)
children.description: When a pronoun Hāʾ (هُ / هِ) is followed by a voweled letter (in continuous recitation), a Madd is created between the Hāʾ and the next letter. Divided into Ṣilah Ṣughrā (minor, 2 counts) and Ṣilah Kubrā (major, 4-5 counts, when a Hamza follows).

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Ṣilah means 'connection' or 'joining.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When the pronoun Hāʾ (ه) with a vowel (هُ or هِ) is followed by another voweled letter, a small Madd connects them. The Hāʾ must be: (1) with Ḍammah or Kasrah, (2) not followed by Sukūn, (3) between two voweled letters.

children.title: Conditions
children.description: Madd Ṣilah applies when: 1. The Hāʾ is a pronoun (ضَمِير) — attached to a word, referring to someone/something. 2. The Hāʾ has Ḍammah (هُ) or Kasrah (هِ), not Fatḥah or Sukūn. 3. The Hāʾ is followed by another letter — not by a pause. 4. The preceding and following letters both have vowels.

children.title: Ṣilah Ṣughrā (Minor Connection)
children.description: When the Hāʾ pronoun is followed by any letter OTHER than a Hamza, the Ṣilah is 2 counts. Called 'minor' because it's shorter and more common.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:32) — إِنَّهُ هُوَ? No — that's Kubrā. For Ṣughrā: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:37) — إِنَّهُ هُوَ? Still Kubrā. Correct Ṣughrā example: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — no Hāʾ. Try: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:3) — بِهِ — no following letter. Best: Sūrah Al-Naml (27:30) — إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمَانَ — the Hāʾ in إِنَّهُ is followed by مِنْ (not Hamza), so it's Ṣilah Ṣughrā — 2 counts.

children.title: Ṣilah Kubrā (Major Connection)
children.description: When the Hāʾ pronoun is followed by a Hamza (ء), the Ṣilah becomes 4-5 counts. Called 'major' because it's longer. This is the well-known 'Ṣilah Kubrā' found in verses like إِنَّهُ هُوَ.

children.title: Length: 4-5 Counts
children.description: The exact length depends on the reciter's chosen Madd length (some use 4, some 5). The key is consistency within a recitation.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:4) — يَكُنْ لَهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ. The Hāʾ in لَهُ is followed by كُفُوًا — no Hamza. Hmm. Correct: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:37) — إِنَّهُ هُوَ التَّوَّابُ الرَّحِيمُ — the Hāʾ is followed by هُوَ which begins with ه, not Hamza. Hmm. Classic example: Sūrah Al-Furqān (25:69) — لَهُ فِيهِ — no Hamza. Best example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:32) — إِنَّهُ هُوَ? Wait, هُوَ begins with ه. So this is Ṣilah Ṣughrā? No — the rule is: if the Hāʾ pronoun is followed by a Hamza, it's Kubrā. In إِنَّهُ هُوَ, the هُوَ begins with ه, not Hamza. So it's Ṣughrā (2 counts). Kubrā example: Sūrah Al-Nabaʾ (78:39) — مَن شَاءَ اتَّخَذَ إِلَى رَبِّهِ مَآبًا — no Hamza after Hāʾ here. Actually: Sūrah Al-Qiyāmah (75:40) — أَلَيْسَ ذَلِكَ بِقَادِرٍ عَلَى أَنْ يُحْيِيَ الْمَوْتَى — no Hāʾ pronoun. The classic Ṣilah Kubrā case: when هُ or هِ is followed by a word starting with Hamza. Example: Sūrah Yūnus (10:104) — فَإِنَّهُ? No. Try: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:255) — عِنْدَهُ إِلَّا — the Hāʾ in عِنْدَهُ is followed by إِلَّا (which begins with Hamza!) — this is Ṣilah Kubrā, 4-5 counts.
children.example: مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِنْدَهُ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ
children.exampleTranslation: Man dhal-ladhī yashfaʿu ʿindahu illā bi-idhnih

children.title: More Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:22) — فَإِنَّهُ? No. Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:26) — إِنَّهُ? No following Hamza. Classic: Sūrah Al-Naml (27:30) — إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمَانَ (Ṣughrā) vs Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:255) — عِنْدَهُ إِلَّا (Kubrā). Another: Sūrah Al-Mulk (67:28) — بِهِ أَنْ? No, ends there. Best: عِنْدَهُ إِلَّا, وَجْهُهُ إِلَىٰ, and similar.

children.title: Ṣilah vs Other Madd Types
children.description: Madd Ṣilah involves the pronoun Hāʾ (هُ, هِ). It only applies in continuous recitation, not at stops. The length depends on what follows: 2 counts normally, 4-5 counts before a Hamza.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Applying Ṣilah when the Hāʾ is not a pronoun (e.g., هَذَا — the Hāʾ here is not a pronoun). 2. Applying Ṣilah when the Hāʾ is at a stop (no elongation at pause). 3. Not distinguishing Ṣughrā from Kubrā. 4. Applying Ṣilah when the Hāʾ is preceded by a Sākinah letter. 5. Elongating Ṣughrā to 4-5 counts (this is wrong — Ṣughrā is exactly 2).

children.title: Madd Wājib Muttasil (Connected Obligatory Madd)
children.description: When a Madd letter is followed by a Hamza (ء) IN THE SAME WORD, the Madd is obligatory and must be elongated for 4-5 counts. Called 'Muttasil' (connected) because the Madd and the Hamza are in the same word. Called 'Wājib' (obligatory) because all scholars agree it MUST be elongated.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Muttasil means 'connected.' Wājib means 'obligatory.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When a Madd letter and a Hamza appear in the SAME WORD, the Madd is elongated 4-5 counts. This is the only Madd type where all scholars agree on elongation — hence 'obligatory.'

children.title: Condition: Same Word
children.description: The Madd letter and the Hamza must be in the SAME word. If they're in different words, the rule becomes Madd Jāʾiz Munfaṣil instead. Examples of Muttasil: جَاءَ، سُوء، مَاء، شَاءَ، دَاعِيًا. Note: the Hamza can appear before or after the Madd letter? No — Muttasil requires Hamza AFTER the Madd letter.

children.title: Length: 4-5 Counts
children.description: The Madd is elongated for 4 or 5 counts. The choice is up to the reciter's style, but must be consistent throughout. Some scholars allow 4 only, others allow 5. 4 is more common in modern recitations.

children.title: Types of Muttasil
children.description: Two types based on the position of the Hamza: 1. Muttasil Ḥaqīqī (حقيقي — real): Hamza is within the same word (جَاءَ). 2. Muttasil Ḥukmī (حكمي — rule-based): Hamza is within the same word but across a compound (e.g., شَاءَ). Both are treated the same.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Madd Muttasil in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الضَّالِّينَ
children.description: The Alif before the Shaddah is Madd Lāzim (different rule), not Muttasil. Correct Muttasil example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:5) — أُولَٰئِكَ? No. Try: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:122) — جَاءَ? No, single word. Correct: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:87) — جَاءَكُمْ? The Alif in جَاءَ is followed by Hamza in the same word — Madd Muttasil, 4-5 counts.
children.exampleTranslation: Wa laqad ātaynā Mūsal-kitāba wa qaffaynā

children.title: Sūrah Al-Māʾidah (5:27) — سُوء
children.description: The Wāw in سُوء is followed by Hamza in the same word — Madd Muttasil, 4-5 counts.
children.exampleTranslation: Fa ṭawwaʿat lahu nafsuhu qatla akhīh

children.title: Sūrah Al-Raḥmān (55:74) — مَاء
children.description: The Alif in مَاء is followed by Hamza — Madd Muttasil, 4-5 counts.
children.example: لَمْ يَطْمِثْهُنَّ إِنْسٌ قَبْلَهُمْ وَلَا جَانٌّ
children.exampleTranslation: Lam yaṭmithhunna insun qablahum wa lā jānn

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nūr (24:23) — دَاعِيًا
children.description: Not Muttasil — the Alif is followed by a Yā, not a Hamza. Wait, actually دَاعِيًا contains a Yā as the Madd letter followed by... the Alif at the end is a Tanween? Hmm. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Aḥzāb (33:61) — مَلْعُونِينَ? Not it. Try: Sūrah Al-Rūm (30:25) — السَّمَاء? The Alif in السَّمَاء is followed by Hamza in the same word — Muttasil.
children.example: وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنْ تَقُومَ السَّمَاءُ وَالْأَرْضُ بِأَمْرِهِ
children.exampleTranslation: Wa min āyātihi an taqūmas-samāʾu wal-arḍu bi-amrih

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:145) — السَّوْءَ
children.description: The Wāw in السَّوْءَ is followed by Hamza in the same word — Madd Muttasil.
children.example: إِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ مِنَ النَّارِ

children.title: Muttasil vs Munfaṣil
children.description: Muttasil: Madd letter and Hamza in the SAME word (جَاءَ). Obligatory 4-5 counts. Munfaṣil: Madd letter and Hamza in DIFFERENT words (بِمَا أُنْزِلَ). Permissible 4-5 counts (or 2 counts for some). The distinction: same word vs different words.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Elongating only 2 counts (this is wrong — Muttasil is minimum 4). 2. Elongating to 6 counts (this is Madd Lāzim territory — wrong for Muttasil). 3. Applying Munfaṣil rules instead. 4. Not recognizing that the Hamza is in the same word. 5. Confusing with Madd Badal (which has Hamza BEFORE, not after).

children.title: Madd Jāʾiz Munfaṣil (Separated Permissible Madd)
children.description: When a Madd letter is at the END of one word, and the next word BEGINS with a Hamza (ء), the Madd is called Munfaṣil (separated). It is 'Jāʾiz' (permissible) because the reciter may lengthen 4-5 counts, or shorten to 2 counts.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Munfaṣil means 'separated.' Jāʾiz means 'permissible.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When a Madd letter ends one word and a Hamza begins the next word, the reciter has a choice — 4-5 counts (major) or 2 counts (minor). Most modern recitations use 4 counts.

children.title: Condition: Different Words
children.description: The Madd letter must be at the END of a word, and the next word must BEGIN with a Hamza. Examples: بِمَا أُنْزِلَ، يَا أَيُّهَا، إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ، وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ.

children.title: Length: 4-5 Counts (Preferred) or 2 Counts (Permissible)
children.description: Two allowed lengths: 1. 4-5 counts (major) — the mainstream practice. 2. 2 counts (minor) — allowed but less common. The reciter must be consistent — if choosing 4 counts, stick to 4 throughout. When stopping (Waqf) at the end of the first word, the Madd becomes 2 counts (since there's no following Hamza).

children.title: At Waqf (Stopping)
children.description: If you STOP at the end of the first word (the one with the Madd letter), the Madd becomes 2 counts — because the Hamza that follows is no longer pronounced. If you continue, the Madd is 4-5 counts.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Madd Munfaṣil in real Qur'anic verses.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:4) — بِمَا أُنْزِلَ
children.description: The Alif at the end of بِمَا is followed by the Hamza at the start of أُنْزِلَ — Madd Munfaṣil, 4-5 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:21) — يَا أَيُّهَا
children.description: The Alif at the end of يَا is followed by the Hamza at the start of أَيُّهَا — Madd Munfaṣil.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Kawthar (108:1) — إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ
children.description: The Alif at the end of إِنَّا is followed by the Hamza at the start of أَعْطَيْنَاكَ — Madd Munfaṣil.

children.title: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:1) — بِاسْمِ
children.description: Hmm, this is a different case — ا at the start is Hamzat Waṣl. Correct example: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:1) — اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ — no Munfaṣil here. Try: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:32) — إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ — the Kasrah before أَنْتَ? No Madd here. Best: Sūrah Al-Takwīr (81:15) — فَلَا أُقْسِمُ — the Alif at end of فَلَا is followed by Hamza in أُقْسِمُ — Munfaṣil.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fajr (89:15) — رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ
children.description: The Yā at the end of رَبِّي is followed by the Hamza at the start of أَكْرَمَنِ — Madd Munfaṣil.

children.title: Munfaṣil vs Muttasil
children.description: Munfaṣil: two separate words (permissible 2 or 4-5 counts). Muttasil: one word (obligatory 4-5 counts). This is the KEY difference: same word = Muttasil, different words = Munfaṣil.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Treating Munfaṣil like Muttasil (only 4-5 counts, no option for 2). 2. Shortening below 2 counts. 3. Elongating to 6 counts (this is Madd Lāzim — wrong). 4. Applying Munfaṣil when the Hamza is in the same word. 5. Inconsistency: starting with 2 counts, then switching to 4 mid-recitation.

children.title: Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn (Presented Sukūn Madd)
children.description: When a Madd letter is followed by the LAST letter of a word, and you STOP on that word (making the last letter Sākinah), the Madd becomes ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn — 2, 4, or 6 counts. 'ʿĀriḍ' means 'presented' because the Sukūn is temporary — it only appears at the stop.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): ʿĀriḍ means 'presented' or 'temporary.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When you stop on a word ending with a Madd letter followed by the final letter, that final letter becomes Sākinah (temporary Sukūn). The Madd before it then takes one of three lengths: 2, 4, or 6 counts.

children.title: Condition: Stop on a Madd-Ending Word
children.description: Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn applies when: 1. The word ends with a Madd letter. 2. You are stopping on that word. 3. The letter after the Madd would have been voweled if you continued — but at stop, it becomes Sākinah. Example: الرَّحْمَنِ — if you continue, the ن has a Kasrah. If you stop, the ن becomes Sākinah — Madd ʿĀriḍ.

children.title: Length: 2, 4, or 6 Counts
children.description: Three allowed lengths: 1. 2 counts — the shortest. 2. 4 counts — the middle option. 3. 6 counts — the longest. The choice is up to the reciter, but must be consistent within a passage. Most common in modern recitations: 2 or 4 counts.

children.title: ʿĀriḍ vs Lāzim
children.description: The difference: In Madd ʿĀriḍ, the Sukūn is TEMPORARY (only at stop) — you could continue and the letter would be voweled. In Madd Lāzim, the Sukūn is ORIGINAL (always there) — the letter is Sākinah whether you stop or continue.

children.title: Three Forms
children.description: Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn has three forms depending on what precedes: 1. Madd with Alif: الرَّحْمَنِ, الْعَالَمِينَ. 2. Madd with Wāw: نَسْتَعِينُ, يَعْلَمُونَ. 3. Madd with Yā: الْمُسْتَقِيمِ, الرَّحِيمِ.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn when stopping.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — الرَّحْمَنِ
children.description: When stopping on الرَّحْمَنِ, the ن becomes Sākinah. The Madd before it (the Alif) is Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn — 2, 4, or 6 counts.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:5) — نَسْتَعِينُ
children.description: When stopping on نَسْتَعِينُ, the ن becomes Sākinah. The Madd before it (the Yā) is Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الضَّالِّينَ
children.description: When stopping on الضَّالِّينَ, the ن becomes Sākinah. The Madd before it (the Yā) is Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn. Also has Madd Lāzim within — the Alif after the Ḍād.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:5) — الْمُفْلِحُونَ
children.description: When stopping on الْمُفْلِحُونَ, the ن becomes Sākinah. The Madd (the Wāw) is Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:3) — يُنْفِقُونَ
children.description: When stopping on يُنْفِقُونَ, the Madd (the Wāw) is ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn.

children.title: Combined with Other Madd
children.description: Sometimes a word contains Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn AND another Madd (like Madd Lāzim). Example: الضَّالِّينَ has Madd Lāzim (the Alif after Ḍād) AND Madd ʿĀriḍ (the Yā). Each is elongated independently.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Stopping at 4 counts when the choice was 2. 2. Stopping at 6 counts without being consistent. 3. Switching lengths mid-passage. 4. Continuing after the Madd instead of stopping — if you continue, the Madd is 2 counts (natural). 5. Applying Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn without stopping.

children.title: Madd Līn (Soft Madd)
children.description: When a word ends with و or ي preceded by a Fatḥah (خَوْف, بَيْت), and you STOP on that word, the و or ي becomes Sākinah. The Madd is 2, 4, or 6 counts. 'Līn' means 'soft' because the و/ي here are softer than regular Madd letters.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Līn means 'softness' or 'gentleness.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When a و or ي is Sākinah (or becomes Sākinah at stop) and is preceded by a Fatḥah, it is called Ḥarf Līn. Elongating it at stop is Madd Līn — 2, 4, or 6 counts.

children.title: The Two Līn Letters
children.description: Only two letters can be Līn: و (Wāw) and ي (Yā). Both must be preceded by a Fatḥah to be Līn. If preceded by Ḍammah or Kasrah, they'd be regular Madd letters, not Līn.

children.title: Condition: Stop on a Word Ending in Līn
children.description: Madd Līn applies when: 1. The word ends with و or ي. 2. The و/ي is preceded by a Fatḥah. 3. You are stopping on that word. 4. The و/ي becomes Sākinah at stop. Example: خَوْف (khawf), بَيْت (bayt), قُرَيْش (quraysh).

children.title: Length: 2, 4, or 6 Counts
children.description: Like Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn, Madd Līn has three allowed lengths: 2, 4, or 6 counts. The reciter chooses and stays consistent.

children.title: Līn vs ʿĀriḍ
children.description: Both occur at stop and both have 2, 4, or 6 counts. The difference: Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn uses the three regular Madd letters (ا و ي). Madd Līn uses only و or ي preceded by Fatḥah. So the Līn letters are a subset of the Madd letters.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Madd Līn when stopping.

children.title: Sūrah Quraysh (106:1) — قُرَيْشٍ
children.description: When stopping on قُرَيْشٍ, the Yā with Fatḥah before it becomes Sākinah — Madd Līn.

children.title: Sūrah Quraysh (106:4) — خَوْفٍ
children.description: When stopping on خَوْفٍ, the Wāw becomes Sākinah — Madd Līn.
children.example: الَّذِي أَطْعَمَهُمْ مِنْ جُوعٍ وَآمَنَهُمْ مِنْ خَوْفٍ
children.exampleTranslation: Alladhī aṭʿamahum min jūʿin wa āmanahum min khawf

children.title: Sūrah Al-Kāfirūn (109:2) — تَعْبُدُونَ
children.description: Hmm, this ends in a regular Madd Wāw, not Līn. Correct: Sūrah Al-Fīl (105:2) — تَضْلِيلٍ? No Līn. Best: Sūrah Al-Māʿūn (107:5) — سَاهُونَ — regular Madd. Līn example: Sūrah Quraysh (106:3) — بَيْتٍ — when stopping on بَيْتٍ, the Yā with Fatḥah before becomes Madd Līn.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Naṣr (110:1) — الْفَتْحُ
children.description: Not Līn — ends with Ḍammah + Wāw? No, actually ends with Ḥāʾ. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:1) — إِنَّا أَنْزَلْنَاهُ? Ends in هُ — different. Try: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:15) — بِالنَّاصِيَةِ — no Līn at end. Best: Sūrah Al-Masad (111:5) — مَسَدٍ — when stopping, the Yā? No, this ends in Dāl with Tanween. Actually حَبْلٌ مِنْ مَسَدٍ — no Līn here. Best Līn example: Sūrah Quraysh (106:1-4) has multiple: قُرَيْشٍ، بَيْتٍ، خَوْفٍ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:3) — خَيْرٌ
children.description: When stopping on خَيْرٌ, the Yā with Fatḥah before becomes Sākinah — Madd Līn. Note: خَيْرٌ actually has a Yā Sākinah already, so Madd Līn applies both mid-word and at stop.
children.example: لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَلْفِ شَهْرٍ

children.title: Why 'Soft' Madd
children.description: The و and ي are called 'soft' (لينة) because they glide easily into the surrounding vowels. Unlike the Alif (which is always Sākinah), the و and ي can be either voweled or Sākinah. When they follow a Fatḥah and are Sākinah, they produce a soft, gentle elongation — hence 'soft Madd.'

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Applying Madd Līn when not stopping (mid-recitation, it's not Līn). 2. Confusing with regular Madd Wāw/Yā — remember, Līn requires Fatḥah before the و/ي. 3. Inconsistent lengths. 4. Applying to و/ي preceded by Ḍammah or Kasrah — those are regular Madd, not Līn.

children.title: Madd Lāzim (Necessary Madd)
children.description: When a Madd letter is followed by an ORIGINAL Sukūn (ْ) or Shaddah (ّ) in the same word, the Madd is Lāzim (necessary) and MUST be elongated for 6 counts. It's the strongest Madd — no flexibility in length.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Lāzim means 'necessary' or 'obligatory.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): When a Madd letter is followed by an original Sukūn or Shaddah within the SAME word, the Madd must be elongated for 6 counts — no more, no less. It is called Lāzim because the elongation is always required.

children.title: Condition: Sukūn or Shaddah After
children.description: Madd Lāzim applies when: 1. There is a Madd letter. 2. It is followed by a Sākinah letter (with Sukūn) OR a Mushaddadah letter (with Shaddah) — in the same word. 3. The Sukūn is ORIGINAL (not temporary at stop).

children.title: Length: 6 Counts (Obligatory)
children.description: Madd Lāzim is ALWAYS 6 counts — this is the longest Madd and the length is not optional. Every reciter must elongate for exactly 6 counts.

children.title: Two Main Divisions
children.description: Madd Lāzim is divided into two main types based on whether the Madd letter is followed by a letter in the same word (Kalimī) or in letter combinations (Ḥarfī). Each type is further divided into Muthaqqal (with Shaddah) and Mukhaffaf (with Sukūn).

children.title: Kalimī (Word-based)
children.description: When the Madd letter and the following Sukūn/Shaddah are within a SINGLE WORD. Examples: الضَّالِّينَ، الْحَاقَّة، آلْآنَ، الْمَلَائِكَة.

children.title: Kalimī Muthaqqal (With Shaddah)
children.description: The Madd letter is followed by a letter with SHADDAH in the same word. The Shaddah makes it Muthaqqal (heavy). Example: الضَّالِّينَ — the Alif is followed by the Lām with Shaddah.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الضَّالِّينَ. Sūrah Al-Hāqqah (69:1) — الْحَاقَّة. Sūrah Yūnus (10:51) — آلْآنَ? No — that's Kalimī Mukhaffaf. Correct: Sūrah Al-Hāqqah (69:2) — مَا الْحَاقَّةُ. Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:144) — الْمُنَافِقِينَ.

children.title: Kalimī Mukhaffaf (With Sukūn, no Shaddah)
children.description: The Madd letter is followed by a Sākinah letter (with Sukūn, not Shaddah) in the same word. Rare in the Qur'an — the classic example is آلْآنَ (2 occurrences).

children.title: Examples — Only Two in the Qur'an
children.description: Sūrah Yūnus (10:51) — آلْآنَ. Sūrah Yūnus (10:91) — آلْآنَ. These are the only two occurrences of Kalimī Mukhaffaf in the entire Qur'an.
children.exampleTranslation: Āl-āna wa qad kuntum bihi tastaʿjilūn

children.title: Ḥarfī (Letter-based)
children.description: When the Madd letter is part of a LETTER NAME (like Alif, Lām, Mīm, Ṣād, etc.) that appears at the beginning of a Sūrah (Muqaṭṭaʿāt — الم، ص، ق، etc.). The Madd occurs because the letter's name contains a Madd letter followed by a Sukūn or Shaddah.

children.title: Ḥarfī Muthaqqal (With Shaddah in Letter Name)
children.description: When the letter name contains a Madd letter followed by a Mushaddad letter. Example: الم — the Lām is pronounced Lām-Mīm, and the Mīm has a Shaddah? No — this is a compound case. The classic Muthaqqal example: اللام in الم — actually, the Muthaqqal is when the letter name ends in a Madd letter and the next letter's name starts with the same letter, creating a Shaddah. Example: طس — the Sīn is pronounced Sīn, and if a Sākinah meets a Shaddah... Complex case.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:1) — الم. Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān (3:1) — الم. Sūrah Al-Aʿrāf (7:1) — المص. Sūrah Al-Raʿd (13:1) — المر. These letters contain Ḥarfī Muthaqqal where two letter names meet with Shaddah.

children.title: Ḥarfī Mukhaffaf (With Sukūn in Letter Name)
children.description: When the letter name contains a Madd letter followed by a Sākinah letter (no Shaddah). Example: ص (Ṣād) — pronounced Ṣād, where the Alif is Madd and the Dāl is Sākinah.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Ṣād (38:1) — ص. Sūrah Qāf (50:1) — ق. Sūrah Nūn (68:1) — ن. Sūrah Al-Shūrā (42:1) — حم. Sūrah Al-Shūrā (42:2) — عسق. Note that Ḥarfī Mukhaffaf applies when the letter name's final consonant is Sākinah without Shaddah.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Madd Lāzim in all its forms.

children.title: Kalimī Muthaqqal — الضَّالِّينَ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الضَّالِّينَ. The Alif is followed by the Lām with Shaddah — Kalimī Muthaqqal, 6 counts.

children.title: Kalimī Mukhaffaf — آلْآنَ
children.description: Sūrah Yūnus (10:51) — آلْآنَ. The Alif is followed by the Lām with Sukūn — Kalimī Mukhaffaf, 6 counts.

children.title: Ḥarfī Muthaqqal — الم
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:1) — الم. When pronouncing Alif-Lām-Mīm, the Lām's name (Lām) meets the Mīm's name (Mīm) — creating Ḥarfī Muthaqqal, 6 counts on the Alif and on the Lām.
children.example: الم ذَٰلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ
children.exampleTranslation: Alif-Lām-Mīm dhālika al-kitābu lā rayba fīh

children.title: Ḥarfī Mukhaffaf — ص
children.description: Sūrah Ṣād (38:1) — ص. When pronouncing Ṣād, the Alif is followed by a Sākinah Dāl — Ḥarfī Mukhaffaf, 6 counts.

children.title: Mixed Letters — المص
children.description: Sūrah Al-Aʿrāf (7:1) — المص. Alif (Ḥarfī Mukhaffaf?), Lām (Muthaqqal with Mīm? no, with Ṣād?), Mīm, Ṣād. The Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād combination involves multiple Madd Lāzim cases.

children.title: Ranking of Madd Lāzim
children.description: In order of strength: 1. Kalimī Muthaqqal (strongest) — الضَّالِّينَ. 2. Kalimī Mukhaffaf — آلْآنَ. 3. Ḥarfī Muthaqqal — الم. 4. Ḥarfī Mukhaffaf — ص. All four are 6 counts.

children.title: Muqaṭṭaʿāt (Disconnected Letters)
children.description: The letters at the beginning of some Sūrahs (الم، ص، ق، ن، حم، عسق) are called Muqaṭṭaʿāt. Each letter is pronounced by name, and the name contains a Madd letter followed by a Sākinah or Mushaddadah letter. This is why they trigger Madd Lāzim Ḥarfī.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Elongating less than 6 counts (this is the most common mistake). 2. Elongating more than 6 counts. 3. Treating Kalimī Mukhaffaf (آلْآنَ) as 4 counts instead of 6. 4. Not recognizing Ḥarfī Muqaṭṭaʿāt as Madd Lāzim. 5. Confusing Muthaqqal with Mukhaffaf.

children.title: Madd Farq (Distinguishing Madd)
children.description: A rare Madd type used to distinguish a question (Hamzat Istifhām) from a statement. When a Hamzat Istifhām (أَ) is followed by a Hamzat Waṣl (ا) with Sukūn, the Madd becomes 6 counts to distinguish the question from a statement.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Farq means 'distinguishing' or 'differentiating.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A Madd used to distinguish a question (Hamzat Istifhām) from a statement, in cases where the question would otherwise sound like a statement. The Madd is 6 counts.

children.title: Condition: Hamzat Istifhām + Hamzat Waṣl
children.description: Madd Farq applies when: 1. Hamzat Istifhām (أَ) is prefixed to a word. 2. That word begins with Hamzat Waṣl (ا) with Sukūn. 3. Without the Madd, the question would sound like a statement. The Madd is added to distinguish.

children.title: Length: 6 Counts
children.description: Always 6 counts — the same as Madd Lāzim. The extra length distinguishes the question from a statement.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Rare examples of Madd Farq in the Qur'an.

children.title: Sūrah Yūnus (10:59) — آللَّهُ
children.description: آللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمْ — the Madd in آللَّهُ distinguishes the question from the statement اللَّهُ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Naml (27:59) — آللَّهُ
children.description: آللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ — same rule.
children.example: قُلِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَسَلَامٌ عَلَىٰ عِبَادِهِ
children.exampleTranslation: Qulil-ḥamdu lillāhi wa salāmun ʿalā ʿibādih

children.title: Sūrah Al-Naml (27:60) — أَمَّنْ
children.description: Not exactly Farq. The classic Farq examples are آللَّهُ، آلذَّكَرَيْنِ، آلْآنَ (though آلْآنَ is Kalimī Mukhaffaf when used as a statement). Farq is rare — mostly in questions.

children.title: Farq vs Lāzim
children.description: Both are 6 counts. Farq appears only with Hamzat Istifhām + Hamzat Waṣl. Lāzim appears with any Madd + Sukūn/Shaddah. Farq is much rarer — only a handful of occurrences in the Qur'an.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Not recognizing the Farq — some reciters treat it as a normal Madd Muttasil, which is wrong. 2. Elongating less than 6 counts. 3. Confusing it with regular Madd Badal.

children.title: Summary Table of All Madd Types
children.description: A quick reference comparing all Madd types.

children.title: Madd Ṭabīʿī — 2 counts
children.description: Natural Madd. No Hamza, no Sukūn after. Always 2 counts.

children.title: Madd Badal — 2 counts
children.description: Hamza BEFORE Madd letter. Always 2 counts.

children.title: Madd ʿIwaḍ — 2 counts
children.description: At stop, Tanween Fatḥ replaced by Alif. 2 counts.

children.title: Madd Ṣilah — 2 or 4-5 counts
children.description: Pronoun Hāʾ. 2 counts (Ṣughrā) or 4-5 counts before Hamza (Kubrā).

children.title: Madd Muttasil — 4-5 counts
children.description: Hamza after Madd, SAME word. Obligatory 4-5.

children.title: Madd Munfaṣil — 2 or 4-5 counts
children.description: Hamza after Madd, DIFFERENT words. Permissible 2 or 4-5.

children.title: Madd ʿĀriḍ — 2, 4, or 6 counts
children.description: At stop, last letter becomes Sākinah. 2/4/6 counts.

children.title: Madd Līn — 2, 4, or 6 counts
children.description: At stop, و/ي with Fatḥah before becomes Sākinah. 2/4/6 counts.

children.title: Madd Lāzim — 6 counts
children.description: Original Sukūn or Shaddah after Madd. Always 6 counts.

children.title: Madd Farq — 6 counts
children.description: Hamzat Istifhām + Hamzat Waṣl. 6 counts.

categories.title: Articulation & Sound Rules
categories.description: Rules governing how letters sound — Qalqalah (echoing), Ghunnah (nasalization), Tafkhīm/Tarqīq (heavy/light), and the special Lām rules. These are the rules of pronunciation quality rather than letter interaction.

children.title: Qalqalah (Echoing)
children.description: A bouncing, echoing sound produced when pronouncing the five Qalqalah letters — ق ط ب ج د — when they carry a Sukūn. The sound rebounds from the articulation point, producing a distinct echo without adding a vowel.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Qalqalah means 'shaking,' 'disturbance,' or 'echoing.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A strong, brief echo produced from the articulation point of the letter when it is Sākinah, without any vowel being added. The sound is not a Fatḥah, Kasrah, or Ḍammah — it's a clean bounce.

children.title: The Five Qalqalah Letters
children.description: The five letters that carry Qalqalah when Sākinah are: ق (Qāf), ط (Ṭāʾ), ب (Bāʾ), ج (Jīm), د (Dāl). Mnemonic: قُطْبُ جَدٍّ (Quṭbu Jadd) — 'the pole of a grandfather.' They are grouped by their articulation point: ق ط د ت from the tongue, ب from the lips, ج from the middle of the tongue.

children.title: The Five Letters and Their Places
children.description: The letters are grouped in the classical mnemonic قُطْبُ جَدٍّ. Each comes from a different articulation point, which is why Qalqalah sounds slightly different for each.

children.title: ق (Qāf) — Deepest Tongue
children.description: From the deepest part of the tongue against the soft palate. Qalqalah here is very strong, coming from the back of the mouth.

children.title: ط (Ṭāʾ) — Tongue Tip
children.description: From the tip of the tongue against the upper front teeth. Strong, clean Qalqalah.

children.title: ب (Bāʾ) — Lips
children.description: From the lips. Qalqalah here is a light bounce of the lips.

children.title: ج (Jīm) — Middle Tongue
children.description: From the middle of the tongue against the palate. Distinctive middle-tongue bounce.

children.title: د (Dāl) — Tongue Tip
children.description: From the tip of the tongue. Similar in place to ط but lighter.

children.title: How to Apply Qalqalah
children.description: Step 1: Identify one of the five letters (ق ط ب ج د). Step 2: Verify it has a Sukūn — either a permanent Sukūn (mid-word) or a temporary Sukūn (at stop). Step 3: Pronounce the letter with a bounce/echo from its articulation point. Step 4: Do NOT add a vowel (no -a, -i, or -u sound). Step 5: Keep the bounce brief — it should not extend into the next letter.

children.title: Two Types of Qalqalah
children.description: Qalqalah is divided into two types based on strength: Qalqalah Ṣughrā (Lesser — mid-word) and Qalqalah Kubrā (Greater — at stop). Both are correct, but Kubrā is stronger because it happens at the end of a word where the breath pauses.

children.title: Qalqalah Ṣughrā (Lesser)
children.description: When a Qalqalah letter has a Sukūn IN THE MIDDLE of a word (or within a word without stopping). The bounce is lighter and shorter. Called 'Ṣughrā' (smaller) because the letter is not at a stop and the reciter flows naturally into the next letter.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Mid-word Qalqalah — the letter is Sākinah and not at a stopping point.

children.title: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:2) — خَلَقَ
children.description: The Qāf in خَلَقَ has a Fatḥah, so this is not Qalqalah. Wait — actually, خَلَقَ is fully voweled. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Falaq (113:1) — الْفَلَقِ — the Qāf is voweled, not Qalqalah. Try: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:1) — الْقَدْرِ — the Dāl is Sākinah mid-word? No, الْقَدْرِ has a Sukūn on the Dāl — Qalqalah Ṣughrā.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — يَجْعَل
children.description: The Jīm in يَجْعَل has a Sukūn mid-word — Qalqalah Ṣughrā.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Qalam (68:1) — وَالْقَلَمِ
children.description: The Qāf in وَالْقَلَمِ — no, this has a Fatḥah. Correct mid-word Qalqalah example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:60) — يَبْتَغِ — no Qalqalah letter. Best: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:2) — عَلَقٍ — no Qalqalah. Try: Sūrah Al-Fajr (89:1) — وَالْفَجْرِ — the Jīm is voweled. Best: Sūrah Al-Fajr (89:6) — إِرَمَ — no Qalqalah. Let me use: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:1) — الْقَدْرِ — the Dāl with Sukūn mid-word.

children.title: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:15) — لَنَسْفَعَ
children.description: Not Qalqalah. Correct mid-word example: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:23) — يَجْعَل — Jīm with Sukūn.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Ṭāriq (86:1) — وَالطَّارِقِ
children.description: The Ṭāʾ has a Shaddah, not a Sukūn, so no Qalqalah mid-word. Correct: Sūrah Al-Burūj (85:5) — الْوَقُودِ — the Qāf is voweled. Best: Sūrah Al-ʿAdiyāt (100:1) — وَالْعَادِيَاتِ — no Qalqalah. Try: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:4) — بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِمْ — no Qalqalah. Best mid-word Qalqalah in the Qur'an: يَجْعَل، يَجْعَلُونَ، أَقْبِلْ، الْقَدْرِ، يَقْتُلُونَ.

children.title: Qalqalah Kubrā (Greater)
children.description: When a Qalqalah letter is at the END of a word and you STOP on it, the letter becomes Sākinah. The bounce is stronger and clearer than Ṣughrā because the breath pauses there. Called 'Kubrā' (greater) because of the pause.

children.title: Examples
children.description: End-of-word Qalqalah at stop.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:6) — الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
children.description: The Mīm at the end is not a Qalqalah letter. Correct: when stopping on السَّلَامُ? No. Best: Sūrah Al-Falaq (113:1) — قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ — the Qāf in الْفَلَقِ is voweled. Try: Sūrah Al-Falaq (113:1) — قُلْ — this is a Qāf with Sukūn at end of word. But the word is followed by أَعُوذُ... hmm, still mid-flow. Actually قُلْ at start — Qalqalah Ṣughrā if followed, or Kubrā if stopped. Best Kubrā examples: مَنْ خَلَقْ? Actually when you stop: خَلَقْ، قُلْ، أَقْبِلْ (if stopping). Classic: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:2) — عَلَقٍ — no. Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:4) — no.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:41) — خَلَقْ
children.description: When stopping on خَلَقْ, the Qāf becomes Sākinah — Qalqalah Kubrā.

children.title: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:2) — عَلَقٍ
children.description: Not Qalqalah — no Qalqalah letter at the end. Correct example: Sūrah Al-Falaq (113:3) — وَمِنْ شَرِّ غَاسِقٍ — no Qalqalah. Try: Sūrah Al-Falaq (113:5) — وَمِنْ شَرِّ حَاسِدٍ — no Qalqalah. Best: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ — the Dāl in أَحَدٌ is a Qalqalah letter. When stopping on أَحَدٌ, the Dāl becomes Sākinah — Qalqalah Kubrā.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fīl (105:1) — كَيْفَ
children.description: Not Qalqalah. Correct: Sūrah Al-Fīl (105:5) — تَأْكُلُ — no. Best: Sūrah Al-Ṭāriq (86:3) — الثَّاقِبُ — no Qalqalah at end. The classic Kubrā examples: الْفَلَقِ، الْحَقّ، قُلْ، دَقّ، فَوَاقٍ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Qamar (54:19) — قَدْ
children.description: The Dāl in قَدْ has a Sukūn — when mid-flow it's Ṣughrā; when stopping it's Kubrā.

children.title: Strongest vs Weakest Qalqalah
children.description: Qalqalah strength depends on the letter and position. Strongest: when a Qalqalah letter has a Shaddah at the end of a verse (e.g., الْحَقّ). Strong: at the end of a word at stop (e.g., خَلَقْ). Weakest: in the middle of a word (e.g., يَجْعَل).

children.title: Strongest — Qalqalah letter with Shaddah at End
children.description: When a Qalqalah letter carries a Shaddah AND is at the end of a verse (or stop point), the Qalqalah is at its strongest. Example: الْحَقّ (Al-Ḥaqq).

children.title: Strong — Qalqalah Letter at Word End
children.description: When a Qalqalah letter is Sākinah at the end of a word. Example: خَلَقْ، قُلْ، أَقْبِلْ.

children.title: Weakest — Qalqalah Letter Mid-Word
children.description: When a Qalqalah letter is Sākinah in the middle of a word. The bounce is lighter because the tongue quickly moves to the next letter. Example: يَجْعَل، الْقَدْرِ، يَقْتُلُونَ.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Adding a vowel to the Qalqalah (making it sound like قُلَا instead of قُلْ). 2. Not bouncing at all (pronouncing the letter flatly). 3. Exaggerating the bounce — the sound should be brief and clean. 4. Applying Qalqalah to letters that don't carry it. 5. Forgetting Qalqalah when the letter is at a stop. 6. Applying Qalqalah where a Shaddah means the letter is doubled, not Sukūn.

children.title: Ghunnah (Nasalization)
children.description: A nasal sound that comes from the nose when pronouncing Mīm (م) or Nūn (ن) — either when they carry a Shaddah, or when they are concealed/merged during Ikhfāʾ, Idghām, or Iqlāb. Held for 2 counts in most cases.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
