children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Ghunnah means a sound that resonates in the nasal cavity. Technically (اصطلاحاً): A nasal sound produced from the Khayshūm (الخيشوم — nasal cavity) when pronouncing Mīm or Nūn. It is held for 2 counts, except in specific cases (Idghām, Ikhfāʾ, Iqlāb) where it also applies.

children.title: The Two Ghunnah Letters
children.description: Only two letters produce Ghunnah: م (Mīm) and ن (Nūn). This is because their articulation points involve partial closure of the mouth, allowing air to escape through the nose and produce the nasal sound.

children.title: When Ghunnah Applies
children.description: Ghunnah applies in five main situations: 1. Mīm or Nūn with Shaddah (strongest). 2. Ikhfāʾ (Noon/Tanween hidden before 15 letters). 3. Idghām with Ghunnah (Noon/Tanween merged into ي ن م و). 4. Iqlāb (Noon/Tanween becomes Mīm before ب). 5. Ikhfāʾ Shafawī (Mīm before ب).

children.title: Ghunnah Mushaddadah — Mīm or Nūn with Shaddah
children.description: The strongest form of Ghunnah. When Mīm or Nūn carries a Shaddah, the nasal sound is held for 2 counts. This is the most complete form of Ghunnah because the letter is doubled and the nasal resonance is fully present.

children.title: Nūn with Shaddah (نّ)
children.description: When Nūn has a Shaddah, hold the Ghunnah for 2 counts. Example: إِنَّ (inna), إِنَّا (innā).

children.title: Mīm with Shaddah (مّ)
children.description: When Mīm has a Shaddah, hold the Ghunnah for 2 counts. Example: ثُمَّ (thumma), أَمَّا (ammā).

children.title: Ghunnah in Ikhfāʾ — 2 counts
children.description: When Noon Sākinah or Tanween is concealed before one of the 15 Ikhfāʾ letters, the Ghunnah is held for 2 counts. Example: أَنْتُمْ (antum), مِنْ قَبْلِ (mim qabli).

children.title: Ghunnah in Idghām — 2 counts
children.description: When Noon Sākinah or Tanween merges into ي ن م و, the Ghunnah is held for 2 counts. Example: مَنْ يَعْمَلْ (may yaʿmal), مِنْ وَلِيٍّ (miw waliyy).

children.title: Ghunnah in Iqlāb — 2 counts
children.description: When Noon Sākinah or Tanween converts to Mīm before ب, the Ghunnah is held for 2 counts. Example: مِنْ بَعْدِ (mim baʿdi), أَنْبِئْهُمْ (ambihum).

children.title: Ghunnah in Ikhfāʾ Shafawī — 2 counts
children.description: When Mīm Sākinah is concealed before ب, the Ghunnah is held for 2 counts. Example: تَرْمِيهِمْ بِحِجَارَةٍ (tarmīhim biḥijārah).

children.title: Rankings of Ghunnah (مراتب الغنة)
children.description: Classical scholars rank the strength of Ghunnah from strongest to weakest. The strength depends on whether the Noon or Mīm is Mushaddadah, concealed, merged, or converted.

children.title: 1. Strongest — Mushaddad (نّ or مّ)
children.description: The strongest Ghunnah. Complete nasal resonance with full Shaddah. Example: إِنَّ، ثُمَّ.

children.title: 2. Strong — Ikhfāʾ Ḥaqīqī
children.description: Ghunnah before one of the 15 Ikhfāʾ letters. Nearly as strong as Mushaddad but the letter is concealed rather than doubled.

children.title: 3. Medium — Iqlāb
children.description: Ghunnah when Noon/Tanween converts to Mīm before ب. The nasal sound is moderate because the Mīm is hidden.

children.title: 4. Weak — Idghām with Ghunnah
children.description: Ghunnah when Noon/Tanween merges into ي ن م و. The Ghunnah is present but the emphasis shifts to the merged letter.

children.title: 5. Weakest — Ikhfāʾ Shafawī
children.description: Ghunnah when Mīm is concealed before ب. The lips are close together, so the nasal resonance is at its minimum while still being present.

children.title: Duration of Ghunnah
children.description: Ghunnah is ALWAYS held for 2 counts — never more, never less. This is the standard. If the reciter lengthens it beyond 2 counts, it becomes excessive. If shorter than 2 counts, the nasal sound is incomplete. Exception: when Ghunnah coincides with a Madd (e.g., a Nūn with Shaddah followed by Madd), the Madd extends but the Ghunnah itself remains 2 counts.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Ghunnah in each of its five main cases.

children.title: Mushaddadah — إِنَّ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — the Nūn in إِنَّ has a Shaddah — Ghunnah Mushaddadah.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ — مِنْ قَبْلِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:25) — the Nūn in مِنْ is concealed before ق — Ikhfāʾ Ghunnah.

children.title: Idghām — مَنْ يَعْمَلْ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Zalzalah (99:7) — the Nūn in مَنْ merges into ي with Ghunnah.
children.example: فَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ
children.exampleTranslation: Faman yaʿmal mithqāla dharratin khayran yarah

children.title: Iqlāb — مِنْ بَعْدِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:27) — the Nūn in مِنْ converts to Mīm before ب — Iqlāb Ghunnah.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ Shafawī — تَرْمِيهِمْ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fīl (105:4) — the Mīm in تَرْمِيهِمْ is concealed before ب — Ikhfāʾ Shafawī Ghunnah.

children.title: Al-Khayshūm (The Nasal Cavity)
children.description: Ghunnah emerges from a specific articulation point called Al-Khayshūm — the nasal cavity at the back of the nose. This is the 17th of the classical Makhārij (articulation points). The air escapes through the nose while the mouth is partially closed, producing the resonant nasal sound.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Holding Ghunnah for longer than 2 counts (except when combined with Madd). 2. Not producing Ghunnah at all (a common mistake with non-native Arabic speakers). 3. Holding Ghunnah through the lips instead of the nose. 4. Confusing Mushaddadah Ghunnah with Ikhfāʾ Ghunnah. 5. Applying Ghunnah to letters that don't carry it (e.g., other Sākinah letters). 6. Not applying Ghunnah in Idghām/Ikhfāʾ/Iqlāb contexts. 7. Elongating the Ghunnah in a way that sounds like a vowel (adding -a, -i, or -u).

children.title: Tafkhīm & Tarqīq (Heavy & Light)
children.description: Tafkhīm means making a letter heavy (thick) — pronounced with the back of the tongue raised toward the palate. Tarqīq means making a letter light (thin) — pronounced with the tongue flat. Seven letters are ALWAYS heavy; others are always light; and a few are context-dependent.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Tafkhīm means 'to make fat/thick.' Tarqīq means 'to make thin/light.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Tafkhīm is raising the back of the tongue toward the palate, producing a heavier, fuller sound. Tarqīq is keeping the tongue flat, producing a lighter sound.

children.title: The Seven Always-Heavy Letters
children.description: Seven letters are ALWAYS pronounced heavily regardless of context: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق. These are called Ḥurūf al-Istiʿlāʾ (حروف الاستعلاء). Mnemonic: خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ (Khuṣṣa ḍaghṭin qiẓ). These seven letters involve raising the back of the tongue toward the palate.

children.title: Strongest Tafkhīm
children.description: The strongest Tafkhīm is with ط ض ظ ق — because they combine Istiʿlāʾ (elevation) with Iṭbāq (full closure of the tongue against the palate).

children.title: Medium Tafkhīm
children.description: غ خ — they have Istiʿlāʾ but not Iṭbāq. Heavy, but less than ط ض ظ ق.

children.title: Weakest Tafkhīm
children.description: ص — sometimes lighter depending on context, but still heavy.

children.title: Letters That Are Sometimes Heavy
children.arabicTitle: الحروف التي تارة ترقق وتارة تفخم
children.description: Three letters change weight depending on context: ا (Alif), ر (Rā), ل (Lām). Their weight depends on the surrounding vowels and the letters before/after them.

children.title: Alif (ا)
children.description: Alif is never heavy by itself — it follows the weight of the letter BEFORE it. If the letter before is one of the seven heavy letters, the Alif is heavy. Otherwise, the Alif is light. Example: قَالَ (heavy Alif because of Qāf), كَانَ (light Alif because of Kāf).

children.title: Rāʾ (ر)
children.description: Rāʾ is heavy in some contexts and light in others. It is heavy when: (1) it has a Fatḥah (رَ), (2) it has a Ḍammah (رُ), (3) it is Sākinah preceded by a Fatḥah or Ḍammah, (4) it is Sākinah preceded by a Kasrah but followed by a heavy letter. It is light when: (1) it has a Kasrah (رِ), (2) it is Sākinah preceded by a Kasrah and followed by a light letter. See the dedicated Rāʾ rules node for details.

children.title: Lām (ل)
children.description: Lām is usually light, but is heavy in one specific case: in the Name of Allah (اللَّهُ) when preceded by a Fatḥah (اللَّهُ) or Ḍammah (رَسُولُ اللَّهِ). After a Kasrah (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ), it is light. See the Lām of Allah node for details.

children.title: Istiʿlāʾ vs Iṭbāq
children.description: Two Ṣifāt (characteristics) explain Tafkhīm: Istiʿlāʾ (elevation of the back of the tongue) and Iṭbāq (the tongue touching the palate). Letters with both are strongest. Letters with only Istiʿlāʾ are medium.

children.title: Both Istiʿlāʾ and Iṭbāq — Strongest
children.description: ط ض ظ ق — the tongue both rises (Istiʿlāʾ) and touches the palate (Iṭbāq). This produces the heaviest sound.

children.title: Only Istiʿlāʾ — Medium
children.description: غ خ — the tongue rises but does not fully touch the palate. Heavy but less so.

children.title: Only Iṭbāq — Rare
children.description: ص — has Iṭbāq but not full Istiʿlāʾ in the classical sense. Still heavy.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of heavy and light letters in the Qur'an.

children.title: Always Heavy — قَالَ
children.description: The Qāf is always heavy. The Alif after it also becomes heavy.

children.title: Always Light — كَانَ
children.description: The Kāf is always light. The Alif after it stays light.

children.title: Rāʾ Heavy — رَحْمَة
children.description: Rāʾ with Fatḥah is heavy.

children.title: Rāʾ Light — فِرْعَوْن
children.description: Rāʾ with Kasrah (فِرْعَوْن) is light.
children.exampleTranslation: Wa idh najjaynākum min āli Firʿawn

children.title: Lām of Allah Heavy — قَالَ اللَّهُ
children.description: After Fatḥah, the Lām in اللَّهُ is heavy.

children.title: Lām of Allah Light — بِسْمِ اللَّهِ
children.description: After Kasrah, the Lām in اللَّهِ is light.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Making always-heavy letters light (e.g., saying ص lightly). 2. Making always-light letters heavy (e.g., saying ك heavily). 3. Not making Rāʾ heavy where it should be heavy. 4. Making Rāʾ heavy where it should be light. 5. Forgetting the Lām of Allah rules. 6. Making the Alif heavy after light letters. 7. Confusing Istiʿlāʾ with Iṭbāq.

children.title: Rāʾ Rules (Tafkhīm & Tarqīq of ر)
children.description: The letter ر is sometimes heavy (Mufakhkham) and sometimes light (Muraqqaq), depending on its vowel and the surrounding letters. This is one of the most nuanced rules in Tajweed.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Rāʾ (ر) is one of the letters that can be either heavy or light. The determination depends on its own vowel, the vowel before it, and the letter after it. Classical scholars define several cases for each type.

children.title: Cases Where Rāʾ is HEAVY (مفخمة)
children.description: Rāʾ is heavy in five main cases. All of them are based on the vowel of Rāʾ or the vowel before it.

children.title: 1. Rāʾ with Fatḥah (رَ)
children.description: Rāʾ with Fatḥah is always heavy. Example: رَحْمَة، رَبّ، رَسُول.

children.title: 2. Rāʾ with Ḍammah (رُ)
children.description: Rāʾ with Ḍammah is always heavy. Example: رُوح، رُسُل.

children.title: 3. Rāʾ Sākinah preceded by Fatḥah or Ḍammah
children.description: When Rāʾ has a Sukūn and the letter before it has a Fatḥah (ـَرْ) or Ḍammah (ـُرْ), the Rāʾ is heavy. Example: مَرْيَم (Maryam), قُرْآن (Qurʾān), وَالْأَرْض (wal-arḍ).

children.title: 4. Rāʾ Sākinah preceded by Kasrah but followed by a Heavy Letter
children.description: When Rāʾ is Sākinah, preceded by a Kasrah (ـِرْ), but followed by one of the seven heavy letters, the Rāʾ becomes heavy. Example: فِرْقَة (firqah) — followed by Qāf, so heavy. مِرْصَاد (mirṣād) — followed by Ṣād, so heavy.

children.title: 5. Rāʾ Sākinah at Stop preceded by Fatḥah, Ḍammah, or Alif
children.description: When you stop on a word ending in Rāʾ Sākinah that was preceded by a Fatḥah (ـَرْ) or Ḍammah (ـُرْ) or Alif (ـَارْ), the Rāʾ is heavy. Example: الْأَبْتَر (al-abtar), يَنْصُر (yanṣur), الدَّار (ad-dār).

children.title: Cases Where Rāʾ is LIGHT (مرققة)
children.description: Rāʾ is light in four main cases, mostly involving Kasrah before the Rāʾ or a Kasrah on the Rāʾ itself.

children.title: 1. Rāʾ with Kasrah (رِ)
children.description: Rāʾ with Kasrah is always light. Example: رِزْق، رِحْلَة، فِرْعَوْن.
children.exampleTranslation: Wa idh najjaynākum min āli Firʿawn

children.title: 2. Rāʾ Sākinah preceded by Kasrah (ـِرْ) and followed by a Light Letter
children.description: When Rāʾ is Sākinah, preceded by a Kasrah, and followed by a light letter, the Rāʾ is light. Example: فِرْعَوْن (Firʿawn) — followed by ʿAyn, light. شِرْك (shirk) — followed by Kāf, light.

children.title: 3. Rāʾ Sākinah at Stop preceded by Kasrah or Yāʾ Sākinah
children.description: When you stop on a word ending in Rāʾ Sākinah preceded by a Kasrah (ـِرْ) or a Yāʾ Sākinah (ـَيْرْ), the Rāʾ is light. Example: لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ (light Rāʾ at stop), خَيْر (light Rāʾ at stop).
children.example: لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَلْفِ شَهْرٍ

children.title: 4. Rāʾ in the word فِرْقٍ when followed by a light letter
children.description: Special case: the Rāʾ in فِرْقٍ in Sūrah Al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:63) — preceded by Kasrah and followed by Qāf, so heavy? Actually this is a special case where scholars differ. The majority rule: فِرْقٍ has a heavy Rāʾ because Qāf follows.
children.example: فَانفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples demonstrating Rāʾ heavy and light in real verses.

children.title: Heavy — رَبِّ (Rāʾ with Fatḥah)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ. The Rāʾ is heavy.

children.title: Heavy — رُوح (Rāʾ with Ḍammah)
children.description: Sūrah Al-Naḥl (16:102) — the Rāʾ in الرُّوح has a Ḍammah, so it's heavy.

children.title: Heavy — قُرْآن (Sākinah preceded by Ḍammah)
children.description: The Rāʾ in قُرْآن is Sākinah preceded by a Ḍammah, so it's heavy.

children.title: Light — فِرْعَوْن (Rāʾ with Kasrah)
children.description: The Rāʾ in فِرْعَوْن has a Kasrah, so it's light.
children.exampleTranslation: Wa idh najjaynākum min āli Firʿawn

children.title: Light — شِرْك (Sākinah preceded by Kasrah)
children.description: The Rāʾ in شِرْك is Sākinah preceded by Kasrah and followed by Kāf (light letter) — so light.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Making Rāʾ with Fatḥah light (should be heavy). 2. Making Rāʾ with Kasrah heavy (should be light). 3. Forgetting the rule about Sākinah Rāʾ preceded by Kasrah but followed by a heavy letter (should be heavy). 4. Inconsistent Rāʾ treatment in the same verse. 5. Not knowing that Rāʾ can change weight based on the following letter.

children.title: Lām of Allah (Tafkhīm & Tarqīq)
children.description: The Lām in the Name of Allah (اللَّهُ / اللَّهِ) is pronounced either heavy (Tafkhīm) or light (Tarqīq) depending on the vowel immediately before it.

children.title: Definition
children.description: The Name of Allah (اللَّهُ) contains a Lām that is doubled (with Shaddah). This Lām is pronounced either Tafkhīm (heavy) or Tarqīq (light), depending on the vowel of the letter that precedes the Name.

children.title: Heavy (Tafkhīm) — After Fatḥah or Ḍammah
children.description: When the letter immediately before the Name of Allah has a Fatḥah or Ḍammah, the Lām is heavy. Examples: قَالَ اللَّهُ (Fatḥah before), رَسُولُ اللَّهِ (Ḍammah before), عَبْدُ اللَّهِ (Ḍammah before).

children.title: After Fatḥah — قَالَ اللَّهُ
children.description: The Fatḥah in قَالَ is followed by the Name of Allah. The Lām is heavy. Sūrah Al-Māʾidah (5:116).

children.title: After Ḍammah — رَسُولُ اللَّهِ
children.description: The Ḍammah in رَسُولُ is followed by the Name of Allah. The Lām is heavy. Sūrah Al-Fatḥ (48:29).

children.title: Light (Tarqīq) — After Kasrah
children.description: When the letter immediately before the Name of Allah has a Kasrah, the Lām is light. Example: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ (Kasrah before). The light Lām sounds thinner and cleaner.

children.title: After Kasrah — بِسْمِ اللَّهِ
children.description: The Kasrah in بِسْمِ is followed by the Name of Allah. The Lām is light. Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1).

children.title: At the Beginning of Recitation
children.description: When starting recitation directly with the Name of Allah (اللَّهُ) without a preceding vowel, the Lām is HEAVY by default because the starting vowel is assumed to be a Fatḥah.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of the Lām of Allah heavy and light.

children.title: Heavy — قَالَ اللَّهُ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Māʾidah (5:116) — قَالَ اللَّهُ. Heavy Lām after Fatḥah.
children.example: وَإِذْ قَالَ اللَّهُ يَا عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ
children.exampleTranslation: Wa idh qālallāhu yā ʿĪsabna Maryam

children.title: Heavy — عَبْدُ اللَّهِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Jinn (72:19) — عَبْدُ اللَّهِ. Heavy Lām after Ḍammah.
children.example: وَأَنَّهُ لَمَّا قَامَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ يَدْعُوهُ
children.exampleTranslation: Wa annahu lammā qāma ʿabdullāhi yadʿūh

children.title: Light — بِسْمِ اللَّهِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — بِسْمِ اللَّهِ. Light Lām after Kasrah.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Making the Lām heavy after Kasrah (should be light). 2. Making the Lām light after Fatḥah or Ḍammah (should be heavy). 3. Not holding the Shaddah on the Lām (this is a separate rule but commonly missed). 4. Confusing the Lām of Allah with other Lām rules.

children.title: Lām Shamsiyyah & Qamariyyah
children.description: When the definite article ال is prefixed to a word, the Lām is either pronounced (Lām Qamariyyah — Lunar Lām) or silent (Lām Shamsiyyah — Solar Lām), depending on the first letter of the word.

children.title: Definition
children.description: The Arabic definite article ال (al-) has a Lām. When ال is prefixed to a word, the Lām is either pronounced or silent depending on the first letter of that word.

children.title: Lām Shamsiyyah (Solar Lām) — Silent
children.description: When the letter after ال is one of the 14 'Sun Letters,' the Lām is silent and the following letter takes a Shaddah. Called 'Shamsiyyah' because the word الشَّمْس (ash-shams — the sun) demonstrates this rule.

children.title: The 14 Sun Letters
children.description: The 14 letters that trigger Lām Shamsiyyah: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن. Mnemonic: طِبْ ثُمَّ صِلْ رَحِمًا تَفُزْ ضِفْ ذَا نِعَمْ * دَعْ سُوءَ ظَنٍّ زُرْ شَرِيفًا لِلْكَرَمْ.

children.title: Examples
children.description: الشَّمْس (ash-shams), الرَّحْمَن (ar-Raḥmān), الرَّحِيم (ar-Raḥīm), الدِّين (ad-dīn), الصِّرَاط (aṣ-ṣirāṭ), الطَّارِق (aṭ-ṭāriq).

children.title: Lām Qamariyyah (Lunar Lām) — Pronounced
children.description: When the letter after ال is one of the 14 'Moon Letters,' the Lām is pronounced clearly with a Sukūn (الْـ). Called 'Qamariyyah' because the word الْقَمَر (al-qamar — the moon) demonstrates this rule.

children.title: The 14 Moon Letters
children.description: The 14 letters that trigger Lām Qamariyyah: أ ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي. Mnemonic: اِبْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ.

children.title: Examples
children.description: الْقَمَر (al-qamar), الْحَمْد (al-ḥamd), الْكِتَاب (al-kitāb), الْمَلِك (al-malik), الْعَالَمِين (al-ʿālamīn), الْمَوْت (al-mawt).

children.title: In the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, the Lām Shamsiyyah is often written without the Sukūn (الـ), and the following letter carries a Shaddah (الشَّمْس). The Lām Qamariyyah is written with a Sukūn (الْقَمَر), which is the visual cue.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of both Lām types in the Qur'an.

children.title: Shamsiyyah — الشَّمْس
children.description: Sūrah Al-Shams (91:1) — وَالشَّمْسِ. Silent Lām.

children.title: Shamsiyyah — الرَّحْمَن
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — الرَّحْمَنِ. Silent Lām.

children.title: Qamariyyah — الْقَمَر
children.description: Sūrah Al-Qamar (54:1) — الْقَمَرُ. Pronounced Lām.

children.title: Qamariyyah — الْحَمْد
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — الْحَمْدُ. Pronounced Lām.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Pronouncing the Lām in a Shamsiyyah case (should be silent). 2. Not pronouncing the Lām in a Qamariyyah case (should be clear). 3. Not applying Shaddah to the Sun Letter after Lām Shamsiyyah. 4. Confusing the two categories. 5. Not knowing the two mnemonics.

categories.title: Waqf (Stopping) Rules
categories.description: Rules for stopping and continuing during Qur'anic recitation. The Muṣḥaf contains specific signs (علامات الوقف) that guide the reciter on where to stop, where to continue, and where either is permissible. Mastering Waqf preserves the meaning of the verse and beautifies the recitation.

children.title: Introduction to Waqf
children.description: Waqf (الوقف) means 'stopping' or 'pausing' during recitation. It is the act of cutting off the sound at the end of a word for a period of time, usually to take a breath, and then resuming. Waqf is important because stopping at the wrong place can change the meaning of the verse — sometimes drastically.

children.title: Definition (اللغة والاصطلاح)
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Waqf means to stop, halt, or pause. Technically (اصطلاحاً): Cutting off the sound at the end of a word for a period of time (usually to breathe), then resuming recitation. Waqf is different from Sakt (a brief pause without breath) and from Qaṭʿ (a complete break).

children.title: Why Waqf Matters
children.description: Stopping at the wrong place can: 1. Change the meaning of a verse (e.g., attributing an action to the wrong subject). 2. Break a grammatical connection between words. 3. Distort the intended message of the Qur'an. Stopping correctly preserves the meaning and beautifies the recitation. The classical scholars said: 'Al-Waqf is the ornament of the reciter.'

children.title: The Six Categories of Waqf Signs
children.description: The Muṣḥaf contains six main signs that indicate different types of Waqf. Each sign tells the reciter whether stopping is obligatory, permissible, forbidden, or preferred.
children.exampleTranslation: Mīm Jīm Lā Qalā Ṣallā Muʿānaqah

children.title: 1. Waqf Lāzim (م) — Must Stop
children.description: The sign 'م' (Mīm) means Waqf Lāzim — you MUST stop here. Continuing would distort the meaning.

children.title: 2. Waqf Jāʾiz (ج) — Permissible
children.description: The sign 'ج' (Jīm) means Waqf Jāʾiz — you may stop or continue, both are equally acceptable.

children.title: 3. Waqf Mamnūʿ (لا) — Do Not Stop
children.description: The sign 'لا' (Lā) means Waqf Mamnūʿ — you must NOT stop here. The meaning depends on the continuation.

children.title: 4. Waqf Aulā (قلى) — Better to Stop
children.description: The sign 'قلى' (Qalā) means Waqf Aulā — stopping is preferred, though continuing is permissible.

children.title: 5. Waqf Murakhkhaṣ (صلى) — Better to Continue
children.description: The sign 'صلى' (Ṣallā) means it is BETTER to continue, though stopping is permissible.

children.title: 6. Waqf Muʿānaqah (∴ ∴) — Stop at One Only
children.description: The triple-dot sign (∴) appears TWICE in the same verse. You must stop at ONE of them, but NOT at both. Stopping at both would break the meaning.

children.title: Waqf vs Sakt vs Qaṭʿ
children.description: Three related concepts: 1. Waqf (وقف): Stopping with breath, then resuming. 2. Sakt (سكت): A brief pause WITHOUT breath, then continuing. 3. Qaṭʿ (قطع): A complete break — the reciter stops and does not resume (or starts a new section). Each has its own place in Tajweed.

children.title: Waqf at Verse End (رأس الآية)
children.description: Stopping at the end of a verse is the most common form of Waqf. The Sunnah is to stop at the end of each verse, then continue with the next. Verse-end Waqf is called Waqf Tāmm (وقف تام — complete stop) when the meaning is complete.

children.title: Waqf and Madd Interaction
children.description: When you stop on a word with a Madd letter at the end, the Madd type can change. For example: Madd Munfaṣil (4-5 counts) becomes Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn (2/4/6) at stop. Madd Ṭabīʿī (2 counts) becomes Madd ʿĀriḍ li-Sukūn (2/4/6) at stop. Always check the Madd rule when stopping.

children.title: Waqf Lāzim (م) — Compulsory Stop
children.description: The sign 'م' in the Muṣḥaf indicates Waqf Lāzim — a COMPULSORY stop. The reciter MUST stop here. Continuing would distort the meaning of the verse, often by connecting words that should remain separate.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Lāzim means 'necessary' or 'obligatory.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A place in the Qur'an where stopping is COMPULSORY because continuing would: 1. Change the meaning of the verse. 2. Attribute a statement to the wrong speaker. 3. Break a grammatical relationship. The sign is a small 'م' (Mīm) above the word.

children.title: Rule
children.description: When you see 'م' in the Muṣḥaf: STOP. Take a breath, then continue. Do not try to skip the sign — the meaning depends on stopping.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Well-known Waqf Lāzim examples.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Zumar (39:9) — إِنَّمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ
children.description: The verse contains a Waqf Lāzim sign, indicating a required stop between two grammatical segments.
children.example: هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ وَالَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ
children.exampleTranslation: Hal yastawil-ladhīna yaʿlamūna walladhīna lā yaʿlamūn

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:2) — لَا رَيْبَ
children.description: Some Muṣḥafs place Waqf Lāzim here to clarify that 'the Book' is separate from 'no doubt.'

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:1) — إِنَّ اللَّهَ
children.description: Waqf Lāzim before the statement about Allah being watchful over you.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Ignoring the Waqf Lāzim sign and continuing — this distorts the meaning. 2. Stopping at a place where other signs apply instead of the Lāzim. 3. Confusing Waqf Lāzim with other Mawāḍiʿ (places). 4. Not knowing which Muṣḥafs use 'م' and which use 'ل' (some use Lām instead of Mīm).

children.title: Waqf Jāʾiz (ج) — Permissible Stop
children.description: The sign 'ج' in the Muṣḥaf indicates Waqf Jāʾiz — the reciter may either stop or continue. Both are equally acceptable and do not distort the meaning.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Jāʾiz means 'permissible' or 'allowed.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A place in the Qur'an where stopping and continuing are both equally acceptable. Neither choice distorts the meaning.

children.title: Rule
children.description: When you see 'ج' in the Muṣḥaf: you have a choice. Stop for a breath and continue, or read straight through. Both are correct.

children.title: Sub-types of Jāʾiz
children.description: Some Muṣḥafs use additional variants of the Jāʾiz sign: ج with no marks (fully permissible), or with a small letter above indicating preference. The basic rule is: 'ج' = both are equally allowed.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Waqf Jāʾiz in real verses.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ
children.description: Permissible to stop at الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ and continue with رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ, or to read straight through.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:2) — ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ
children.description: Permissible to stop after ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ and continue, or read straight through.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Treating every word break as Waqf Jāʾiz — only places marked with 'ج' are permissible for stopping. 2. Avoiding stops even when they improve breath control. 3. Stopping at random places without checking the sign.

children.title: Waqf Mamnūʿ (لا) — Forbidden Stop
children.description: The sign 'لا' in the Muṣḥaf indicates Waqf Mamnūʿ — stopping is FORBIDDEN. If you stop here, the meaning of the verse is broken or distorted. You must continue.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Mamnūʿ means 'forbidden' or 'prevented.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A place in the Qur'an where stopping is FORBIDDEN because the meaning depends on the continuation. Stopping here would distort the verse's message. The sign is 'لا' (Lā).

children.title: Rule
children.description: When you see 'لا' in the Muṣḥaf: DO NOT stop. Keep reciting. If you must stop for breath (e.g., during a long verse), continue from the same word — do not break the meaning.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Well-known Waqf Mamnūʿ examples.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:187) — لَا تُبَاشِرُوهُنَّ
children.description: In some verses, stopping mid-clause would break the connection between two parts of a single statement.
children.example: وَلَا تُبَاشِرُوهُنَّ وَأَنْتُمْ عَاكِفُونَ فِي الْمَسَاجِدِ
children.exampleTranslation: Wa lā tubāshirūhunna wa antum ʿākifūna fil-masājid

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:226) — لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ
children.description: Stopping between the subject and its predicate would break the grammatical structure.
children.example: لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ
children.exampleTranslation: Lilladhīna yuʾlūna min nisāʾihim tarabbuṣu arbaʿati ashhur

children.title: If You Need to Breathe
children.description: If the verse is long and you must stop for breath at a Mamnūʿ place: 1. Breathe quickly. 2. Resume from the SAME word, not the next. 3. Or, if you've already passed the word, go back to the beginning of the connected phrase and repeat. The meaning must not be broken.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Stopping at a Mamnūʿ sign because the verse is long. 2. Continuing past a Waqf Lāzim (which is the opposite sign). 3. Not knowing which sign is which. 4. Ignoring the sign entirely.

children.title: Waqf Aulā (قلى) — Better to Stop
children.description: The sign 'قلى' in the Muṣḥaf indicates Waqf Aulā — stopping is PREFERRED, though continuing is permissible. The reciter should stop if possible.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Aulā means 'better' or 'more appropriate.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A place where stopping is PREFERRED but not compulsory. The meaning is complete if you stop; continuing would still be correct but less ideal.

children.title: Rule
children.description: When you see 'قلى': Stop if you can. If you're out of breath and need to continue, continuing is permissible. The preference is to stop.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Waqf Aulā.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:21) — يَا أَيُّهَا
children.description: Preference to stop after يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ before اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمْ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:1) — يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ
children.description: Stopping after the call is preferred before the command.

children.title: Aulā vs Jāʾiz
children.description: Both allow stopping. The difference: Jāʾiz = no preference (stopping and continuing are equal). Aulā = stopping is PREFERRED. Choose to stop when you see قلى.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Confusing قلى with ج (both look similar to beginners). 2. Not stopping when قلى appears (missing the preference). 3. Treating it like a Mamnūʿ (which forbids stopping).

children.title: Waqf Murakhkhaṣ (صلى) — Better to Continue
children.description: The sign 'صلى' in the Muṣḥaf indicates that CONTINUING is PREFERRED, though stopping is permissible. The reciter should continue if possible.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Murakhkhaṣ means 'licensed' or 'permitted.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A place where CONTINUING is PREFERRED. Stopping is permitted but not ideal. The sign 'صلى' is used in some Muṣḥafs; others use a different marker.

children.title: Rule
children.description: When you see 'صلى': continue if you can. Stopping is allowed but less preferred. The meaning flows better when you continue.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Waqf Murakhkhaṣ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — الرَّحْمَنِ
children.description: Some Muṣḥafs mark a preference to continue from الرَّحْمَنِ to الرَّحِيمِ rather than stop.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Confusing 'صلى' with 'قلى' — they look similar but mean opposite preferences. 2. Stopping when the sign says to continue. 3. Not knowing the sign at all.

children.title: Waqf Muʿānaqah (∴ ∴) — Stop at One Only
children.description: The triple-dot sign (∴) appears TWICE in the same verse (or sometimes more). The rule is: stop at ONE of them, but NOT at both. Stopping at both breaks the meaning. Called 'Muʿānaqah' (embracing) because the two stops 'embrace' each other — you choose one.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Muʿānaqah means 'embracing' or 'hugging.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Two or three dots placed at different points in the same verse. The reciter chooses ONE of them to stop at, but NOT both. Stopping at both would break the meaning or repeat what should be said once.

children.title: Rule
children.description: When you see two or more sets of dots (∴) in the same verse: 1. Choose ONE place to stop. 2. Do NOT stop at the other. 3. Complete the verse from your chosen stop. The choice is yours — pick whichever gives you a cleaner breath.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Well-known Waqf Muʿānaqah examples.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:2) — ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ
children.description: Two dots mark alternative stopping points: after ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ or after لَا رَيْبَ. Stop at one, not both.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nūr (24:35) — اللَّهُ نُورُ السَّمَاوَاتِ
children.description: Multiple stopping points marked with dots. Choose one.

children.title: When You Need to Breathe Twice
children.description: If the verse is very long and you need two breaths: choose one of the Muʿānaqah stops as your first breath, and the other as your second. But you must not stop at BOTH places in sequence without a valid reason. In practice, pick one — usually the longer one.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Stopping at BOTH Muʿānaqah dots (this breaks the meaning). 2. Not stopping at either (missing the choice entirely). 3. Confusing the triple-dot with other signs. 4. Stopping at the first dot every time without considering the meaning.

children.title: Waqf at Verse Ends (رأس الآية)
children.description: Stopping at the end of each verse is a Sunnah and is recommended. The end-of-verse mark is a small circle (۝) with the verse number inside. Waqf Tāmm (وقف تام) means a complete stop — the meaning is fully independent of the next verse.

children.title: Definition
children.description: The end of each verse is marked with a circle (۝). Stopping here is a Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ and helps preserve the verse's meaning. Waqf Tāmm (complete Waqf) is when the verse ends a complete thought independent of the next verse.

children.title: Sunnah of Stopping at Verse Ends
children.description: The Prophet ﷺ used to stop at the end of each verse. The classical scholars recommend this. It preserves the integrity of each verse and provides natural breathing points.

children.title: Three Types of Verse-End Waqf
children.description: Based on the relationship between the verse you're stopping at and the next verse: 1. Waqf Tāmm (تام): Complete — no grammatical or semantic link to next verse. 2. Waqf Kāfī (كافي): Sufficient — a link exists but stopping is still valid. 3. Waqf Ḥasan (حسن): Good — a link exists; better to continue but stopping is allowed.

children.title: Waqf Tāmm (تام) — Complete
children.description: The verse is a complete thought. No grammatical or semantic connection to the next verse. Stopping here is preferred.

children.title: Waqf Kāfī (كافي) — Sufficient
children.description: A weak grammatical link exists between this verse and the next. Stopping is still valid and common.

children.title: Waqf Ḥasan (حسن) — Good
children.description: A stronger connection exists to the next verse. Stopping is allowed but continuing is preferred.

children.title: Waqf Qabīḥ (قبيح) — Ugly Stop (Avoid)
children.description: Stopping here distorts the meaning — often separating words that should be together. Example: stopping after لَا in لَا إِلَٰهَ. Never do this.

children.title: Verse-End Sign in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: The verse-end mark is a small circle (۝) containing the verse number. In some Muṣḥafs it's called 'Rās al-Āyah' (رأس الآية — head of the verse). Every printed Muṣḥaf uses it consistently.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Not stopping at verse ends (this breaks the Sunnah). 2. Stopping at other places instead. 3. Not knowing the difference between Tāmm, Kāfī, and Ḥasan. 4. Racing through verses to finish faster.

children.title: Summary of Waqf Signs
children.description: A quick reference to all Waqf signs and their meanings.

children.title: م — Waqf Lāzim (Must Stop)
children.description: Compulsory stop. Continuing distorts the meaning.

children.title: ج — Waqf Jāʾiz (Permissible)
children.description: Stopping or continuing — both are acceptable.

children.title: لا — Waqf Mamnūʿ (Do Not Stop)
children.description: Stopping is forbidden. Continuing is required.

children.title: قلى — Waqf Aulā (Better to Stop)
children.description: Stopping is preferred. Continuing is permissible.

children.title: صلى — Waqf Murakhkhaṣ (Better to Continue)
children.description: Continuing is preferred. Stopping is permissible.

children.title: ∴ ∴ — Waqf Muʿānaqah (Stop at One)
children.description: Two dots in the same verse. Stop at one, not both.

children.title: ۝ — Verse End (Waqf Tāmm)
children.description: End of verse. Stopping is a Sunnah.

children.title: Additional Waqf Topics
children.description: Related topics that affect Waqf decisions.

children.title: Sakt (سكت) — Brief Pause Without Breath
children.description: A Sakt is a brief pause (usually 1 count) WITHOUT taking a breath, followed by resumption. Unlike Waqf, Sakt does not involve breathing. Sakt occurs in four specific places in the Qur'an (e.g., Sūrah Al-Kahf 18:1-2).

children.title: Ibtidāʾ — Detailed Starting Rules
children.description: Ibtidāʾ means 'starting' — the rules for where to begin recitation after stopping. Just as Waqf governs where to stop, Ibtidāʾ governs where to start. Starting in the wrong place can also distort the meaning.

children.title: The Rule
children.description: When starting recitation (whether at the beginning of a Sūrah or after a Waqf), choose a point that: 1. Makes grammatical sense. 2. Preserves the meaning. 3. Does not split essential phrases. 4. Follows the Basmalah (if starting a new Sūrah).

children.title: Types of Ibtidāʾ
children.description: Ibtidāʾ is classified similarly to Waqf: 1. Ibtidāʾ Tāmm — complete start. 2. Ibtidāʾ Kāfī — sufficient start. 3. Ibtidāʾ Ḥasan — good start. 4. Ibtidāʾ Qabīḥ — ugly start (distorts meaning). Avoid Qabīḥ.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Good: starting at the beginning of a verse (e.g., اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ). Bad: starting with أَنْعَمْتَ without الَّذِينَ — distorts the meaning.

children.title: Breath Control During Recitation
children.description: Waqf is often dictated by breath. The reciter should plan their stops to align with the Waqf signs and manage their breathing. If a breath is needed at a Mamnūʿ place, the reciter resumes from the same word or repeats the connected phrase.

categories.title: Makhārij al-Ḥurūf (Articulation Points)
categories.description: The science of where each Arabic letter originates — the 17 specific articulation points across 5 main areas: Al-Jawf (empty space), Al-Ḥalq (throat), Al-Lisān (tongue), Al-Shafatān (lips), and Al-Khayshūm (nasal cavity). Mastering Makhārij is the foundation of correct Tajweed.

children.title: Introduction to Makhārij
children.description: Makhārij (singular: Makhraj) means 'exit' or 'place of emission.' It refers to the specific point in the mouth, throat, or nose where each Arabic letter is produced. Classical scholars identified 17 Makhārij grouped into 5 main areas.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Makhraj means 'the place of exit.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): The specific point of articulation where a letter is produced, or the point where the sound of a letter is distinguished from other letters.

children.title: The Five Main Areas
children.description: All 17 Makhārij fall into 5 main areas: 1. Al-Jawf (الجوف) — the empty space in the mouth and throat (1 Makhraj). 2. Al-Ḥalq (الحلق) — the throat (3 Makhārij). 3. Al-Lisān (اللسان) — the tongue (10 Makhārij). 4. Al-Shafatān (الشفتان) — the two lips (2 Makhārij). 5. Al-Khayshūm (الخيشوم) — the nasal cavity (1 Makhraj).

children.title: Why Makhārij Matter
children.description: Pronouncing a letter from the wrong Makhraj changes its sound — sometimes to a different letter entirely, which can change the meaning. Example: ق and ك are both from the tongue but different Makhārij. Mixing them turns قَلْب (qalb — heart) into كَلْب (kalb — dog).

children.title: 1. Al-Jawf (الجوف) — The Empty Space
children.description: The empty space in the mouth and throat where air flows freely without obstruction. This is where the three Madd letters originate — they have no specific contact point; they simply flow through the open cavity.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Al-Jawf literally means 'the cavity' or 'the hollow.' It refers to the empty space in the mouth and throat through which air passes freely. This is the ONLY Makhraj that has no contact point — the letters emerge from the open space.

children.title: The Three Jawf Letters
children.description: The three letters that emerge from Al-Jawf are: ا (Alif), و (Wāw Sākinah preceded by Ḍammah), ي (Yā Sākinah preceded by Kasrah). These are the three Madd letters — they emerge from the empty space and are elongated.

children.title: Alif (ا)
children.description: Alif is ALWAYS Sākinah and preceded by a Fatḥah. Example: قَالَ (qāla).

children.title: Wāw (و) — Madd
children.description: Wāw Sākinah preceded by a Ḍammah. Example: يَقُولُ (yaqūlu).

children.title: Yā (ي) — Madd
children.description: Yā Sākinah preceded by a Kasrah. Example: قِيلَ (qīla).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Examples of the three Jawf letters in the Qur'an.

children.title: Alif — الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ
children.description: The Alif in رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ is a Jawf letter — it emerges from the empty space.

children.title: Wāw — نَسْتَعِينُ
children.description: The Wāw in يَعْبُدُ? No — the Wāw in نَسْتَعِينُ? Actually نَسْتَعِينُ has a Yā Madd. The Wāw example: يَقُولُ (yaqūlu) in Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8).

children.title: Yā — الرَّحِيمِ
children.description: The Yā in الرَّحِيمِ is a Jawf letter — Sākinah preceded by Kasrah.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Pronouncing the Madd letters from the throat or tongue instead of the empty space. 2. Mixing Madd letters with their non-Madd counterparts (e.g., a voweled و is not a Jawf letter). 3. Not elongating the Madd letters fully. 4. Confusing Alif with Hamza (which comes from the throat).

children.title: 2. Al-Ḥalq (الحلق) — The Throat
children.description: The throat contains THREE distinct Makhārij, each producing two letters. Moving from the deepest part of the throat outward to the mouth: Aqṣā al-Ḥalq (deepest), Wasaṭ al-Ḥalq (middle), and Adnā al-Ḥalq (nearest to the mouth).
children.example: أ ه ع ح غ خ
children.exampleTranslation: Hamza, Hā, ʿAyn, Ḥā, Ghayn, Khā

children.title: Definition
children.description: Al-Ḥalq is the throat — a passage extending from the chest up to the mouth. It contains three articulation points, producing six letters total (two from each point).

children.title: Aqṣā al-Ḥalq (أقصى الحلق) — Deepest Throat
children.description: The deepest part of the throat, closest to the chest. Two letters emerge from here: ء (Hamza) and ه (Hā).

children.title: Hamza (ء)
children.description: A complete closure of the throat at the deepest point, then release. Example: أَحَد (aḥad).

children.title: Hā (ه)
children.description: A soft breath from the deepest throat without full closure. Example: هُوَ (huwa), هَادَ (hāda).

children.title: Wasaṭ al-Ḥalq (وسط الحلق) — Middle Throat
children.description: The middle part of the throat. Two letters emerge from here: ع (ʿAyn) and ح (Ḥā).

children.title: ʿAyn (ع)
children.description: A constriction at the middle of the throat. Example: عَبْد (ʿabd), عِلْم (ʿilm).

children.title: Ḥā (ح)
children.description: A soft, whispered constriction at the middle throat. Example: حَمْد (ḥamd), حَقّ (ḥaqq).

children.title: Adnā al-Ḥalq (أدنى الحلق) — Nearest Throat
children.description: The part of the throat closest to the mouth. Two letters emerge from here: غ (Ghayn) and خ (Khā).

children.title: Ghayn (غ)
children.description: A voiced constriction at the nearest throat. Example: غَفُور (ghafūr), غَيْب (ghayb).

children.title: Khā (خ)
children.description: A whispered constriction at the nearest throat. Example: خَيْر (khayr), خَلَقَ (khalaqa).

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of each throat letter in real verses.
children.example: أ ه ع ح غ خ
children.exampleTranslation: Hamza, Hā, ʿAyn, Ḥā, Ghayn, Khā

children.title: Hamza — أَحَد
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — أَحَدٌ. The Hamza comes from the deepest throat.

children.title: Hā — هُوَ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — هُوَ. The Hā comes from the deepest throat.

children.title: ʿAyn — نَعْبُدُ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:5) — نَعْبُدُ. The ʿAyn comes from the middle throat.

children.title: Ḥā — الْحَمْدُ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — الْحَمْدُ. The Ḥā comes from the middle throat.

children.title: Ghayn — غَفُور
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:173) — غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ. The Ghayn comes from the nearest throat.

children.title: Khā — خَبِير
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:234) — خَبِيرٌ. The Khā comes from the nearest throat.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Mixing Ḥā (ح) with Hā (ه) — very common for non-Arabic speakers. 2. Mixing ʿAyn (ع) with Hamza (ء). 3. Mixing Ghayn (غ) with Khā (خ). 4. Pronouncing all throat letters from the same point instead of their distinct points. 5. Using the mouth (not throat) to produce throat letters.
children.example: أ ه ع ح غ خ
children.exampleTranslation: Hamza, Hā, ʿAyn, Ḥā, Ghayn, Khā

children.title: 3. Al-Lisān (اللسان) — The Tongue
children.description: The tongue is the source of TEN articulation points — the most in the mouth. It produces 18 Arabic letters. The tongue is divided into sections: deepest (closest to throat), middle, edges, and tip.
children.example: ق ك ج ش ي ض ل ن ر ط د ت ص ز س ظ ذ ث

children.title: Definition
children.description: Al-Lisān is the tongue. It has 10 Makhārij distributed across its deepest part, middle, edges, and tip. The tongue is the most versatile articulation organ — 18 letters emerge from it.

children.title: Deepest Tongue (أقصى اللسان) — ق ك
children.description: The deepest part of the tongue (near the throat) against the soft palate. Two letters emerge here: ق (Qāf) and ك (Kāf).

children.title: Qāf (ق)
children.description: Deepest part of the tongue against the soft palate — slightly deeper than Kāf. Example: قَالَ (qāla), قَلْب (qalb).

children.title: Kāf (ك)
children.description: Slightly forward of Qāf, still on the deepest tongue. Example: كِتَاب (kitāb), كَانَ (kāna).

children.title: Middle Tongue (وسط اللسان) — ج ش ي
children.description: The middle of the tongue against the hard palate. Three letters emerge here: ج (Jīm), ش (Shīn), ي (Yā — non-Madd).

children.title: Jīm (ج)
children.description: Middle tongue against the hard palate. Example: جَعَلَ (jaʿala), الْجَنَّة (al-jannah).

children.title: Shīn (ش)
children.description: Middle tongue against the hard palate, producing a hissing sound. Example: شَمْس (shams), شَيْء (shayʾ).

children.title: Yā (ي) — Non-Madd
children.description: Middle tongue when Yā has a vowel (يَ، يِ، يُ). Note: Yā Sākinah with Kasrah before is a Jawf letter, not a Makhraj letter.

children.title: Tongue Edges (حافة اللسان) — ض
children.description: The edge of the tongue (usually the left edge) against the upper molars and premolars. One letter emerges here — and only here: ض (Ḍād). This is the most unique Makhraj in Arabic.

children.title: Ḍād (ض)
children.description: The left edge of the tongue against the upper molars. Arabic is called 'the language of Ḍād' (لغة الضاد) because no other language has this unique letter. Example: ضَلَّ (ḍalla), الْأَرْض (al-arḍ).

children.title: Tongue Edge Near Tip (حافة اللسان قريباً من طرفه) — ل
children.description: The front edge of the tongue (near the tip) against the upper gums. One letter emerges here: ل (Lām).

children.title: Lām (ل)
children.description: The front edge of the tongue against the upper gums above the front teeth. Example: لَهُ (lahu), اللَّهُ (Allāhu).

children.title: Tongue Tip (طرف اللسان) — 11 Letters
children.description: The tip of the tongue is used for many letters, distributed across five sub-points: against the upper front teeth (ث ذ ظ), against the gums behind the front teeth (ن ر), against the upper front teeth (ط د ت), between the teeth (ص ز س), and against the tips of the upper front teeth (ظ ذ ث).
children.example: ن ر ط د ت ص ز س ظ ذ ث
children.exampleTranslation: Nūn, Rā, Ṭā, Dāl, Tā, Ṣād, Zāy, Sīn, Ẓā, Dhāl, Thā

children.title: Nūn (ن) — Tongue Tip + Gums
children.description: Tongue tip against the gums behind the upper front teeth, with Ghunnah. Example: نُور (nūr), نَعْبُدُ (naʿbudu).

children.title: Rā (ر) — Tongue Tip + Gums
children.description: Tongue tip against the gums behind the upper front teeth. It has slight vibration (Takrīr). Example: رَبّ (rabb), رَحْمَة (raḥmah).

children.title: Ṭā (ط) — Tongue Tip + Upper Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the roots of the upper front teeth, heavy letter. Example: طَارِق (ṭāriq), طَيِّب (ṭayyib).

children.title: Dāl (د) — Tongue Tip + Upper Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the roots of the upper front teeth, lighter than Ṭā. Example: دِين (dīn), دَار (dār).

children.title: Tā (ت) — Tongue Tip + Upper Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the roots of the upper front teeth, lightest of the ط د ت group. Example: تَوَّاب (tawwāb), تَقْوَى (taqwā).

children.title: Ṣād (ص) — Tongue Tip + Lower Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the tips of the lower front teeth, heavy letter with whistling sound. Example: صِرَاط (ṣirāṭ), صَلَاة (ṣalāh).

children.title: Zāy (ز) — Tongue Tip + Lower Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the tips of the lower front teeth, light whistling sound. Example: زَكَاة (zakāh), زَيْتُون (zaytūn).

children.title: Sīn (س) — Tongue Tip + Lower Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the tips of the lower front teeth, lightest whistling sound. Example: سَمِيع (samīʿ), سَلَام (salām).

children.title: Ẓā (ظ) — Tongue Tip + Upper Teeth (Emphatic)
children.description: Tongue tip against the tips of the upper front teeth, heavy emphatic letter. Example: ظُلْم (ẓulm), ظَهَرَ (ẓahara).

children.title: Dhāl (ذ) — Tongue Tip + Upper Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the tips of the upper front teeth, light. Example: ذِكْر (dhikr), ذَلِكَ (dhālika).

children.title: Thā (ث) — Tongue Tip + Upper Teeth
children.description: Tongue tip against the tips of the upper front teeth, light with a lisping sound. Example: ثَوَاب (thawāb), ثَلَاثَة (thalātha).

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of tongue letters from each sub-point in real verses.
children.example: ق ك ج ش ي ض ل ن ر ط د ت ص ز س ظ ذ ث

children.title: Qāf — قُلْ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — قُلْ. Qāf from the deepest tongue.

children.title: Kāf — كِتَاب
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:2) — الْكِتَابُ. Kāf from the deepest tongue.

children.title: Jīm — جَعَلَ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fajr (89:6) — جَعَلَ? Actually جَعَلَ appears in many verses. The Jīm from middle tongue.

children.title: Shīn — الشَّمْس
children.description: Sūrah Al-Shams (91:1) — وَالشَّمْسِ. Shīn from middle tongue.

children.title: Ḍād — الضَّالِّينَ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الضَّالِّينَ. Ḍād from the tongue edge — unique to Arabic.

children.title: Lām — لِلَّهِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — لِلَّهِ. Lām from the tongue edge near the tip.

children.title: Nūn — نَعْبُدُ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:5) — نَعْبُدُ. Nūn from tongue tip + gums.

children.title: Rā — رَبِّ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — رَبِّ. Rā from tongue tip + gums.

children.title: Sīn — السَّلَام
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ḥashr (59:23) — السَّلَامُ. Sīn from tongue tip + lower teeth.
children.example: هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ

children.title: Ṣād — الصِّرَاط
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:6) — الصِّرَاطَ. Ṣād from tongue tip + lower teeth.

children.title: Ẓā — ظُلْم
children.description: Sūrah Luqmān (31:13) — لَظُلْمٌ. Ẓā from tongue tip + upper teeth (emphatic).

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Mixing ق and ك (both from deepest tongue but different points). 2. Mixing ط and ت (both tongue tip but different emphasis). 3. Mixing ص and س (both tongue tip + lower teeth but different emphasis). 4. Mixing ظ and ذ (both tongue tip + upper teeth but different emphasis). 5. Not pronouncing Ḍād from the tongue edge (a very common error). 6. Confusing ن and ر. 7. Not producing the Rā with proper vibration.
children.example: ق ك ط ت ص س ظ ذ ض ن ر

children.title: 4. Al-Shafatān (الشفتان) — The Two Lips
children.description: The two lips (upper and lower) produce FOUR Arabic letters across TWO Makhārij: ف (Fā) from the lower lip against the upper front teeth, and ب م و from the two lips together.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Al-Shafatān literally means 'the two lips.' Two Makhārij are located here, producing four letters total (ف and the group ب م و).

children.title: Fāʾ (ف) — Lower Lip + Upper Teeth
children.description: The lower lip against the tips of the upper front teeth. One letter emerges here: ف (Fā).

children.title: Fā — Detail
children.description: The inside of the lower lip touches the tips of the upper front teeth, allowing air to pass through creating the 'f' sound. Example: فَاتِحَة (fātiḥah), فِي (fī).

children.title: Bāʾ (ب), Mīm (م), Wāw (و) — Two Lips Together
children.description: The two lips together produce three letters: ب (Bā), م (Mīm), and و (Wāw — non-Madd, i.e., voweled or with Sukūn and not preceded by Ḍammah).

children.title: Bāʾ (ب)
children.description: The two lips fully close, then release with a distinct sound. Example: بَاب (bāb), بَيْت (bayt).

children.title: Mīm (م)
children.description: The two lips close, and the sound emerges from the nose with Ghunnah. Example: مَالِك (mālik), مُحَمَّد (Muḥammad).

children.title: Wāw (و) — Non-Madd
children.description: The two lips round and slightly protrude when Wāw has a vowel (وَ، وِ، وُ) or is Sākinah with a Fatḥah before (Līn). Not to be confused with Wāw Madd (which is Jawf). Example: وَاحِد (wāḥid), وَعْد (waʿd).

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of lip letters in real verses.

children.title: Fā — فَاتِحَة
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — the Fā in the title. From lower lip + upper teeth.

children.title: Bā — بِسْمِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — بِسْمِ. From the two lips.

children.title: Mīm — مَالِكِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:4) — مَالِكِ. From the two lips with Ghunnah.

children.title: Wāw — وَاحِد
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:163) — وَاحِدٌ. Wāw with Fatḥah — from the two lips.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Pronouncing Fā from the throat instead of the lips. 2. Confusing Fā and Bā (both involve lips but Fā uses teeth). 3. Pronouncing Wāw Madd from the lips instead of Al-Jawf. 4. Not producing Ghunnah with Mīm. 5. Not fully closing the lips for Bā and Mīm.

children.title: 5. Al-Khayshūm (الخيشوم) — The Nasal Cavity
children.description: The nasal cavity at the back of the nose. This is where Ghunnah (nasalization) emerges. It is the ONLY Makhraj for Ghunnah — no letter originates here, but the nasal sound of Mīm and Nūn does.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Al-Khayshūm is the nasal cavity — the passage at the back of the nose. It is a Makhraj for the Ghunnah sound that accompanies Mīm and Nūn. It does not produce any letter itself; it only resonates.

children.title: Ghunnah from Al-Khayshūm
children.description: When Mīm or Nūn carries Ghunnah (either Mushaddadah, concealed, merged, or converted), the sound resonates in the nasal cavity for 2 counts. This is the Makhraj of Ghunnah.

children.title: The Two Ghunnah Letters
children.description: The two letters that produce Ghunnah are م (Mīm) and ن (Nūn). Both have their primary Makhraj elsewhere (Mīm from the lips, Nūn from the tongue tip), but their Ghunnah emerges from Al-Khayshūm.

children.title: Mīm (م) — Ghunnah from Nose
children.description: Mīm's primary Makhraj is the lips; its Ghunnah comes from the nose. Example: إِنَّ، ثُمَّ.

children.title: Nūn (ن) — Ghunnah from Nose
children.description: Nūn's primary Makhraj is the tongue tip; its Ghunnah comes from the nose. Example: إِنَّ، إِنَّا.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Ghunnah from Al-Khayshūm.

children.title: Nūn with Shaddah — إِنَّ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — إِنَّ. The Nūn's Ghunnah resonates in the nose.

children.title: Mīm with Shaddah — ثُمَّ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:28) — ثُمَّ. The Mīm's Ghunnah resonates in the nose.

children.title: Ikhfāʾ — مِنْ قَبْلِ
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:25) — مِنْ قَبْلِ. The Nūn is concealed with Ghunnah from the nose.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Not producing Ghunnah from the nose at all (very common). 2. Producing Ghunnah from the throat or mouth instead. 3. Holding Ghunnah for the wrong length. 4. Confusing the nasal sound with a vowel sound. 5. Not producing Ghunnah when it's required (Mushaddadah, Ikhfāʾ, Idghām, Iqlāb).

children.title: Summary of the 17 Makhārij
children.description: A quick reference table of all 17 articulation points.

children.title: Al-Jawf — 1 Makhraj
children.description: The empty space. Letters: ا و ي (Madd letters). Total: 3 letters.

children.title: Aqṣā al-Ḥalq — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Deepest throat. Letters: ء ه. Total: 2 letters.

children.title: Wasaṭ al-Ḥalq — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Middle throat. Letters: ع ح. Total: 2 letters.

children.title: Adnā al-Ḥalq — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Nearest throat. Letters: غ خ. Total: 2 letters.

children.title: Aqṣā al-Lisān — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Deepest tongue. Letters: ق ك. Total: 2 letters.

children.title: Wasaṭ al-Lisān — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Middle tongue. Letters: ج ش ي. Total: 3 letters.

children.title: Ḥāfat al-Lisān — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Tongue edge. Letter: ض. Total: 1 letter.

children.title: Ḥāfat al-Lisān near tip — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Tongue edge near tip. Letter: ل. Total: 1 letter.

children.title: Ṭaraf al-Lisān + Gums — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Tongue tip against gums. Letters: ن ر. Total: 2 letters.

children.title: Ṭaraf al-Lisān + Upper Teeth (roots) — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Tongue tip against upper teeth roots. Letters: ط د ت. Total: 3 letters.

children.title: Ṭaraf al-Lisān + Lower Teeth — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Tongue tip against lower teeth tips. Letters: ص ز س. Total: 3 letters.

children.title: Ṭaraf al-Lisān + Upper Teeth (tips) — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Tongue tip against upper teeth tips. Letters: ظ ذ ث. Total: 3 letters.

children.title: Al-Shafatān (Fā) — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Lower lip + upper teeth. Letter: ف. Total: 1 letter.

children.title: Al-Shafatān (Bā-Mīm-Wāw) — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Two lips together. Letters: ب م و. Total: 3 letters.

children.title: Al-Khayshūm — 1 Makhraj
children.description: Nasal cavity. Produces Ghunnah for م and ن.

children.title: Classical Mnemonics
children.description: Classical scholars used mnemonics to help memorize the Makhārij and their letters.

children.title: Throat Letters — أ خ ه ع ح غ
children.description: The six throat letters collected in: أَخِي هَاكَ عِلْمًا حَازَهُ غَيْرُ خَاسِرٍ (Akhī hāka ʿilman ḥāzahu ghayru khāsir).
children.example: أ خ ه ع ح غ
children.exampleTranslation: Hamza, Khā, Hā, ʿAyn, Ḥā, Ghayn

children.title: Tongue Letters — Various Groups
children.description: Groups on the tongue: ق ك, ج ش ي, ض, ل, ن ر, ط د ت, ص ز س, ظ ذ ث.
children.example: ق ك ج ش ي ض ل ن ر ط د ت ص ز س ظ ذ ث

children.title: Lip Letters — ف ب م و
children.description: The four lip letters: ف ب م و. Fā uses lower lip + upper teeth; ب م و use both lips.

children.title: Most Common Makhraj Mistakes
children.description: The most common mistakes made by non-Arabic speakers and how to fix them.

children.title: Mixing Hā (ه) and Ḥā (ح)
children.description: Hā comes from the deepest throat (breath only); Ḥā from the middle throat (constriction). Practice: هَادَ (hāda) vs. حَادَ (ḥāda).

children.title: Mixing ʿAyn (ع) and Hamza (ء)
children.description: ʿAyn is a middle-throat constriction; Hamza is a deep-throat closure. Practice: عَبْد (ʿabd) vs. أَبْد — the latter doesn't exist in Arabic but the sound difference is clear.

children.title: Mixing Ghayn (غ) and Khā (خ)
children.description: Both from nearest throat, but Ghayn is voiced and Khā is whispered. Practice: غَفُور (ghafūr) vs. خَفُور (khafūr).

children.title: Mixing Qāf (ق) and Kāf (ك)
children.description: Both from deepest tongue, but Qāf is slightly deeper and heavier. Practice: قَلْب (qalb — heart) vs. كَلْب (kalb — dog).

children.title: Mixing Ḍād (ض) and Dhāl (ذ)
children.description: Ḍād comes from the tongue edge; Dhāl from the tongue tip against teeth. Practice: ضَلَّ (ḍalla) vs. ذَلَّ (dhalla).

children.title: Mixing Ḍād (ض) and Ẓā (ظ)
children.description: Ḍād from the tongue edge; Ẓā from the tongue tip. Practice: ضَلَّ (ḍalla) vs. ظَلَّ (ẓalla).

children.title: Mixing Ṣād (ص) and Sīn (س)
children.description: Both from tongue tip + lower teeth; Ṣād is emphatic (heavy), Sīn is light. Practice: صَيْف (ṣayf — summer) vs. سَيْف (sayf — sword).

children.title: Mixing ط (Ṭā) and ت (Tā)
children.description: Both from tongue tip + upper teeth; Ṭā is emphatic (heavy), Tā is light. Practice: طَيْن (ṭayn — clay) vs. تَيْن (tayn).

children.title: Mixing ث (Thā) and ذ (Dhāl)
children.description: Both from tongue tip + upper teeth; Thā is whispered, Dhāl is voiced. Practice: ثَمَّ (thamma) vs. ذَمَّ (dhamma).

categories.title: Ṣifāt al-Ḥurūf (Characteristics of Letters)
categories.description: The science of how each Arabic letter sounds — its permanent characteristics (Ṣifāt). Divided into two groups: Ṣifāt with opposites (الصفات المتضادة) and Ṣifāt without opposites (الصفات غير المتضادة). These distinguish letters that share the same Makhraj.

children.title: Introduction to Ṣifāt
children.description: Ṣifāt (singular: Ṣifah) means 'characteristics' or 'attributes.' They describe HOW a letter sounds when pronounced from its Makhraj. Two letters can share the same Makhraj but sound different because of their Ṣifāt. Example: ط and ت share a Makhraj but ط is heavy and ت is light.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Ṣifah means 'attribute' or 'description.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): The quality or characteristic that describes how a letter is pronounced when it emerges from its Makhraj — such as whether the sound is whispered or voiced, strong or soft, heavy or light.

children.title: The Two Groups of Ṣifāt
children.description: Ṣifāt are divided into two main groups: 1. Ṣifāt Mutāḍādah (صفات متضادة) — Ṣifāt WITH opposites. These come in pairs: if a letter has one, it lacks the opposite. 2. Ṣifāt Ghayr Mutāḍādah (صفات غير متضادة) — Ṣifāt WITHOUT opposites. These stand alone with no contrasting quality.

children.title: Why Ṣifāt Matter
children.description: Two letters might share the same Makhraj (like ط and ت) but sound completely different because of their Ṣifāt. Mastering Ṣifāt ensures you pronounce each letter distinctly, which is essential for correct recitation and preventing changes in meaning.

children.title: The Five Pairs (With Opposites)
children.description: The Ṣifāt with opposites come in five pairs: 1. Hams / Jahr (whispered / voiced). 2. Shiddah / Rakhāwah (strong / soft, with intermediate Tawassuṭ). 3. Istiʿlāʾ / Istifāl (elevated / lowered). 4. Iṭbāq / Infitāḥ (closed / open). 5. Idhlāq / Iṣmāt (fluent / firm).
children.example: الهمس والجهر الشدة والرخاوة الاستعلاء والاستفال الإطباق والانفتاح الإذلاق والإصمات

children.title: Ṣifāt with Opposites (الصفات المتضادة)
children.description: Five pairs of opposing characteristics. Each pair describes a binary quality — a letter either has one or the other (or, in one case, is in between).

children.title: 1. Hams (الهمس) — Whispered
children.description: Hams means 'whispering' — the breath continues to flow when the letter is pronounced. Because the articulation point is weak or the letter is whispered, air escapes. Letters with Hams have weak contact at their Makhraj.

children.title: The 10 Hams Letters
children.description: The Hams letters are: ف ح ث ه ش خ ص س ك ت. Mnemonic: فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ (Faḥaththahu shakhṣun sakat — 'So encourage him; a person was silent'). These are whispered — the breath continues when pronounced.
children.example: ف ح ث ه ش خ ص س ك ت
children.exampleTranslation: Fā, Ḥā, Thā, Hā, Shīn, Khā, Ṣād, Sīn, Kāf, Tā

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — the ص in الصِّرَاطَ? No, الصِّرَاطَ has Ṣād which is Hams. Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:6) — الصِّرَاطَ. The Sīn in الْمُسْتَقِيمَ. The Kāf in مَالِكِ. The Tā in نَسْتَعِينُ.

children.title: 2. Jahr (الجهر) — Voiced
children.description: Jahr means 'to announce' or 'to be voiced' — the breath is withheld when the letter is pronounced. The articulation point is strong, so no air escapes. Jahr is the opposite of Hams.

children.title: The 18 Jahr Letters
children.description: The remaining 18 Arabic letters carry Jahr — they are all letters not in the Hams group: أ ب ج د ذ ر ز ض ط ظ ع غ ق ل م ن و ي. These are voiced — the breath is withheld.
children.example: أ ب ج د ذ ر ز ض ط ظ ع غ ق ل م ن و ي

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — the د in الْحَمْدُ. The ب in رَبِّ. The ل in لِلَّهِ. These are voiced — no breath escapes.

children.title: 3. Shiddah (الشدة) — Strong
children.description: Shiddah means 'strength' — the sound is completely blocked at the Makhraj, then released forcefully. Air does not flow during the letter; it's trapped until released. Shiddah is the opposite of Rakhāwah.

children.title: The 8 Shiddah Letters
children.description: The Shiddah letters are: أ ج د ق ط ب ك ت. Mnemonic: أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ (Ajid qaṭin bakat — 'I found only a cat cried'). These letters completely stop the sound at their Makhraj before releasing.
children.example: أ ج د ق ط ب ك ت
children.exampleTranslation: Hamza, Jīm, Dāl, Qāf, Ṭā, Bā, Kāf, Tā

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — the ق in قُلْ. The د in أَحَدٌ. The ج in يَجْعَل. These letters produce a strong, abrupt sound.

children.title: 4. Tawassuṭ (التوسط) — Intermediate
children.description: Tawassuṭ means 'middle' or 'intermediate.' Five letters are neither fully Shiddah nor fully Rakhāwah — they are in between. The sound flows partially, then stops. Tawassuṭ sits between Shiddah and Rakhāwah.

children.title: The 5 Tawassuṭ Letters
children.description: The five intermediate letters are: ل ن ع م ر. Mnemonic: لِنْ عُمَرَ (Lin ʿUmar — 'Be soft, Umar'). These letters have a partial flow of sound — neither fully blocked nor fully flowing.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:5) — the ن in نَعْبُدُ and نَسْتَعِينُ. The ل in لِلَّهِ. The م in مَالِكِ. These are intermediate — the sound flows partially.

children.title: 5. Rakhāwah (الرخاوة) — Soft
children.description: Rakhāwah means 'softness' or 'gentleness.' The sound flows continuously at the Makhraj without being blocked. Air continues to escape during the letter. Rakhāwah is the opposite of Shiddah.

children.title: The 15 Rakhāwah Letters
children.description: The Rakhāwah letters are all remaining letters after removing Shiddah (8) and Tawassuṭ (5): ث ح خ ذ ز س ش ص ض ظ غ ف ه و ي. That's 15 letters. These flow continuously — air keeps escaping.
children.example: ث ح خ ذ ز س ش ص ض ظ غ ف ه و ي

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — the س in بِسْمِ. The ر in الرَّحْمَنِ? No, ر is Tawassuṭ. The ح in الرَّحْمَنِ. The ش in الشَّمْسِ. These flow continuously.

children.title: 6. Istiʿlāʾ (الاستعلاء) — Elevated
children.description: Istiʿlāʾ means 'elevation.' The back of the tongue rises toward the upper palate when pronouncing these letters, producing a heavier, deeper sound. Also called Tafkhīm (heavy). Istiʿlāʾ is the opposite of Istifāl.

children.title: The 7 Istiʿlāʾ Letters
children.description: The seven elevated (heavy) letters are: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق. Mnemonic: خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ (Khuṣṣa ḍaghṭin qiẓ — 'Distinguish the pressure, be alert'). These letters raise the back of the tongue toward the palate.
children.example: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق
children.exampleTranslation: Khā, Ṣād, Ḍād, Ṭā, Ẓā, Ghayn, Qāf

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — the ض in الضَّالِّينَ. The ط in الصِّرَاطَ. The ق in الْمُسْتَقِيمَ. These are heavy — the back of the tongue is raised.

children.title: 7. Istifāl (الاستفال) — Lowered
children.description: Istifāl means 'lowering.' The back of the tongue stays flat (lowered) when pronouncing these letters, producing a lighter, thinner sound. Also called Tarqīq (light). Istifāl is the opposite of Istiʿlāʾ.

children.title: The 22 Istifāl Letters
children.description: All remaining letters after removing the 7 Istiʿlāʾ letters carry Istifāl — that's 22 letters. These are light — the back of the tongue stays flat.
children.example: أ ب ت ث ج ح د ذ ر ز س ش ع ف ك ل م ن ه و ي

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — the م in الْحَمْدُ. The د in الْحَمْدُ. The ك in مَالِكِ. These are light — the tongue stays flat.

children.title: 8. Iṭbāq (الإطباق) — Closed (Full Contact)
children.description: Iṭbāq means 'closing' or 'covering.' The tongue touches the upper palate over a large area when pronouncing these letters, producing the heaviest sounds. Iṭbāq is a stronger form of heaviness than Istiʿlāʾ alone. Iṭbāq is the opposite of Infitāḥ.

children.title: The 4 Iṭbāq Letters
children.description: The four letters with Iṭbāq are: ص ض ط ظ. These four letters combine Istiʿlāʾ (elevation) with Iṭbāq (full contact of the tongue against the palate), making them the heaviest letters in Arabic.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — the ض in الضَّالِّينَ. The ط in الصِّرَاطَ. These are the heaviest letters — tongue fully touches the palate.

children.title: 9. Infitāḥ (الانفتاح) — Open
children.description: Infitāḥ means 'opening' — the tongue does NOT fully touch the palate. The sound is more open. Infitāḥ is the opposite of Iṭbāq.

children.title: The 25 Infitāḥ Letters
children.description: All remaining letters after removing the 4 Iṭbāq letters carry Infitāḥ — that's 25 letters. These do not have full tongue-palate contact.
children.example: أ ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ر ز س ش ع غ ف ق ك ل م ن ه و ي

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — the ح in الْحَمْدُ. The ك in مَالِكِ. These are open — the tongue does not fully touch the palate.

children.title: 10. Idhlāq (الإذلاق) — Fluency
children.description: Idhlāq means 'fluency' or 'smoothness.' These letters come easily from the tip of the tongue or the lips — they flow off quickly. Idhlāq is the opposite of Iṣmāt.

children.title: The 6 Idhlāq Letters
children.description: The six fluent letters are: ف ر ل ن ب م. Mnemonic: فِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ (Firra min lubb — 'Flee from the core'). These letters flow off the tongue tip or lips quickly.
children.example: ف ر ل ن ب م
children.exampleTranslation: Fā, Rā, Lām, Nūn, Bā, Mīm

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — the ل in لِلَّهِ. The ر in رَبِّ. The م in مَالِكِ. The ن in نَعْبُدُ. The ب in رَبِّ. These flow easily.

children.title: 11. Iṣmāt (الإصمات) — Firmness
children.description: Iṣmāt means 'firmness' or 'prevention.' These letters do NOT flow easily — they are heavier, more firmly rooted in their Makhraj. Iṣmāt is the opposite of Idhlāq.

children.title: The 23 Iṣmāt Letters
children.description: All remaining letters after removing the 6 Idhlāq letters carry Iṣmāt — that's 23 letters: أ ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ع غ ق ك ه و ي. These do not flow easily.
children.example: أ ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ع غ ق ك ه و ي

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — the ص in الصِّرَاطَ. The ط in الصِّرَاطَ. These are firm — they don't flow off the tongue.

children.title: Ṣifāt without Opposites (الصفات غير المتضادة)
children.description: Seven characteristics that stand alone — they have no contrasting quality. Each describes a specific feature of certain letters.

children.title: 1. Ṣafīr (الصفير) — Whistling
children.description: Ṣafīr means 'whistling.' Three letters produce a whistling sound as air passes through a narrow opening: ص ز س. The whistling is strongest with ص, medium with ز, lightest with س.

children.title: The 3 Ṣafīr Letters
children.description: The three whistling letters are: ص (Ṣād), ز (Zāy), س (Sīn). These produce a high-pitched whistle as air flows past the tongue tip and lower teeth.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:6) — the ص in الصِّرَاطَ. The س in الْمُسْتَقِيمَ. These have a distinct whistling quality.

children.title: 2. Qalqalah (القلقلة) — Echoing
children.description: Qalqalah means 'echoing' or 'bouncing.' Five letters produce a bouncing echo when they are Sākinah: ق ط ب ج د. Mnemonic: قُطْبُ جَدٍّ (Quṭbu jadd). This Ṣifah is covered in detail in the Qalqalah rule.

children.title: The 5 Qalqalah Letters
children.description: The five letters with Qalqalah are: ق ط ب ج د. Mnemonic: قُطْبُ جَدٍّ (Quṭbu jadd — 'The pole of a grandfather').

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — the ق in قُلْ. The د in أَحَدٌ at stop.

children.title: 3. Līn (اللين) — Softness
children.description: Līn means 'softness' or 'gentleness.' Two letters produce a soft, gliding sound when they are Sākinah and preceded by a Fatḥah: و ي (in specific cases). Example: خَوْف، بَيْت.

children.title: The 2 Līn Letters
children.description: The two Līn letters are: و (Wāw) and ي (Yā) — when they are Sākinah and preceded by a Fatḥah. This is different from their Madd usage (which is Jawf).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Quraysh (106:1-2) — the ي in قُرَيْشٍ, the و in خَوْفٍ. These glide softly.

children.title: 4. Inḥirāf (الانحراف) — Deviation
children.description: Inḥirāf means 'deviation' or 'turning aside.' Two letters have this quality: ل and ر. When pronounced, the sound deviates from its Makhraj — for Lām, it slides toward the tongue tip; for Rā, it vibrates and rebounds.

children.title: The 2 Inḥirāf Letters
children.description: The two letters with Inḥirāf are: ل (Lām) and ر (Rā). Lām's sound deviates from the tongue edge toward the tip. Rā's sound deviates and vibrates.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — the ل in لِلَّهِ. The ر in رَبِّ.

children.title: 5. Takrīr (التكرير) — Repetition (Vibration)
children.description: Takrīr means 'repetition' or 'trilling.' Only one letter has this quality: ر (Rā). When pronouncing Rā, the tip of the tongue vibrates against the gums briefly. Excessive vibration (more than 2 trills) is discouraged in Tajweed.

children.title: The 1 Takrīr Letter
children.description: Only ر (Rā) has Takrīr. The tongue tip vibrates briefly, but excessive trilling is considered a defect in Tajweed. Ideally, the Rā should have a single, controlled vibration.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — the ر in رَبِّ. The vibration is brief — do not trill excessively.

children.title: 6. Tafashshī (التفشي) — Spread
children.description: Tafashshī means 'spreading' or 'diffusion.' Only one letter has this quality: ش (Shīn). When pronouncing Shīn, the air spreads across the palate, producing a hissing, spreading sound.

children.title: The 1 Tafashshī Letter
children.description: Only ش (Shīn) has Tafashshī. The air diffuses across the roof of the mouth, creating a broad, spreading sound.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Shams (91:1) — the ش in وَالشَّمْسِ. The sound spreads across the palate.

children.title: 7. Istiṭālah (الاستطالة) — Extension
children.description: Istiṭālah means 'extension' or 'elongation.' Only one letter has this quality: ض (Ḍād). The sound extends along the entire edge of the tongue — from the front edge to the back molars. This is why Ḍād is one of the longest letters to pronounce.

children.title: The 1 Istiṭālah Letter
children.description: Only ض (Ḍād) has Istiṭālah. The sound extends from the front of the tongue edge to the back, involving the entire side of the tongue.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — the ض in الضَّالِّينَ. The sound extends along the tongue edge.

children.title: How Ṣifāt Distinguish Letters
children.description: Examples showing how letters sharing a Makhraj are distinguished by their Ṣifāt.

children.title: ط and ت — Same Makhraj, Different Ṣifāt
children.description: Both ط and ت come from the tongue tip + upper teeth. But ط has Istiʿlāʾ, Iṭbāq, and Shiddah (heavy, closed, strong). ت has Istifāl, Infitāḥ, and Shiddah (light, open, strong). The result: ط is heavy, ت is light. Practice: طَيْن (ṭayn) vs. تَيْن (tayn).

children.title: د and ذ — Same Makhraj, Different Ṣifāt
children.description: Both د and ذ come from the tongue tip near upper teeth. But د is Shiddah (strong) and Jahr (voiced) with no Istiʿlāʾ. ذ is Rakhāwah (soft) and Jahr. Practice: دَار (dār) vs. ذَار (dhār).

children.title: ص and س — Same Makhraj, Different Ṣifāt
children.description: Both ص and س come from the tongue tip + lower teeth. But ص has Istiʿlāʾ and Iṭbāq (heavy, closed). س has Istifāl and Infitāḥ (light, open). Practice: صَيْف (ṣayf — summer) vs. سَيْف (sayf — sword).
