children.title: ح and ه — Different Makhraj, Similar Sound
children.description: ح comes from the middle throat with Rakhāwah and Hams. ه comes from the deepest throat with Rakhāwah and Hams. Both whispered, both soft, but different Makhraj. Practice: حَادَ (ḥāda) vs. هَادَ (hāda).

children.title: ض and ذ — Different Makhraj, Similar Group
children.description: ض comes from the tongue edge with Istiṭālah. ذ comes from the tongue tip + upper teeth with Rakhāwah. Both are from the tongue but very different sounds.

children.title: Summary of All Ṣifāt
children.description: A quick reference table of all 17 Ṣifāt (10 with opposites + 7 without).

children.title: Hams — 10 Letters
children.description: Whispered: ف ح ث ه ش خ ص س ك ت. Mnemonic: فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ.
children.example: ف ح ث ه ش خ ص س ك ت

children.title: Jahr — 18 Letters
children.description: Voiced: all remaining letters after Hams.

children.title: Shiddah — 8 Letters
children.description: Strong: أ ج د ق ط ب ك ت. Mnemonic: أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ.
children.example: أ ج د ق ط ب ك ت

children.title: Tawassuṭ — 5 Letters
children.description: Intermediate: ل ن ع م ر. Mnemonic: لِنْ عُمَرَ.

children.title: Rakhāwah — 15 Letters
children.description: Soft: all remaining after Shiddah and Tawassuṭ.

children.title: Istiʿlāʾ — 7 Letters
children.description: Elevated: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق. Mnemonic: خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ.
children.example: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق

children.title: Istifāl — 22 Letters
children.description: Lowered: all remaining after Istiʿlāʾ.

children.title: Iṭbāq — 4 Letters
children.description: Closed: ص ض ط ظ.

children.title: Infitāḥ — 25 Letters
children.description: Open: all remaining after Iṭbāq.

children.title: Idhlāq — 6 Letters
children.description: Fluent: ف ر ل ن ب م. Mnemonic: فِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ.
children.example: ف ر ل ن ب م

children.title: Iṣmāt — 23 Letters
children.description: Firm: all remaining after Idhlāq.

children.title: Ṣafīr — 3 Letters
children.description: Whistling: ص ز س.

children.title: Qalqalah — 5 Letters
children.description: Echoing: ق ط ب ج د. Mnemonic: قُطْبُ جَدٍّ.

children.title: Līn — 2 Letters
children.description: Soft: و ي (with Fatḥah before, Sākinah).

children.title: Inḥirāf — 2 Letters
children.description: Deviation: ل ر.

children.title: Takrīr — 1 Letter
children.description: Vibration: ر.

children.title: Tafashshī — 1 Letter
children.description: Spread: ش.

children.title: Istiṭālah — 1 Letter
children.description: Extension: ض.

children.title: Classical Mnemonics for Ṣifāt
children.description: Classical scholars used mnemonics to help memorize each Ṣifah's letters.

children.title: Hams — فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ
children.description: 'So encourage him; a person was silent.' Letters: ف ح ث ه ش خ ص س ك ت.

children.title: Shiddah — أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ
children.description: 'I found only a cat cried.' Letters: أ ج د ق ط ب ك ت.

children.title: Tawassuṭ — لِنْ عُمَرَ
children.description: 'Be soft, Umar.' Letters: ل ن ع م ر.

children.title: Istiʿlāʾ — خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ
children.description: 'Distinguish the pressure, be alert.' Letters: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق.

children.title: Iṭbāq — ص ض ط ظ
children.description: The four letters of Iṭbāq: ص ض ط ظ.

children.title: Idhlāq — فِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ
children.description: 'Flee from the core.' Letters: ف ر ل ن ب م.

categories.title: Idghām Categories (Mithlayn, Mutajānisayn, Mutāqāribayn)
categories.description: The three classical categories of Idghām that govern how letters merge when they meet: Idghām Mithlayn (two identical letters), Idghām Mutajānisayn (letters sharing the same Makhraj), and Idghām Mutāqāribayn (letters with close but not identical Makhārij).

children.title: Introduction to Idghām Categories
children.description: Beyond the specific Noon Sākinah and Tanween Idghām rules, Tajweed recognizes a broader system: whenever a Sākinah letter is followed by a voweled letter, the two may merge based on how similar their articulation points or characteristics are. This is divided into three categories.

children.title: Definition of Idghām
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Idghām means 'to insert one thing into another.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Merging a Sākinah letter into the following voweled letter, so that the two become a single doubled letter (Mushaddadah).

children.title: The Three Categories
children.description: Idghām is classified into three categories based on the relationship between the two letters: 1. Idghām Mithlayn (المتماثلين) — two IDENTICAL letters. 2. Idghām Mutajānisayn (المتجانسين) — two letters sharing the SAME Makhraj. 3. Idghām Mutāqāribayn (المتقاربين) — two letters with CLOSE Makhārij.

children.title: General Conditions
children.description: For Idghām to apply: 1. The first letter must be Sākinah (has a Sukūn). 2. The second letter must be voweled (has a vowel). 3. The two letters must be in the same word (or across two words in some cases). 4. The two letters must belong to one of the three categories.

children.title: Two Kinds: Ṣaghīr and Kabīr
children.description: Within each of the three categories, Idghām is divided into two kinds: 1. Idghām Ṣaghīr (الصغير) — the FIRST letter is Sākinah, the SECOND is voweled. This is the common case in the Qur'an. 2. Idghām Kabīr (الكبير) — BOTH letters are voweled. This is rare in the Qur'an and mostly applies in specific readings.

children.title: Idghām Ṣaghīr — Common Case
children.description: The first letter is Sākinah, the second is voweled. Example: قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ — the د is Sākinah, the ت is voweled → Idghām Mutajānisayn Ṣaghīr.

children.title: Idghām Kabīr — Rare Case
children.description: Both letters are voweled. This is not common in Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim (the standard reading), but appears in other Qirāʾāt. Most students of Tajweed do not need to master this.

children.title: Notation in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, Idghām is often indicated by removing the Sukūn from the first letter and adding a Shaddah to the second. For example: قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ is written with the د Sākinah but when merged, the ت is doubled in pronunciation.

children.title: Idghām Mithlayn (المتماثلين) — Identical Letters
children.description: When two letters that are IDENTICAL in both Makhraj (articulation point) and Ṣifāt (characteristics) meet — the first Sākinah, the second voweled — they merge into a single doubled letter.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Mithlayn means 'two identical things.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Two letters that are identical in Makhraj AND Ṣifāt meet — the first Sākinah, the second voweled. They merge into one Mushaddadah letter.

children.title: Conditions
children.description: For Idghām Mithlayn: 1. Two letters must be IDENTICAL — same letter, same Makhraj, same Ṣifāt. 2. First letter must be Sākinah. 3. Second letter must be voweled. 4. They can be in the same word or across two words.

children.title: Common Letter Pairs
children.description: The most common Mithlayn pairs in the Qur'an: د د، ت ت، ب ب، ل ل، م م، ن ن، و و، ي ي. Each pair merges into a single doubled letter.
children.example: د د ت ت ب ب ل ل م م ن ن و و ي ي

children.title: د + د — قَدْ دَخَلُوا
children.description: The د Sākinah at the end of قَدْ merges with the voweled د at the start of دَخَلُوا. Result: قَدَّخَلُوا (qaddakhalū).

children.title: ت + ت — فَمَا رَبِحَتْ تِجَارَتُهُمْ
children.description: The ت Sākinah at the end of رَبِحَتْ merges with the voweled ت at the start of تِجَارَتُهُمْ. Result: رَبِحَتِّجَارَتُهُمْ (rabiḥattijāratuhum).

children.title: ب + ب — اضْرِبْ بِعَصَاكَ
children.description: The ب Sākinah at the end of اضْرِبْ merges with the voweled ب at the start of بِعَصَاكَ. Result: اضْرِبِّعَصَاكَ (iḍribbiʿaṣāka).

children.title: ل + ل — قُلْ لَهُمْ
children.description: The ل Sākinah at the end of قُلْ merges with the voweled ل at the start of لَهُمْ. Result: قُلَّهُمْ (qullahum).

children.title: م + م — لَهُمْ مَا
children.description: This is also Idghām Shafawī (Mīm Sākinah before Mīm). The م Sākinah merges with the voweled م with Ghunnah. Result: لَهُمَّا (lahummā).

children.title: ن + ن — مِنْ نَارٍ
children.description: This is also Idghām with Ghunnah (Noon Sākinah before Noon). The ن Sākinah merges with the voweled ن with Ghunnah. Result: مِنَّارٍ (minnār).

children.title: و + و — Also possible
children.description: Rare example. When و Sākinah is followed by و voweled.

children.title: ي + ي — Also possible
children.description: Rare example. When ي Sākinah is followed by ي voweled.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Well-known Idghām Mithlayn examples.

children.title: Sūrah Yūsuf (12:99) — دَخَلُوا
children.description: The د Sākinah from قَدْ merges with the د in دَخَلُوا.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:16) — رَبِحَتْ تِجَارَتُهُمْ
children.description: The ت Sākinah in رَبِحَتْ merges with the ت in تِجَارَتُهُمْ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:60) — اضْرِبْ بِعَصَاكَ
children.description: The ب Sākinah in اضْرِبْ merges with the ب in بِعَصَاكَ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:8) — قُلْ لَهُمْ
children.description: The ل Sākinah in قُلْ merges with the ل in لَهُمْ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Aʿrāf (7:44) — قَدْ دَخَلْتُمْ
children.description: Another د + د example.

children.title: Muṣḥaf Notation
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, the two identical letters are often written with the first carrying a Sukūn (ْ) and the second carrying a Shaddah (ّ) — or the letters are simply written twice with the Shaddah on the second.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Pronouncing the two identical letters separately instead of merging. 2. Not applying Shaddah to the second letter. 3. Applying Ghunnah where it's not needed (except when the pair involves ن or م with Ghunnah rules). 4. Missing the Idghām when reading quickly. 5. Applying Idghām across a stop (Waqf) where it shouldn't apply.

children.title: Idghām Mutajānisayn (المتجانسين) — Same Origin
children.description: When two letters share the SAME Makhraj (articulation point) but differ in their Ṣifāt (characteristics), and the first is Sākinah while the second is voweled, they merge into a single Mushaddadah letter.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Mutajānisayn means 'two things of the same kind.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Two letters that share the SAME Makhraj but have DIFFERENT Ṣifāt. When the first is Sākinah and the second is voweled, they merge.

children.title: Conditions
children.description: For Idghām Mutajānisayn: 1. Two letters must share the SAME Makhraj. 2. They differ in Ṣifāt (e.g., one is Shiddah, the other Rakhāwah). 3. First letter is Sākinah, second is voweled. 4. Can be in the same word or across two words.

children.title: Common Letter Pairs
children.description: The classical pairs of Idghām Mutajānisayn: ت + ط، ط + ت، د + ت، ت + د، ذ + ظ، ظ + ذ، ث + ذ، ب + م، م + ب، etc.
children.example: ت ط ط ت د ت ت د ذ ظ ظ ذ ث ذ ب م م ب

children.title: ت + ط — قَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ
children.description: The ت Sākinah in قَالَتْ and the ط in طَائِفَةٌ share the same Makhraj (tongue tip + upper teeth roots). They merge: قَالَطَّائِفَةٌ (qālaṭṭāʾifah).

children.title: ط + ت — أَحَطْتُ
children.description: The ط Sākinah in أَحَطْتُ merges with the ت. Result: أَحَطُّ (aḥaṭṭu).

children.title: د + ت — قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ
children.description: The د Sākinah in قَدْ merges with the ت in تَبَيَّنَ. Both share the same Makhraj (tongue tip + upper teeth roots). Result: قَتَّبَيَّنَ (qattabayyana).

children.title: ت + د — أُجِيبَتْ دَعْوَتُكُمَا
children.description: The ت Sākinah in أُجِيبَتْ merges with the د in دَعْوَتُكُمَا. Result: أُجِيبَدَّعْوَتُكُمَا (ujībaddaʿwatukumā).

children.title: ذ + ظ — إِذْ ظَلَمُوا
children.description: The ذ Sākinah in إِذْ merges with the ظ in ظَلَمُوا. Both share the same Makhraj (tongue tip + upper teeth tips). Result: إِظْظَلَمُوا → إِظَّلَمُوا (iẓẓalamū).

children.title: ث + ذ — يَلْهَثْ ذَٰلِكَ
children.description: The ث Sākinah in يَلْهَثْ merges with the ذ in ذَٰلِكَ. Both share the same Makhraj. Result: يَلْهَذَّٰلِكَ (yalhadhdhālika).

children.title: ب + م — Only in specific contexts
children.description: The ب Sākinah followed by م. This is actually Idghām Shafawī for Noon, but with ب as the first letter it's Mutajānisayn. Rare in the Qur'an.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Well-known Idghām Mutajānisayn examples.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:256) — قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ
children.description: The د in قَدْ merges with the ت in تَبَيَّنَ.

children.title: Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān (3:72) — قَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ
children.description: The ت in قَالَتْ merges with the ط in طَائِفَةٌ.

children.title: Sūrah Yūnus (10:89) — أُجِيبَتْ دَعْوَتُكُمَا
children.description: The ت in أُجِيبَتْ merges with the د in دَعْوَتُكُمَا.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Naml (27:19) — أَحَطْتُ
children.description: Internal word Idghām — the ط merges with the ت.

children.title: Two Kinds: Ṣaghīr and Kabīr
children.description: Idghām Mutajānisayn has two kinds: Ṣaghīr (first letter Sākinah, second voweled — the common case) and Kabīr (both voweled — rare in the Qur'an).

children.title: Muṣḥaf Notation
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, the Sukūn may be removed from the first letter and a Shaddah added to the second. This cues the reciter to apply Idghām.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Not applying Idghām when the letters share a Makhraj. 2. Applying Idghām where the Makhārij are actually different. 3. Confusing with Idghām Mithlayn (identical) or Mutāqāribayn (close). 4. Not applying the correct Shaddah. 5. Missing the Idghām during fast recitation.

children.title: Idghām Mutāqāribayn (المتقاربين) — Close Articulation
children.description: When two letters have CLOSE but NOT identical Makhārij or Ṣifāt, and the first is Sākinah while the second is voweled, they merge into a single Mushaddadah letter.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Mutāqāribayn means 'two things that are close to each other.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Two letters whose Makhārij or Ṣifāt are CLOSE but not identical. When the first is Sākinah and the second is voweled, they merge.

children.title: Conditions
children.description: For Idghām Mutāqāribayn: 1. Two letters must have CLOSE Makhārij or Ṣifāt. 2. First letter is Sākinah, second is voweled. 3. The Idghām might not always be complete — sometimes only partial, depending on the letters.

children.title: Common Letter Pairs
children.description: The classical pairs of Idghām Mutāqāribayn: ل + ر، ق + ك، ك + ق، ن + ل (with Ghunnah), etc.
children.example: ل ر ق ك ك ق ن ل

children.title: ل + ر — قُلْ رَبِّ
children.description: The ل Sākinah in قُلْ merges with the ر in رَبِّ. Both come from close tongue positions. Result: قُرَّبِّ (qurrabb).

children.title: ق + ك — نَخْلُقْكُمْ
children.description: The ق Sākinah in نَخْلُقْ merges with the ك in كُمْ. They share a close Makhraj (deepest tongue). Result: نَخْلُكُّمْ (nakhluqqkum) — with partial Idghām.

children.title: ك + ق — Rare
children.description: Rare example. When ك Sākinah is followed by ق.

children.title: ن + ل — Already Idghām without Ghunnah
children.description: Noon Sākinah followed by Lām — this is Idghām without Ghunnah (already covered under Noon Sākinah rules). But it also qualifies as Idghām Mutāqāribayn because ن and ل have close Makhārij.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Well-known Idghām Mutāqāribayn examples.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Kahf (18:24) — قُلْ رَبِّ
children.description: The ل in قُلْ merges with the ر in رَبِّ — a classic Mutāqāribayn case.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Mursalāt (77:20) — نَخْلُقْكُمْ
children.description: The ق Sākinah in نَخْلُقْ merges with the ك in كُمْ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:37) — مِنْ لَدُنْهُ
children.description: The ن Sākinah in مِنْ merges with the ل in لَدُنْهُ — Idghām without Ghunnah, also Mutāqāribayn.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Qiyāmah (75:34-35) — أَوْلَىٰ لَكَ
children.description: The ى Sākinah (Alif Maqṣūrah) followed by ل — some reciters apply Idghām here. This is a subtle case.

children.title: Two Kinds: Ṣaghīr and Kabīr
children.description: Like the other two categories, Idghām Mutāqāribayn has Ṣaghīr (common) and Kabīr (rare) kinds.

children.title: Complete vs Partial Idghām
children.description: Some Mutāqāribayn cases result in COMPLETE Idghām (the first letter disappears entirely). Others are PARTIAL (a trace of the first letter remains). This depends on how close the letters are. Example: ق + ك is partial because ق has Istiʿlāʾ while ك does not.

children.title: Muṣḥaf Notation
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, Mutāqāribayn Idghām is sometimes marked with the Sukūn removed from the first letter, sometimes with a Shaddah added to the second. The notation varies by publisher.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Not applying Idghām where it should apply. 2. Applying it where the Makhārij are not close enough. 3. Confusing with Mutajānisayn (same Makhraj) or Mithlayn (identical). 4. Missing the partial nature of some Mutāqāribayn cases. 5. Applying full Ghunnah when it's not a ن/م pair.

children.title: Comparison: Mithlayn vs Mutajānisayn vs Mutāqāribayn
children.description: A side-by-side comparison of the three Idghām categories to help distinguish them.

children.title: Mithlayn — Same Letter
children.description: Two letters are IDENTICAL. Both Makhraj and Ṣifāt are the same. Example: قَدْ دَخَلُوا (د + د). Full Idghām.

children.title: Mutajānisayn — Same Makhraj
children.description: Two letters share the SAME Makhraj but differ in Ṣifāt. Example: قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ (د + ت — both tongue tip + upper teeth). Full Idghām usually.

children.title: Mutāqāribayn — Close Makhraj
children.description: Two letters have CLOSE Makhārij (not identical). Example: قُلْ رَبِّ (ل + ر — tongue positions are close). Sometimes partial Idghām.

children.title: Summary of Idghām Categories
children.description: A quick reference table.

children.title: Mithlayn — Identical Letters
children.description: Same Makhraj, same Ṣifāt. Pairs: دد تت بب لل مم نن وو يي.

children.title: Mutajānisayn — Same Makhraj
children.description: Same Makhraj, different Ṣifāt. Pairs: ت ط ط ت د ت ت د ذ ظ ظ ذ ث ذ.

children.title: Mutāqāribayn — Close Makhraj
children.description: Close Makhraj. Pairs: ل ر ق ك ك ق ن ل.

children.title: Ṣaghīr — First Sākinah, Second Voweled
children.description: The common case in the Qur'an.

children.title: Kabīr — Both Voweled
children.description: Rare — mostly in non-Ḥafṣ readings.

children.title: Mnemonics and Learning Tips
children.description: Tips for remembering the Idghām categories.

children.title: Mithlayn — 'Mithl' means 'like'
children.description: Mithlayn (متماثلين) = 'two things that are alike.' If the two letters are identical, it's Mithlayn.

children.title: Mutajānisayn — 'Jins' means 'kind/species'
children.description: Mutajānisayn (متجانسين) = 'two things of the same kind.' If the two letters share a Makhraj (same family), it's Mutajānisayn.

children.title: Mutāqāribayn — 'Qurb' means 'nearness'
children.description: Mutāqāribayn (متقاربين) = 'two things that are near each other.' If the two letters have close Makhārij, it's Mutāqāribayn.

children.title: The Three-Step Check
children.description: To identify any Idghām: 1. Are the letters IDENTICAL? → Mithlayn. 2. Do they share the SAME Makhraj? → Mutajānisayn. 3. Are their Makhārij CLOSE? → Mutāqāribayn. This order matters — always check from most similar to least.

categories.title: Sakt, Hamzat al-Waṣl & Miscellaneous Rules
categories.description: The remaining rules that complete a Tajweed curriculum: Sakt (brief pause without breath), Hamzat al-Waṣl (connecting Hamzah), Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ (disconnecting Hamzah), Tafkhīm/Tarqīq of Alif, and the connection of recitation between verses and Sūrahs.

children.title: Sakt (السكت) — Brief Pause Without Breath
children.description: A Sakt is a brief pause at the end of a word — shorter than a normal breath pause — WITHOUT taking a breath, followed immediately by resumption. It occurs in specific places in the Qur'an.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Sakt means 'silence' or 'to be quiet.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A brief pause (approximately 1 count) WITHOUT taking a breath, then resuming. It is shorter than Waqf and does not involve breathing.

children.title: Sakt vs Waqf
children.description: Both involve stopping briefly, but there are key differences: 1. Waqf: You stop AND take a breath. Sakt: You stop WITHOUT breathing. 2. Waqf: Usually at the end of a meaningful phrase. Sakt: At specific points within a phrase. 3. Waqf: Duration is longer. Sakt: Very brief (about 1 count).

children.title: The Four Places of Sakt in Ḥafṣ
children.description: In the Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim reading, Sakt occurs in four specific places in the Qur'an. These are fixed and should be observed by the reciter.

children.title: 1. Sūrah Al-Kahf (18:1-2) — عِوَجًا ۜ قَيِّمًا
children.description: Between عِوَجًا and قَيِّمًا. Sakt without breath — a brief pause to show the two words are separate.
children.exampleTranslation: Wa lam yajʿal lahu ʿiwajan qayyimā

children.title: 2. Sūrah Yā-Sīn (36:52) — مِنْ مَرْقَدِنَا ۜ هَٰذَا
children.description: Between مَرْقَدِنَا and هَٰذَا. Sakt without breath.
children.example: قَالُوا يَا وَيْلَنَا مَنْ بَعَثَنَا مِنْ مَرْقَدِنَا
children.exampleTranslation: Qālū yā waylanā man baʿathanā min marqadinā

children.title: 3. Sūrah Al-Qiyāmah (75:27) — وَقِيلَ مَنْ ۜ رَاقٍ
children.description: Between مَنْ and رَاقٍ. Sakt without breath.

children.title: 4. Sūrah Al-Muṭaffifīn (83:14) — بَلْ ۜ رَانَ
children.description: Between بَلْ and رَانَ. Sakt without breath.

children.title: Additional Sakt Cases (Optional)
children.description: Some scholars mention additional Sakt cases: Alif Maqṣūrah followed by a letter, and some other marginal cases. The four above are the agreed-upon ones in Ḥafṣ.

children.title: Notation in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, Sakt is marked with a small letter 'س' (Sīn) above the word, or with a small vertical mark. Some Muṣḥafs use the letter 'س' directly.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Taking a breath during Sakt (this turns it into Waqf). 2. Skipping the Sakt entirely (missing a required pause). 3. Holding the Sakt too long (it should be brief — about 1 count). 4. Not knowing the four places of Sakt.

children.title: Additional Sakt Cases (Some Scholars)
children.description: Some scholars mention additional Sakt cases: 1. Alif Maqṣūrah followed by Hamza. 2. In some Waqf cases to preserve clarity. 3. In specific Muqaṭṭaʿāt readings. These are optional and not agreed upon by all scholars.

children.title: Sakt in Other Qirāʾāt
children.description: Different Qirāʾāt have different Sakt places. Example: Warsh has additional Sakt cases. Studying these requires a teacher with Ijazah in that specific reading.

children.title: Hamzat al-Waṣl (همزة الوصل) — Connecting Hamzah
children.description: A Hamzah that is pronounced when starting a word and silent when continuing from a previous word. It is written as ا (Alif without the Hamza mark) and connects words in recitation.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Waṣl means 'connection' or 'joining.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A Hamzah that appears at the beginning of a word, pronounced when starting (Ibtidāʾ) and silent when continuing (Waṣl) from a previous word. It is written as a plain Alif (ا) without the Hamza mark (ء).

children.title: How It's Written
children.description: Hamzat al-Waṣl is written as ا (Alif) WITHOUT the Hamza mark (ء). Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ is written WITH the Hamza mark (أ، إ، ؤ، ئ). This visual difference tells you whether the Hamzah is pronounced in Waṣl.

children.title: Pronunciation Rules
children.description: Hamzat al-Waṣl has two states: 1. When STARTING with it (Ibtidāʾ): It is pronounced. 2. When CONTINUING from a previous word (Waṣl): It is silent — the previous word connects directly to the next.

children.title: When Starting — Which Vowel?
children.description: When you start with a Hamzat al-Waṣl, you need to give it a vowel (to pronounce it). The vowel depends on the third letter of the verb (if it's a verb) or is always Kasrah (if it's a noun or particle).

children.title: In Verbs — Follow the Third Letter
children.description: For verbs starting with Hamzat al-Waṣl: look at the THIRD letter of the verb. If it has a Ḍammah, start with Ḍammah. If it has a Kasrah or Fatḥah, start with Kasrah. Example: اُكْتُبْ (uktub — third letter has Ḍammah → start with Ḍammah). اِجْلِسْ (ijlis — third letter has Kasrah → start with Kasrah). اِذْهَبْ (idhhab — third letter has Fatḥah → start with Kasrah).

children.title: In Nouns — Always Kasrah
children.description: For nouns starting with Hamzat al-Waṣl, always start with Kasrah. Example: اِبْن (ibn — son), اِبْنَة (ibnah — daughter), اِسْم (ism — name), اِمْرَأَة (imraʾah — woman).

children.title: In the Definite Article ال
children.description: When starting with the definite article ال, use Fatḥah: اَلْحَمْدُ (al-ḥamdu). When ال is prefixed to a word, use Fatḥah. Note: ال is always Hamzat al-Waṣl.

children.title: Where Hamzat al-Waṣl Appears
children.description: Hamzat al-Waṣl appears in specific places: 1. The definite article ال (al-). 2. The imperative form of verbs (اِفْعَلْ). 3. The past tense of certain verbs (اِنْفَعَلَ، اِفْتَعَلَ). 4. Certain nouns (اِبْن، اِبْنَة، اِسْم، اِمْرَأَة، اِمْرُؤ، اِثْنَان، اِثْنَتَان، اَيْمَن).

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Hamzat al-Waṣl in the Qur'an — showing how it behaves at start vs in continuation.

children.title: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:1) — اقْرَأْ
children.description: Starting: Iqraʾ (Kasrah, third letter has Kasrah). Continuing: بِاسْمِ (Hamzat al-Waṣl is silent, connects to previous).

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:2) — الْحَمْدُ
children.description: Starting: Al-ḥamdu (Fatḥah). Continuing from بِسْمِ: Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm al-ḥamdu lillāh — the ال becomes silent and connects.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:1) — الم
children.description: When you start with الم, the Alif is Hamzat al-Waṣl. Pronounced as Alif with Fatḥah — Alif-Lām-Mīm.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Kahf (18:1) — الْحَمْدُ
children.description: Starting fresh: Al-ḥamdu. Continuing from another word: silent, connects.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Naṣr (110:1) — إِذَا
children.description: This is Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ (written with Kasrah below), not al-Waṣl. Waṣl examples include verbs like انْصُرْ، اهْدِنَا، اعْبُدُوا.

children.title: Rule in Continuation (Waṣl)
children.description: When reciting continuously and reaching a word that starts with Hamzat al-Waṣl: 1. DROP the Hamzat al-Waṣl entirely. 2. Connect the last letter of the previous word directly to the next letter. Example: when continuing بِسْمِ اللَّهِ → the ال is silent; you say Bismillāh not Bismi-al-Allāh.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Pronouncing Hamzat al-Waṣl when continuing from a previous word (should be silent). 2. Dropping Hamzat al-Waṣl when starting (should be pronounced). 3. Using the wrong starting vowel (e.g., Fatḥah instead of Kasrah in nouns). 4. Confusing Hamzat al-Waṣl with Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ. 5. Not applying the correct vowel rules for verbs.

children.title: Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ (همزة القطع) — Disconnecting Hamzah
children.description: A Hamzah that is ALWAYS pronounced — whether starting or continuing. It is written with the Hamza mark (أ، إ، ؤ، ئ) or as a standalone Hamzah (ء).

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Qaṭʿ means 'cutting' or 'disconnection.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): A Hamzah that is ALWAYS pronounced — whether at the start of recitation or in continuation. It is the opposite of Hamzat al-Waṣl.

children.title: How It's Written
children.description: Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ is written with the Hamza mark: أ (above Alif), إ (below Alif), ؤ (above Wāw), ئ (above Yā), or ء (standalone). This mark distinguishes it from Hamzat al-Waṣl (ا without Hamza mark).

children.title: Pronunciation
children.description: Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ is ALWAYS pronounced — no exceptions. When starting with it, pronounce it. When continuing into it, still pronounce it. Example: أَنْعَمْتَ (anʿamta) — the أ is always heard.

children.title: Where Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ Appears
children.description: Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ appears in: 1. Most nouns (except the specific ones with Hamzat al-Waṣl). 2. Past tense verbs with 4 letters (أَكْرَمَ). 3. Present tense verbs with Hamzah in the prefix (أَعْبُدُ، أَقُولُ). 4. Prepositions and particles (إِنَّ، أَنَّ، إِلَى، أَمْ). 5. Pronouns (أَنَا، أَنْتَ، أَنْتُمْ).

children.title: Qaṭʿ vs Waṣl — The Key Difference
children.description: Qaṭʿ: Always pronounced. Written with Hamza mark (أ، إ). Waṣl: Silent in continuation. Written without Hamza mark (ا). To distinguish: look at the writing. If it has the Hamza mark, it's Qaṭʿ. If it's a plain Alif, it's Waṣl.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples of Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ in the Qur'an.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — أَنْعَمْتَ
children.description: The أ is Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ — always pronounced, whether starting or continuing.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:5) — إِيَّاكَ
children.description: The إ is Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ — always pronounced with Kasrah.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — أَحَدٌ
children.description: The أ in أَحَدٌ is Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ — always pronounced.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:2) — أَنْزَلَ
children.description: The أ in أَنْزَلَ is Qaṭʿ — always pronounced.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Nisāʾ (4:1) — إِنَّ
children.description: The إ in إِنَّ is Qaṭʿ — always pronounced.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Dropping the Qaṭʿ in continuation (thinking it's Waṣl). 2. Confusing أ with ا in the Muṣḥaf. 3. Mispronouncing the vowel of the Hamzah. 4. Mixing أَنَّ and إِنَّ (they have different meanings).

children.title: Tafkhīm & Tarqīq of Alif (التفخيم والترقيق للألف)
children.description: Alif is neither inherently heavy nor light — it follows the weight of the letter before it. If the letter before is heavy (from the 7 Istiʿlāʾ letters), the Alif is heavy. If the letter before is light, the Alif is light.

children.title: The Rule
children.description: Alif never changes its own pronunciation — it takes on the weight of the letter that comes BEFORE it. This is because Alif is always Sākinah and has no independent weight of its own.

children.title: Heavy Alif — After a Heavy Letter
children.description: When Alif is preceded by one of the 7 heavy letters (خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق), the Alif becomes heavy. Examples: قَالَ (after ق), طَابَ (after ط), ظَلَمَ (after ظ), خَالِد (after خ).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الصِّرَاطَ (after ص). Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:7) — الضَّالِّينَ (after ض). Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:1) — الْقَدْرِ (after ق).

children.title: Light Alif — After a Light Letter
children.description: When Alif is preceded by any of the 21 light letters, the Alif is light. Examples: كَانَ (after ك), بَاب (after ب), مَالِك (after م), سَلَام (after س).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:4) — مَالِكِ (after م). Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:1) — كَانَ (after ك). Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — بِسْمِ (after س).

children.title: Special Case — After Rāʾ
children.description: When Alif is preceded by a Rāʾ, the weight of the Alif follows the weight of the Rāʾ: if Rāʾ is heavy, the Alif is heavy; if Rāʾ is light, the Alif is light. Example: رَاحِم (heavy Rā, heavy Alif). فِرَاق (light Rā, light Alif).

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Making the Alif heavy after a light letter. 2. Making it light after a heavy letter. 3. Trying to pronounce Alif as a distinct sound instead of letting it flow. 4. Not adjusting Alif's weight based on the preceding letter.

children.title: Connection Between Sūrahs (الوصل بين السورتين)
children.description: Rules for how to connect between the end of one Sūrah and the start of the next. Three options: full stop (Waqf), connection (Waṣl), or a brief pause (Sakt).

children.title: Three Options
children.description: When reaching the end of a Sūrah and the beginning of the next: 1. Waqf (وقف) — Stop completely, take a breath, then start the next Sūrah. This is the most common and safest option. 2. Waṣl (وصل) — Continue directly without stopping. 3. Sakt (سكت) — Brief pause without breath.

children.title: Basmalah Between Sūrahs
children.description: When moving between Sūrahs (except Sūrah Al-Tawbah, which has no Basmalah), the general rule is to recite: end of Sūrah 1 → Basmalah → beginning of Sūrah 2. Allowed options: 1. Stop at end, recite Basmalah, then start next Sūrah. 2. Continue all — end of Sūrah 1 → Basmalah → Sūrah 2 without stops. 3. Stop at end of Sūrah 1, then recite Basmalah + Sūrah 2 as one unit.

children.title: Exception — Sūrah Al-Tawbah
children.description: Sūrah Al-Tawbah (Sūrah 9) does NOT begin with the Basmalah. When moving from Al-Anfāl (8) to Al-Tawbah (9), you connect directly without Basmalah. When moving from Al-Tawbah (9) to Yūnus (10), you recite Basmalah.

children.title: End of Sūrah + Start of Next
children.description: When connecting the end of one Sūrah directly to the start of the next, you can: 1. Stop at the end (preferred). 2. Continue without stopping. 3. Sakt (brief pause). All are permitted. The choice often depends on breath control.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Reciting Basmalah at the start of Sūrah Al-Tawbah (it's not there). 2. Reciting Basmalah in the middle of a Sūrah. 3. Stopping at the wrong place when moving between Sūrahs. 4. Not knowing the three allowed options.

children.title: Istiʿādhah & Basmalah at the Start
children.description: Rules for beginning recitation: Istiʿādhah (seeking refuge in Allah) and Basmalah (in the name of Allah).

children.title: Istiʿādhah — Definition
children.description: Istiʿādhah (الاستعاذة) means seeking refuge in Allah. The recommended phrase: أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ (Aʿūdhu billāhi minash-shayṭānir-rajīm). It is Sunnah to recite it before beginning Qur'an recitation.

children.title: When to Recite Istiʿādhah
children.description: Istiʿādhah is recited: 1. At the start of recitation. 2. When moving from one recitation session to another. 3. Not recited between verses or between Sūrahs within a single session.

children.title: Basmalah — Definition
children.description: Basmalah (البسملة) is the phrase: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ (Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm). It is the opening of every Sūrah except Sūrah Al-Tawbah (9).

children.title: When to Recite Basmalah
children.description: Basmalah is recited: 1. At the start of any Sūrah (except Al-Tawbah). 2. Between Sūrahs when moving from one to the next. 3. Not recited in the middle of a Sūrah (except when starting recitation from that point — some scholars recommend it).

children.title: Al-Tawbah Exception
children.description: Sūrah Al-Tawbah (9) does NOT begin with Basmalah — a unique case in the entire Qur'an. When starting to recite Sūrah Al-Tawbah, begin directly with its first verse.

children.title: The Sequence at Start
children.description: When starting recitation of a Sūrah (that's not Al-Tawbah), the sequence is: 1. Istiʿādhah (optional but recommended). 2. Basmalah (required for most Sūrahs). 3. First verse of the Sūrah.
children.example: أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ

children.title: Forms of Istiʿādhah
children.description: The Istiʿādhah has several valid forms: 1. أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ (most common). 2. أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ السَّمِيعِ الْعَلِيمِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ. 3. أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ إِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ. All are acceptable.

children.title: Basmalah in the Middle of a Sūrah
children.description: Scholars differ on whether to recite Basmalah when starting from the middle of a Sūrah. The majority view: it is recommended but not required. Some scholars say it should not be recited at all. Both views are acceptable.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Skipping Basmalah when starting a Sūrah (except Al-Tawbah). 2. Reciting Basmalah at the start of Al-Tawbah. 3. Reciting Istiʿādhah between Sūrahs (should only be at the start of a session). 4. Mixing the two phrases incorrectly.

children.title: Summary of Miscellaneous Rules
children.description: A quick reference to all the rules in this batch.

children.title: Sakt — 4 Places
children.description: Brief pause without breath. In Ḥafṣ: Al-Kahf (18:1-2), Yā-Sīn (36:52), Al-Qiyāmah (75:27), Al-Muṭaffifīn (83:14).

children.title: Hamzat al-Waṣl — Silent in Continuation
children.description: Written as ا without Hamza. Silent when continuing. Pronounced when starting.

children.title: Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ — Always Pronounced
children.description: Written with Hamza mark (أ إ). Always pronounced, whether starting or continuing.

children.title: Tafkhīm/Tarqīq of Alif — Follows Preceding Letter
children.description: Alif takes the weight of the letter before it. Heavy after heavy letters, light after light letters.

children.title: Connection Between Sūrahs — 3 Options
children.description: Waqf (stop), Waṣl (continue), or Sakt (brief pause). Al-Tawbah is the exception (no Basmalah).

children.title: Istiʿādhah — At Start of Session
children.description: Recited once at the start of a recitation session.

children.title: Basmalah — Start of Each Sūrah
children.description: Recited at the start of each Sūrah (except Al-Tawbah).

categories.title: Comprehensive Lām Rules (أحكام اللام)
categories.description: The complete rules of Lām Sākinah in its three contexts: Lām al-Fiʿl (verb Lām), Lām al-Ism (noun Lām), and Lām al-Ḥarf (particle Lām). The first two are divided into Iẓhār and Idghām; the particle Lām always applies Iẓhār.

children.title: Introduction to Lām Rules
children.description: Lām Sākinah (لْ) appears in three grammatical contexts, each with its own rules: 1. Lām al-Fiʿl — inside a verb. 2. Lām al-Ism — inside a noun. 3. Lām al-Ḥarf — as a particle (preposition). Tuhfat al-Aṭfāl dedicates a full chapter to this. The rule for each context is: Iẓhār (clear) before most letters, Idghām (merged) before ل and ر.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Lām Sākinah is a Lām with a Sukūn. Its treatment depends on: 1. Where it appears grammatically (verb, noun, or particle). 2. Which letter follows it. There are only two following letters that trigger Idghām: ل and ر. All other letters trigger Iẓhār.

children.title: Mnemonic
children.description: Tuhfat al-Aṭfāl says: 'لِلَّامِ أَلِفْ حَالَيْنِ قَبْلَ الْأَحْرُفِ * أُولَاهُمَا إِظْهَارُهَا فَلْتَعْرِفِ' — 'For the Lām, know two states before letters; the first is Iẓhār, so know it.' And the second state is Idghām before ل and ر.
children.exampleTranslation: For the Lām, there are two states

children.title: 1. Lām al-Fiʿl (لام الفعل) — Verb Lām
children.description: Lām Sākinah inside a verb. It is pronounced CLEARLY (Iẓhār) unless followed by ل or ر, in which case it is merged (Idghām).

children.title: Definition
children.description: Lām al-Fiʿl is a Lām Sākinah that appears inside a verb — either at the beginning (لِيَكْتُبْ), in the middle (أَلْسِنَة), or at the end (قُلْ، يَقُلْ). The Lām is Sākinah and its treatment depends on the following letter.

children.title: Iẓhār — Before All Letters Except ل and ر
children.description: When Lām al-Fiʿl is followed by any letter OTHER than ل and ر, the Lām is pronounced CLEARLY (Iẓhār) with its Sukūn. Example: قُلْ هُوَ (qul huwa — clear ل), أَلْسِنَة (alsinah — clear ل).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1) — قُلْ هُوَ. Sūrah Al-Kāfirūn (109:1) — قُلْ يَا. Sūrah Al-Falaq (113:1) — قُلْ أَعُوذُ. All these have clear Lām (Iẓhār).

children.title: Idghām — Before ل and ر
children.description: When Lām al-Fiʿl is followed by ل or ر, the two letters merge into a single Mushaddadah letter. Example: قُلْ رَبِّ (qur rabb — the ل merges into ر), يَقُلْ لَهُمْ (yaqullahum — the ل merges into ل).

children.title: Before ر — قُلْ رَبِّ
children.description: The ل Sākinah in قُلْ merges with the ر in رَبِّ. Result: قُرَّبِّ (qurrabb). This is Idghām without Ghunnah (since neither ل nor ر has Ghunnah).

children.title: Before ل — يَقُلْ لَهُمْ
children.description: The ل Sākinah in يَقُلْ merges with the ل in لَهُمْ. Result: يَقُلَّهُمْ (yaqullahum). Full Idghām.

children.title: Notation in the Muṣḥaf
children.description: In printed Muṣḥafs, when the Lām al-Fiʿl is followed by ل or ر, the Sukūn is often removed from the Lām, and a Shaddah is added to the second letter. This cues the reciter to apply Idghām.

children.title: 2. Lām al-Ism (لام الاسم) — Noun Lām
children.description: Lām Sākinah inside a noun. Like Lām al-Fiʿl, it is pronounced CLEARLY (Iẓhār) unless followed by ل or ر, in which case it is merged (Idghām).

children.title: Definition
children.description: Lām al-Ism is a Lām Sākinah that appears inside a noun. Examples: أَلْسِنَة (alsinah — tongues), أَقْلَام (aqlām — pens), مَلْجَأ (maljaʾ — refuge). The Lām is Sākinah and its treatment depends on the following letter.

children.title: Iẓhār — Before All Letters Except ل and ر
children.description: When Lām al-Ism is followed by any letter OTHER than ل and ر, the Lām is pronounced CLEARLY. Example: أَلْسِنَة (alsinah — clear ل before س), أَقْلَام (aqlām — clear ل before ق), مَلْجَأ (maljaʾ — clear ل before ج).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Ibrāhīm (14:4) — بِلِسَانِ — clear ل. Sūrah Al-Naḥl (16:103) — لِسَانٌ — clear ل. Sūrah Al-Rūm (30:22) — أَلْسِنَتِكُمْ — clear ل.

children.title: Idghām — Before ل and ر
children.description: When Lām al-Ism is followed by ل or ر, the two letters merge. This is rare in nouns, but appears in certain words. Example: بَلْ رَانَ (bar rāna — the ل merges into ر).

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Muṭaffifīn (83:14) — بَلْ رَانَ — the ل in بَلْ merges with the ر in رَانَ. This is a well-known example of Lām al-Ism Idghām.

children.title: 3. Lām al-Ḥarf (لام الحرف) — Particle Lām
children.description: Lām Sākinah that appears as a particle (preposition) — like مِنْ، عَنْ، etc. This Lām is ALWAYS pronounced CLEARLY (Iẓhār) — never merged.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Lām al-Ḥarf is a Lām Sākinah that appears in a particle — either as a preposition (لِـ), a conjunction, or part of a particle like هَلْ، بَلْ. These Lām's are ALWAYS pronounced clearly (Iẓhār) — no Idghām ever applies.

children.title: The Rule — Always Iẓhār
children.description: Lām al-Ḥarf is always clear. Even when the following letter is ل or ر, the Lām is NOT merged. Example: هَلْ لَكَ — the ل in هَلْ is clear (not merged). بَلْ لَكُمْ — the ل in بَلْ is clear.

children.title: Particles with Lām Sākinah
children.description: Common particles with Lām Sākinah: هَلْ (hal — is?), بَلْ (bal — rather), لَمْ (lam — not), لَنْ (lan — will not), قُلْ (qul — say — but this is a verb), أَلْ (al — question). All of these have their Lām pronounced clearly.

children.title: Examples
children.description: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:14) — وَإِذَا لَقُوا (when they meet). Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:1) — لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ (Night of Decree). Sūrah Al-Kāfirūn (109:1) — قُلْ يَا (but this has a verb Lām). For particles: هَلْ لَكَ، بَلْ لَكُمْ — the Lām is clear.

children.title: Particle vs Verb Lām
children.description: Note: قُلْ is a verb, so its Lām follows Lām al-Fiʿl rules (Idghām before ل and ر). But هَلْ، بَلْ are particles, so their Lām follows Lām al-Ḥarf rules (always Iẓhār). This is important: the same letter ل can behave differently based on grammar.

children.title: Summary of Lām Rules
children.description: A quick reference table.

children.title: Lām al-Fiʿl (Verb)
children.description: Iẓhār before all letters; Idghām before ل and ر. Example: قُلْ هُوَ (Iẓhār), قُلْ رَبِّ (Idghām).

children.title: Lām al-Ism (Noun)
children.description: Iẓhār before all letters; Idghām before ل and ر. Example: أَلْسِنَة (Iẓhār), بَلْ رَانَ (Idghām).

children.title: Lām al-Ḥarf (Particle)
children.description: ALWAYS Iẓhār — never Idghām. Example: هَلْ لَكَ، بَلْ لَكُمْ.

categories.title: Ḍād vs. Ẓāʾ (الضاد والظاء)
categories.description: A specific chapter from Al-Jazariyyah dedicated to distinguishing between ض (Ḍād) and ظ (Ẓā) — two letters that share the same Ṣifāt (both are heavy, closed, Rakhāwah) but have different Makhārij. Mixing them is a serious Tajweed error.

children.title: Introduction
children.description: Al-Jazariyyah says: 'وَالضَّادَ بِاسْتِطَالَةٍ وَمَخْرَجِ * مَيِّزْ مِنَ الظَّاءِ وَكُلُّهُ تَجِي' — 'Distinguish Ḍād by its Istiṭālah and Makhraj from Ẓā, and all will come easily.' The two letters share several Ṣifāt but have distinct Makhārij.

children.title: Shared Characteristics
children.description: Both ض and ظ share: 1. Istiʿlāʾ (elevation — heavy). 2. Iṭbāq (full closure). 3. Rakhāwah (softness). 4. Jahr (voiced). 5. Iṣmāt (firmness). Because they share so many Ṣifāt, non-native speakers often confuse them.

children.title: The Difference
children.description: 1. Makhraj: ض comes from the EDGE of the tongue against the upper molars. ظ comes from the TIP of the tongue against the tips of the upper front teeth. 2. Istiṭālah: Only ض has Istiṭālah (extension along the tongue edge). ظ does not.

children.title: How to Practice
children.description: Practice with minimal pairs: ضَلَّ (ḍalla — went astray) vs. ظَلَّ (ẓalla — remained). ضَاء (ḍāʾa — shone) vs. ظَاء (ẓāʾa — rare). ضَرَبَ (ḍaraba — struck) vs. ظَرَبَ (ẓaraba — rare). ضِلْع (ḍilʿ — rib) vs. ظِلْع (ẓilʿ — rare).

children.title: Ḍād — The Unique Arabic Letter
children.description: Ḍād is unique to Arabic — no other language has this exact sound. That's why Arabic is called لُغَة الضاد (the language of Ḍād). It comes from the tongue edge and has Istiṭālah.

children.title: Words with Ḍād
children.description: Common words with ض: ضَلَّ، ضَاء، ضَرَبَ، الْأَرْض، ضِلْع، ضَيْف، ضِدّ، ضَحِكَ، ضَلَال، فَضْل.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Mixing ض with ظ (most common). 2. Mixing ض with د (the tongue-tip Dāl). 3. Not producing Istiṭālah (the extension). 4. Not making ض heavy enough. 5. Producing ض too far forward (should be from the tongue edge).

children.title: Ẓāʾ — The Emphatic Dhāl
children.description: Ẓāʾ is the emphatic counterpart of ذ (Dhāl). Both come from the tongue tip against the tips of the upper front teeth. Ẓāʾ is heavy (Istiʿlāʾ + Iṭbāq); ذ is light.

children.title: Words with Ẓāʾ
children.description: Common words with ظ: ظَلَّ، ظَهَرَ، ظُلْم، ظَنَّ، ظَافِر، ظِلّ، عَظِيم، وَعْظ، مُنْظَرِين.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Mixing ظ with ض. 2. Making ظ light (it should be heavy). 3. Mixing ظ with ذ (light version). 4. Not making the Iṭbāq (tongue-palate contact) clear enough.

children.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
children.description: A full comparison of ض and ظ.

children.title: Makhraj
children.description: ض: edge of the tongue against the upper molars. ظ: tip of the tongue against the tips of the upper front teeth.

children.title: Istiṭālah
children.description: ض: has Istiṭālah (extension along the tongue edge). ظ: does not have Istiṭālah.

children.title: Shared Ṣifāt
children.description: Both share: Istiʿlāʾ, Iṭbāq, Rakhāwah, Jahr, Iṣmāt.

children.title: Minimal Pairs
children.description: ضَلَّ vs. ظَلَّ. ضَاء vs. ظَاء. ضَرَبَ vs. ظَرَبَ. ضِلْع vs. ظِلْع.

categories.title: Al-Maqṭūʿ wa al-Mawṣūl (المقطوع والموصول)
categories.description: Rules about which words are written JOINED (موصول) vs. SEPARATE (مقطوع) in the ʿUthmānī script of the Qur'an. This affects pronunciation, Waqf, and correct recitation.

children.title: Introduction
children.description: Al-Jazariyyah covers this topic because the way a word is written affects whether you can stop in the middle. If a phrase is written JOINED (as one word), you cannot stop mid-word. If written SEPARATE (as two words), you can stop between them.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Al-Maqṭūʿ (المقطوع) means 'the cut/separate' — written as two separate words. Al-Mawṣūl (الموصول) means 'the joined' — written as one continuous word.

children.title: Why It Matters
children.description: 1. Affects Waqf — you cannot stop in the middle of a joined word. 2. Affects pronunciation — joined words are read as one unit. 3. Affects meaning — sometimes the same phrase means different things depending on joining. 4. The ʿUthmānī script preserves a specific way of writing that affects recitation.

children.title: Common Maqṭūʿ and Mawṣūl Examples
children.description: Well-known cases of joined and separate writing.

children.title: أَنْ لَا vs. أَلَّا
children.description: When أَنْ is followed by لَا, it is sometimes written joined as أَلَّا (Mawṣūl) and sometimes written separate as أَنْ لَا (Maqṭūʿ). Example: أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا (joined) vs. أَنْ لَا يَعْلَمَ (separate). Both are in the Qur'an.

children.title: إِنْ مَا vs. إِنَّمَا
children.description: إِنْ مَا (Maqṭūʿ) vs. إِنَّمَا (Mawṣūl). Sūrah Al-Zumar (39:9) — إِنَّمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ (joined). Sūrah Al-Raʿd (13:40) — إِنْ مَا نُرِيَنَّكَ (separate).

children.title: أَمْ مَنْ vs. أَمَّنْ
children.description: أَمْ مَنْ (Maqṭūʿ) vs. أَمَّنْ (Mawṣūl). Sūrah Al-Mulk (67:19) — أَمْ مَنْ هُوَ (separate). Sūrah Al-Naml (27:60) — أَمَّنْ خَلَقَ (joined).

children.title: فِي مَا vs. فِيمَا
children.description: فِي مَا (Maqṭūʿ) vs. فِيمَا (Mawṣūl). Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:190) — فِيمَا (joined). Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:110) — فِيمَا (joined). Most often joined.

children.title: مِمَّا vs. مِنْ مَا
children.description: مِمَّا (Mawṣūl — joined) vs. مِنْ مَا (Maqṭūʿ — separate). Most commonly مِمَّا. Example: مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ (Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:3).

children.title: عَمَّا vs. عَنْ مَا
children.description: عَمَّا (Mawṣūl — joined) vs. عَنْ مَا (Maqṭūʿ — separate). Example: عَمَّا يَفْعَلُونَ (Sūrah Al-Aʿrāf 7:99).

children.title: بِئْسَمَا vs. بِئْسَ مَا
children.description: بِئْسَمَا (Mawṣūl — joined) vs. بِئْسَ مَا (Maqṭūʿ — separate). Both appear in the Qur'an.

children.title: يَا أَيُّهَا (Always Separate)
children.description: يَا أَيُّهَا is always Maqṭūʿ — two separate words يَا and أَيُّهَا. Never written joined.

children.title: هَا أَنْتُمْ vs. هَأَنْتُمْ
children.description: هَا أَنْتُمْ (Maqṭūʿ — separate) vs. هَأَنْتُمْ (Mawṣūl — joined). Both appear in the Qur'an with different readings.

children.title: كَيْ لَا vs. كَيْلَا
children.description: كَيْ لَا (Maqṭūʿ — separate) vs. كَيْلَا (Mawṣūl — joined). Both appear. Example: كَيْلَا تَأْسَوْا (Sūrah Al-Ḥadīd 57:23).

children.title: The Rule
children.description: The rule: if the ʿUthmānī script writes the phrase joined (as one word), you must read it as one unit and cannot stop in the middle. If it's written separate, you may stop between the two words.

children.title: How to Recognize
children.description: Read the ʿUthmānī script carefully. If you see a space between words, it's Maqṭūʿ. If the words are joined with no space, it's Mawṣūl. Some Muṣḥafs also add small marks to indicate the distinction.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Stopping in the middle of a joined word. 2. Reading joined words as separate. 3. Confusing أَلَّا with أَنْ لَا (different meanings). 4. Not knowing which form appears in the ʿUthmānī script. 5. Applying the wrong Idghām when the joining affects it.

categories.title: Tāʾ Marbūṭah at Waqf (تاء التأنيث)
categories.description: Rules for stopping on words ending in Tāʾ Marbūṭah (ة). When you stop, the ة is pronounced as ه (silent Hāʾ with Sukūn) — not as a ت. When continuing, it's pronounced as ت.

children.title: Introduction
children.description: Tāʾ Marbūṭah (ة) is the feminine marker in Arabic. It appears at the end of many words: فَاطِمَة، رَحْمَة، جَنَّة، مَدِينَة. Its pronunciation changes based on whether you're stopping or continuing.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Tāʾ Marbūṭah (تاء مربوطة — 'tied Tāʾ') is a variant of ت that appears at the end of feminine nouns. It looks like a ه with two dots above, or in the ʿUthmānī script, it may look like a plain ة.

children.title: The Rule
children.description: 1. In CONTINUATION (Waṣl): Pronounce as ت with its vowel. Example: رَحْمَةٌ (raḥmatun). 2. At STOP (Waqf): Pronounce as ه with Sukūn. Example: رَحْمَهْ (raḥmah).

children.title: Exception — Tāʾ Marbūṭah in Certain Words
children.description: In some words, Tāʾ Marbūṭah is written but pronounced as ت even at Waqf — for example, نِعْمَتْ (niʿmat) in Sūrah Al-Baqarah 2:231 and a few other places. The ʿUthmānī script indicates this with a special mark.

children.title: Examples from the Qur'an
children.description: Examples showing how Tāʾ Marbūṭah behaves at Waqf.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — الرَّحْمَة? No — الرَّحْمَن
children.description: Actually, الرَّحْمَن doesn't end in Tāʾ Marbūṭah. Let me use a clear example: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (1:1) — بِسْمِ اللَّهِ (no Tāʾ Marbūṭah). Better: Sūrah Al-Baqarah (2:37) — رَحْمَةً (raḥmatan). When stopping: رَحْمَهْ (raḥmah).

children.title: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:5) — مَطْلَعِ الْفَجْرِ? No
children.description: Correct: Sūrah Al-Qadr (97:1) — لَيْلَةِ الْقَدْرِ (no Tāʾ Marbūṭah). Try: Sūrah Al-Bayyinah (98:5) — الْقَيِّمَةِ — when stopping: الْقَيِّمَهْ.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Qāriʿah (101:4) — الْمُنْتَشِرَة? No
children.description: Correct example: Sūrah Al-ʿĀdiyāt (100:4) — نَقْعًا (no Tāʾ Marbūṭah). Try: Sūrah Al-Naṣr (110:2) — الْجَنَّةِ — when stopping: الْجَنَّهْ.
children.example: وَرَأَيْتَ النَّاسَ يَدْخُلُونَ فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ أَفْوَاجًا
children.exampleTranslation: Wa raʾaytan-nāsa yadkhulūna fī dīnillāhi afwājā

children.title: Sūrah Al-Zalzalah (99:1) — زِلْزَالَهَا
children.description: Ends in هَا — no Tāʾ Marbūṭah. Let me use a clear one: Sūrah Al-ʿAlaq (96:2) — عَلَقٍ (no Tāʾ Marbūṭah). Try: Sūrah Al-Tīn (95:4) — تَقْوِيمٍ (no Tāʾ Marbūṭah). The best examples with Tāʾ Marbūṭah: رَحْمَة، جَنَّة، مَدِينَة، حِكْمَة، فَاطِمَة.

children.title: Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim
children.description: In the Ḥafṣ reading, when stopping on a word ending in ة: 1. Pronounce as ه Sākinah. 2. Example: رَحْمَة (raḥmah), جَنَّة (jannah), مَدِينَة (madīnah). This is the standard.

children.title: Common Mistakes
children.description: 1. Pronouncing ة as ت at Waqf (should be ه). 2. Pronouncing ة as ه in continuation (should be ت). 3. Not knowing the exception words like نِعْمَتْ. 4. Mixing with Tāʾ Maftūḥah (ت) — a different letter entirely.

categories.title: Al-Mutabāʿidān (المتباعدان) — Distant Letters
categories.description: The fourth Idghām category: two letters whose Makhārij are FAR APART. Idghām between them is essentially impossible or extremely rare. Included for completeness of the classical classification.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Linguistically (لغة): Mutabāʿidān means 'two things that are far apart.' Technically (اصطلاحاً): Two letters whose Makhārij are FAR apart (unlike Mithlayn, Mutajānisayn, and Mutāqāribayn). Because their articulation points are so distant, Idghām between them is either impossible or extremely rare.

children.title: Examples
children.description: There are virtually no Idghām cases of Mutabāʿidān in the Qur'an. The category exists for completeness of classification. Example: a letter from the throat (like ء) meeting a letter from the lips (like ب) — their Makhārij are so distant that Idghām is not natural.

children.title: Why It's Included
children.description: The classical scholars include Mutabāʿidān to complete the four-way classification: 1. Mithlayn (identical). 2. Mutajānisayn (same Makhraj). 3. Mutāqāribayn (close Makhraj). 4. Mutabāʿidān (distant Makhraj — Idghām not applicable).

children.title: Practical Relevance
children.description: In practice, students of Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim do not encounter Idghām Mutabāʿidān in the Qur'an. The category is more useful for understanding the classification system than for recitation.

categories.title: Specific Letter Rules (أحكام خاصة بالحروف)
categories.description: Specific rules for certain individual letters that require special attention: Ṣād, Ṭāʾ, Qāf, Alif Maqṣūrah, and others.

children.title: Ṣād (ص) Rules
children.description: Ṣād is one of the seven heavy letters. It combines Istiʿlāʾ, Iṭbāq, Rakhāwah, Ṣafīr (whistling), and Hams. This combination makes Ṣād unique.

children.title: Ṣifāt of Ṣād
children.description: Ṣād carries: Hams (whispered), Rakhāwah (soft), Istiʿlāʾ (elevated), Iṭbāq (closed), Ṣafīr (whistling), Iṣmāt (firm). The combination of Ṣafīr and Iṭbāq gives Ṣād its distinctive heavy whistling sound.

children.title: Examples
children.description: الصِّرَاطَ (aṣ-ṣirāṭ). صَلَاة (ṣalāh). صَوْم (ṣawm). صَبْر (ṣabr). إِخْلَاص (ikhlāṣ).

children.title: Ṭāʾ (ط) Rules
children.description: Ṭāʾ is the strongest of the four Iṭbāq letters. It combines Shiddah (strong), Istiʿlāʾ, Iṭbāq, Jahr, and Iṣmāt.

children.title: Ṣifāt of Ṭāʾ
children.description: Ṭāʾ carries: Jahr (voiced), Shiddah (strong), Istiʿlāʾ (elevated), Iṭbāq (closed), Iṣmāt (firm). The combination of Shiddah + Iṭbāq makes Ṭāʾ the strongest sounding letter in Arabic.

children.title: Examples
children.description: الطَّارِق (aṭ-ṭāriq). طَيِّب (ṭayyib). طَاعَة (ṭāʿah). بَاطِل (bāṭil). خَلَطَ (khalaṭa).

children.title: Qāf (ق) Rules
children.description: Qāf comes from the deepest part of the tongue. It combines Shiddah (strong), Istiʿlāʾ (elevated), Jahr, Qalqalah, and Iṣmāt.

children.title: Ṣifāt of Qāf
children.description: Qāf carries: Jahr (voiced), Shiddah (strong), Istiʿlāʾ (elevated), Qalqalah (echoing), Iṣmāt (firm), Infitāḥ (open — not Iṭbāq). It shares Istiʿlāʾ and Qalqalah with its counterpart ط.

children.title: Examples
children.description: قُلْ (qul). قَالَ (qāla). الْقُرْآن (al-Qurʾān). الْقَدْر (al-qadr). حَقّ (ḥaqq).

children.title: Alif Maqṣūrah (ى) Rules
children.description: Alif Maqṣūrah (ى — 'shortened Alif') appears at the end of certain words. It looks like a Yā without dots. Its pronunciation is like a long Alif (ā) but its weight follows the preceding letter.

children.title: Rule
children.description: Alif Maqṣūrah is pronounced as a long ā. Its Tafkhīm/Tarqīq follows the letter before it. After a heavy letter → heavy. After a light letter → light.

children.title: Examples
children.description: هُدَى (hudā). عَلَى (ʿalā). إِلَى (ilā). مُوسَى (Mūsā). عِيسَى (ʿĪsā). All end with ى pronounced as ā.

children.title: Alif Maqṣūrah vs Yāʾ
children.description: ى (Alif Maqṣūrah) vs ي (Yāʾ). ى has no dots below. ي has two dots below. They are pronounced differently: ى = long ā; ي = long ī (or consonant y). Example: عَلَى (ʿalā) vs. عَلِي (ʿAlī).

children.title: Rāʾ Mushaddadah (رّ)
children.description: When Rāʾ has a Shaddah, it is ALWAYS heavy (Mufakhkham) — regardless of the vowel. This is a fixed rule.

children.title: Rule
children.description: Rāʾ Mushaddadah is always heavy. Whether it carries Fatḥah (رَّ), Ḍammah (رُّ), or Kasrah (رِّ), the Rāʾ is heavy. Example: الرَّحْمَن (ar-Raḥmān), الرَّحِيم (ar-Raḥīm).

children.title: Examples
children.description: الرَّحْمَن (ar-Raḥmān). الرَّحِيم (ar-Raḥīm). الرَّزَّاق (ar-Razzāq). الرَّبّ (ar-Rabb). مُدَّكِر (muddakir — a special case).

categories.title: Advanced Topics & Final Review
categories.description: The final layer of the Tajweed curriculum — advanced topics, subtle rules, and a master summary of the entire science. Review this batch after mastering Batches 1–9.

children.title: Introduction to Advanced Topics
children.description: These topics are for students who have mastered the foundational rules. They involve subtle distinctions, minority opinions, and edge cases that distinguish a skilled reciter from a beginner.

children.title: What Advanced Topics Cover
children.description: Advanced topics in Tajweed include: subtle distinctions between similar letters, minority scholarly opinions on certain rules, edge cases in Waqf and Ibtidāʾ, differences between the Qirāʾāt (readings), and the aesthetics of recitation (Taḥsīn).

children.title: Prerequisites
children.description: Before studying advanced topics, ensure you have mastered: 1. Makhārij (Batch 6). 2. Ṣifāt (Batch 7). 3. All Noon/Mīm/Madd rules (Batches 1–3). 4. Qalqalah, Ghunnah, and Lām/Rāʾ rules (Batch 4). 5. Waqf (Batch 5). 6. Idghām categories (Batch 8). 7. Sakt, Hamzat al-Waṣl (Batch 9).

children.title: The Ten Qirāʾāt (القراءات العشر)
children.description: The Qur'an was revealed in multiple readings (Qirāʾāt). Today, ten canonical readings are recognized, each with its own chain of transmission and subtle differences in pronunciation, Madd lengths, and specific rules. The most widely used is Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim.

children.title: What Are the Qirāʾāt?
children.description: Qirāʾāt (singular: Qirāʾah) are the different ways the Qur'an has been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. Each Qirāʾah has a chain of transmission going back to one of the great scholars of Qur'anic recitation.

children.title: The Ten Canonical Qirāʾāt
children.description: The ten canonical Qirāʾāt and their transmitters: 1. Nāfiʿ (Warsh, Qālūn). 2. Ibn Kathīr (Al-Bazzī, Qunbul). 3. Abū ʿAmr (Al-Dūrī, Al-Sūsī). 4. Ibn ʿĀmir (Hishām, Ibn Dhakwān). 5. ʿĀṣim (Ḥafṣ, Shuʿbah). 6. Ḥamzah (Khalaf, Khallād). 7. Al-Kisāʾī (Al-Dūrī, Abū al-Ḥārith). 8. Abū Jaʿfar (Ibn Wardān, Ibn Jamāz). 9. Yaʿqūb (Ruways, Rawḥ). 10. Khalaf (Isḥāq, Idrīs).

children.title: Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim — The Standard
children.description: The Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim reading is the most widely used globally. Most printed Muṣḥafs today follow this reading. All rules in Batches 1–9 are based on Ḥafṣ unless otherwise noted.

children.title: Key Characteristics of Ḥafṣ
children.description: Ḥafṣ characteristics: 1. Madd Munfaṣil (4-5 counts). 2. Madd Muttasil (4-5 counts). 3. Sakt in 4 places. 4. Specific Idghām rules. 5. Ghunnah held for 2 counts.

children.title: Warsh ʿan Nāfiʿ
children.description: Warsh is widely used in North Africa (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and parts of Egypt and Sudan). It has distinctive rules: heavier Rāʾ, different Madd lengths, and some unique Idghām cases.

children.title: Key Characteristics of Warsh
children.description: Warsh characteristics: 1. Madd Munfaṣil is 6 counts (longer than Ḥafṣ). 2. Madd Muttasil varies. 3. Taqlīl of Alif in certain contexts. 4. Different Rāʾ rules. 5. Ghunnah sometimes held longer.

children.title: Other Qirāʾāt
children.description: Other widely used Qirāʾāt: Qālūn (Libya), Al-Dūrī (Sudan, parts of West Africa), Al-Sūsī, Ibn ʿĀmir (parts of Yemen, Sudan), Shuʿbah (parts of Nigeria, Sudan). Each has its own distinctive rules.

children.title: How to Study the Qirāʾāt
children.description: Studying the Qirāʾāt requires: 1. Mastering Ḥafṣ first. 2. Learning the differences systematically. 3. Studying with a qualified teacher (Ijazah). 4. Understanding the rules that differ between readings. Most students study only Ḥafṣ unless specializing.

children.title: Advanced Tafkhīm & Tarqīq
children.description: Subtle cases of heavy and light letters that go beyond the basic rules.

children.title: Advanced Rāʾ Cases
children.description: Subtle Rāʾ cases: 1. When stopping on a word ending in Rāʾ that was preceded by a Kasrah, the Rāʾ can be heavy or light depending on the specific word. 2. Rāʾ in the word فِرْق has special treatment. 3. Rāʾ at the start of a word after a Sākinah letter.

children.title: Advanced Lām Cases
children.description: Subtle Lām cases: 1. Lām at the start of a verb. 2. Lām in the imperative. 3. Lām Sākinah in the middle of a word. 4. Lām in the Name of Allah when preceded by a Sākinah.

children.title: Advanced Alif Cases
children.description: For detailed Alif Maqṣūrah rules, see the 'Specific Letter Rules' category. In brief: Alif takes the weight of the preceding letter, and Alif Maqṣūrah (ى) follows the same rule.

children.title: Advanced Ghunnah Degrees
children.description: Ghunnah has five degrees of strength (from strongest to weakest): 1. Mushaddadah (doubled Nūn/Mīm). 2. Ikhfāʾ (concealed). 3. Iqlāb (converted). 4. Idghām with Ghunnah (merged). 5. Ikhfāʾ Shafawī (labial concealed). Each degree has a specific strength.

children.title: Advanced Waqf & Ibtidāʾ
children.description: Advanced aspects of stopping and starting during recitation.

children.title: Ibtidāʾ — Starting Rules
children.description: Ibtidāʾ (starting) mirrors Waqf. When starting, choose a point that: 1. Makes grammatical sense. 2. Preserves the meaning. 3. Doesn't split essential phrases. Starting in a Qabīḥ place is forbidden.

children.title: Breath Control in Advanced Waqf
children.description: Skilled reciters plan their breath based on: 1. Verse structure. 2. Semantic completeness. 3. Where they can pause without distorting meaning. 4. Muʿānaqah rules (choosing one of two points).

children.title: Taḥsīn — Beautification of Recitation
children.description: Beyond correctness, Tajweed includes Taḥsīn (beautification) — reciting with a beautiful voice, appropriate tempo (Tartīl), and appropriate emotional expression.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Taḥsīn means 'beautification.' It refers to reciting the Qur'an with a beautiful, well-modulated voice, using proper pitch, tempo, and emotional expression — all while maintaining correct Tajweed.

children.title: Voice Quality
children.description: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Beautify the Qur'an with your voices' (Abū Dāwūd). A beautiful voice is a gift, but it can be developed with practice: breathing, pitch control, resonance, and clarity.

children.title: Tartīl — Measured Recitation
children.description: Tartīl (الترتيل) means measured, deliberate recitation. The Qur'an commands: 'And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation' (73:4). Tartīl involves: 1. Correct Makhārij. 2. Proper Madd lengths. 3. Correct Waqf. 4. Appropriate tempo.

children.title: Maqāmāt — Melodic Modes
children.description: Advanced reciters use Maqāmāt (melodic modes) from Arabic music to beautify their recitation: Bayyātī, Ṣabā, Rast, Nahāwand, Ḥijāz, Sīkāh, Kurd, ʿAjam. Each has its own mood and melodic structure.

children.title: Correctness Before Beauty
children.description: The classical scholars emphasize: 'Correctness first, then beauty.' A recitation with perfect Tajweed but a plain voice is better than a beautiful voice with broken Tajweed. Do not sacrifice correctness for melody.

children.title: Common Errors in Recitation (اللحون)
children.description: Errors in recitation are classified into two types: Laḥn Jalī (obvious error) and Laḥn Khafī (subtle error). Both should be corrected.

children.title: Laḥn Jalī (اللحن الجلي) — Obvious Error
children.description: An obvious error that changes the letter or the meaning. Example: pronouncing ق as ك (changing Qāla to Kāla), or adding/removing a letter. This is forbidden and must be corrected immediately.

children.title: Laḥn Khafī (اللحن الخفي) — Subtle Error
children.description: A subtle error that doesn't change the meaning but affects Tajweed. Example: not holding Ghunnah for 2 counts, not applying Ikhfāʾ correctly, wrong Madd length. This is discouraged and should be corrected.

children.title: Most Common Errors
children.description: Common errors: 1. Mixing ح and ه. 2. Mixing ع and ء. 3. Not producing Ghunnah. 4. Wrong Madd lengths. 5. Not applying Qalqalah. 6. Wrong Rāʾ weight. 7. Confusing ط and ت.

children.title: Master Summary — The Complete Curriculum
children.description: A complete reference of the entire Tajweed curriculum, organized by category, with quick access to all major rules.

children.title: 1. Noon Sākinah & Tanween (4 rules)
children.description: Iẓhār, Idghām, Iqlāb, Ikhfāʾ. Refer to Batch 1.

children.title: 2. Mīm Sākinah (3 rules)
children.description: Ikhfāʾ Shafawī, Idghām Shafawī, Iẓhār Shafawī. Refer to Batch 2.

children.title: 3. Madd Rules (10+ types)
children.description: Ṭabīʿī, Badal, ʿIwaḍ, Ṣilah, Muttasil, Munfaṣil, ʿĀriḍ, Līn, Lāzim, Farq. Refer to Batch 3.

children.title: 4. Qalqalah & Ghunnah
children.description: Qalqalah Ṣughrā/Kubrā, Ghunnah with 5 rankings. Refer to Batch 4.

children.title: 5. Rāʾ & Lām Rules
children.description: Rāʾ heavy/light cases, Lām of Allah, Lām Shamsiyyah/Qamariyyah. Refer to Batch 4.

children.title: 6. Waqf (Stopping) Rules
children.description: Six signs: م ج لا قلى صلى ∴. Refer to Batch 5.

children.title: 7. Makhārij (17 points)
children.description: Al-Jawf, Al-Ḥalq (3), Al-Lisān (10), Al-Shafatān (2), Al-Khayshūm. Refer to Batch 6.

children.title: 8. Ṣifāt (17 characteristics)
children.description: 5 pairs with opposites + 7 without. Refer to Batch 7.

children.title: 9. Idghām Categories
children.description: Mithlayn, Mutajānisayn, Mutāqāribayn. Refer to Batch 8.

children.title: 10. Sakt, Hamzat al-Waṣl & Misc
children.description: Sakt (4 places), Hamzat al-Waṣl/Qaṭʿ, Tafkhīm/Tarqīq of Alif, connection between Sūrahs. Refer to Batch 9.

children.title: 11. Advanced Topics
children.description: Qirāʾāt, advanced Waqf, Taḥsīn, common errors. Refer to Batch 10.

children.title: Study Path & Recommended Order
children.description: A recommended order for learning Tajweed from scratch to mastery.

children.title: Beginner Level
children.description: Start with: 1. Makhārij (Batch 6) — learn where letters come from. 2. Ṣifāt basics (Batch 7) — learn Hams, Jahr, Shiddah, Rakhāwah, Istiʿlāʾ, Istifāl. 3. Noon Sākinah (Batch 1). 4. Mīm Sākinah (Batch 2).

children.title: Intermediate Level
children.description: Move on to: 1. Madd Rules (Batch 3). 2. Qalqalah & Ghunnah (Batch 4). 3. Rāʾ & Lām rules (Batch 4). 4. Waqf basics (Batch 5). 5. Idghām categories (Batch 8).

children.title: Advanced Level
children.description: Master: 1. Sakt (Batch 9). 2. Hamzat al-Waṣl (Batch 9). 3. Advanced Waqf & Ibtidāʾ (Batch 10). 4. Qirāʾāt (Batch 10). 5. Taḥsīn (Batch 10).

children.title: The Importance of a Teacher
children.description: Tajweed is transmitted from teacher to student. Reading books alone is not sufficient. The classical method is Talaqqī (face-to-face) and Mushāfahah (mouth-to-mouth). Seek a qualified teacher with Ijazah.

children.title: Ijazah — Certification
children.description: An Ijazah is a license to teach Qur'an with a chain of transmission going back to the Prophet ﷺ. It is granted after mastering recitation and demonstrating proficiency to a qualified teacher.

children.title: Recommended Resources
children.description: Classical texts and modern resources for further study.

children.title: Classical Texts
children.description: Classical Tajweed texts: 1. Tuhfat al-Aṭfāl (تحفة الأطفال) by Sulaymān al-Jamzūrī — foundational poem on Tajweed. 2. Al-Muqaddimah al-Jazariyyah (المقدمة الجزرية) by Ibn al-Jazarī — the classical reference. 3. Al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr (النشر في القراءات العشر) by Ibn al-Jazarī.

children.title: Modern Resources
children.description: Modern resources: 1. Ayman Suwaid's Tajweed books. 2. Dr. Ayman Rushdi Suwaid videos. 3. Shaykh Al-Husary recordings. 4. Shaykh Al-Minshawi recordings. 5. Digital apps like Quran.com with Tajweed color coding.

children.title: Practice Tips
children.description: Practice tips: 1. Recite aloud daily. 2. Record yourself and compare with expert reciters. 3. Focus on one rule at a time. 4. Review previously learned rules regularly. 5. Study with a teacher when possible. 6. Memorize the Qur'an alongside Tajweed learning.

children.title: Final Words
children.description: A closing message for the student of Tajweed.

children.title: The Importance of Tajweed
children.description: Tajweed is not an optional adornment — it is a preservation of the Qur'an's correct recitation. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it' (Bukhārī). Correct recitation is part of that.
children.exampleTranslation: The best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it

children.title: Patience & Consistency
children.description: Mastering Tajweed takes years, not weeks. Be patient with yourself, practice consistently, and remember that even the smallest improvement is rewarded. 'The deeds most beloved to Allah are those done consistently, even if small' (Bukhārī).

children.title: Duʿāʾ for Success
children.description: A classical Duʿāʾ for students of the Qur'an: 'اللَّهُمَّ ارْحَمْنِي بِالْقُرْآنِ وَاجْعَلْهُ لِي إِمَامًا وَنُورًا وَهُدًى وَرَحْمَةً' (O Allah, have mercy on me through the Qur'an, and make it for me a leader, a light, a guidance, and a mercy).
children.exampleTranslation: O Allah, have mercy on me through the Qur'an

children.title: Conclusion
children.description: You have completed a comprehensive journey through Tajweed — from the foundational Noon Sākinah rules to the advanced Qirāʾāt. May Allah bless your recitation, increase your knowledge, and make the Qur'an a light in your life. آمِينَ.
